They signify certain hypocrites who, on account of the disfigurement of their faces and expressions, seem and are, as it were, mere shadows in the Church, or in religion, or in the family; against which, Matthew 6: 'when you fast, be not, as the hypocrites, sad; for they disfigure their faces,' and so on.

Augustine, On Christian Discipline: 'let not your heart be at variance with your face; do not have your face turned upward while your heart is turned downward. How do you deserve that God should turn his face away from your sins, if you yourself do not turn your face away from your own sins?'
That great fish called Leviathan, Job 3 and 40, and Isaiah 27. If, as certain glossators say, it is the whale, there is no need to say more, since it has already been treated fully above.

But if it is the greatest sea-serpent, a bolt and crooked, as though undeceivable and incomprehensible, as seems to be implied in Job 40 and Isaiah 27, where it is said: 'in that day the Lord shall visit with his hard, and great, and strong sword upon Leviathan the bolted serpent, the crooked serpent,' and so on.
So, according to the Gloss there, because it is interpreted as 'their addition.'

It signifies the devil, who is indeed so called 'because, after he has brought in evil guilt by evil suggestion, he does not cease daily to increase it by evil persuasions. For in his crookedness a flowing softness is marked, but in the bolt a hard rigidity. So, that it may signify him both hard and soft, it names him both bolt and serpent. For he is hard through malice and soft through flattery. He is called a bolt because he strikes even unto death. He is called a serpent because he pours in his snares softly.' Thus far the Gloss.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the fifty-sixth place, that fish called the sturgeon is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, being of precious flesh and flavor, it has strong and sharp scales, an elongated head and tail, but a thick and fleshy middle. Whatever it has in it is pleasingly fit for human food, except for the scales.

It signifies grave and learned men in the Church who, being of precious life and edification, are fortified with virtues and sharpened by the goads of divine zeal; they have a mind expanded toward God and a long-suffering perseverance; but an affection enlarged with charity and full of piety, and all that they live, feel, and know is of profit to the churches of Christ and to individual souls.
Such were Peter and Paul, as is clear from their letters and from the Acts of the Apostles.

Such were Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory, who, excelling in the preciousness of their life and in the example of their edification, were virtuous men and zealots in the Church. They also had minds that acted upward, and stood out in long-suffering perseverance, and had affections enlarged with charity and full of piety, as is clear from their writings, and equally from the historical accounts of their deeds.

div.head: Cap. 57: De bellua siue de faste

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the fifty-seventh place, that fish called 'faste' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For water drawn into its mouth becomes sweet, and smaller fish, following it, enter its mouth, which it then suddenly seizes and swallows.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: According to the same author, there is a similar sea-monster which breathes water from its jaws with a fragrant vapor, whose smell fish, sensing it, follow, and enter its jaws for the sake of the fragrance; and this monster, swallowing them, is thus fed by them.

They signify the true preachers of the Gospel, in whose mouth the wisdom that is from heaven grows sweet, and from whose jaws breathes the fragrance of eternal life; and devout persons, sensing or perceiving this, enter, through the effect of teaching, into observance, and are thereby incorporated and carried into the womb of Mother Church, 2 Corinthians 2: 'but thanks be to God, who always triumphs us in Christ Jesus, and manifests the odor of his knowledge by us in every place; for we are the good odor of Christ unto God,' and so on. 'And for these things, who is so sufficient?'

It is sung of the eleven thousand virgins: 'in your fragrance, O Christ, thus these run to their punishments, as though they rejoiced in torments as in delights. They have tasted and seen how sweet you are, Lord, and have gladly spent themselves for your name. These are the flowers of beauty, which the springtime of breathing grace and the summer of charity have brought forth today.'

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the 'petrosa' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For it is so named from the multitude of its stone-like joints. It is a broad fish, tailed like a mouse, of cheap price and equally poor flavor.

It signifies a man bound up with the varied hardnesses of beasts of burden, spread wide toward earthly things, whose end is a beast's end, base in character and tasteless in speech and action, Psalm 48: 'man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to senseless beasts, and made like to them.'
'How very base you have become, repeating your ways.'
'For I know that you are hard, your neck is an iron sinew, and your brow of brass.'
An example is found in Simon Magus, and in Julian the Apostate, and in Nicholas the newcomer from Antioch, of whom is found in the Tripartite and Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the lamprey is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, having a shape somewhat like an eel, though of a varied and more beautiful color on its underside, above the middle it has certain painted and graceful markings, distinct and orderly. It is precious and especially flavorful, and delicate, much accepted among kings and lords among fish, and, comparatively among the kinds of fish, wholesome for healthy men.

It signifies good men, long-suffering in hope, capable of charity, or love, for God and neighbor, and fit for virtues and the gifts of sevenfold grace, beautiful in character and distinguished by the variety of graces freely given, with grace and the edification, or consolation, of others; precious in wisdom, flavorful in eloquence, acceptable to God and angels and men, and wholesome in speech and action.
Such was blessed Stephen, as is found in Acts 6 and 7.
Such was Barnabas, as is found in Acts 9, 13, 14, and 15.
Such were blessed Nicholas, blessed Benedict, and blessed Bernard, as is clear from their deeds and from ecclesiastical histories.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the sixtieth place, that fish called the 'umbrina' is of this condition. For, according to Iorath, On Animals, it is a great fish, precious, long, thick, fleshy, flavorful, solid, fittingly fat.

It signifies, in the Church, great prelates or religious who, after the likeness of this fish, ought to be precious in wisdom, long in perseverance, thick, or full, of probity and virtue, full of piety, flavorful in devotion, and fat with heavenly anointing.
Such were, in the primitive Church, the apostles and disciples, as is found in the Acts and in the Ecclesiastical History.
Such, too, were the good shepherds who came after the apostles, as blessed Gregory tells of many, in the book of the Dialogues, and the Tripartite History names many.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: Those fish called herrings are of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For they are of brief measure, and flavorful, and wholesome, and plentiful, and at certain fixed times draw near to land in the greatest multitude. When their catching is at its height, they eat nothing, but live on water alone. They have a certain very long intestine, golden within, and are, moreover, most translucent and choice.

They signify men humble in habit, sweet in affection, wholesome in speech, abounding in virtues, condescending to the weak at fixed times, precisely when there is greatest need, with holy edification or instruction. They are fed, above all, on the grace of God and the venerable Scripture, and also have a long-suffering desire for golden glory. They are, no less, always open to heavenly influence, or to the rays of eternal wisdom.

Paul, and likewise blessed Ambrose, having all these qualities aforesaid, as Augustine says in the book of the Confessions, served the infirmities of men, 'and the hidden mouth that was in his heart chewed the sweet joys of the heavenly bread.'
Blessed Gregory did likewise, as is found in his Life.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the 'scorpinus' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For it is so named because it has rough spines. Its dwelling, moreover, is among the rocks, and therefore it is very wholesome and flavorful, in no way distasteful.

It signifies religious austere in life and full of zeal, whose way of life is in the wilderness, or in the woods. And therefore they are of wholesome edification to others, and contain and offer a heavenly savor.
Such was the venerable Baptist, as is found in Matthew 3, and Luke 3, and Mark 1.
Such was blessed Anthony the monk, as blessed Jerome sets forth in the book of the Lives of the Fathers.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the 'cochius' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, being of a reddish color and of white and firm flesh, not fatty, it is wholesome and fittingly flavorful. It has a large head in proportion to its body, and a slender, sharp tail.
It signifies a fiery man, bright with chastity, firm in constancy, not wanton in austerity, wholesome in speech, magnanimous in mind, jealous in perseverance.
Timothy, Titus, Dionysius, Clement, as is clear from their deeds and from ecclesiastical histories.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the codfish is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For it is great of body, white of flesh, hard to digest, fittingly firm, flavorful to the taste.
It signifies men magnanimous in mind, bright with chastity, mature or deliberate in judgment, steadfast in fairness, wholesome in speech and learning.
Barnabas, as is found in the Acts.
Gregory, as is found in his Life and gathered from his teaching.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the sixty-fifth place, that fish called the conger eel is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For it is called the sea-eel because of its likeness to lake-eels. It is flavorful and white of flesh, but very loose in texture, and therefore not very wholesome, especially for those prone to its ill effects.

It signifies those who apparently have the savor of truth and the brightness of chastity in the Church, or in religion, and yet do not truly have them; rather they dissolve, corrupting and fermenting whomever they find fit for it, or weak.
Such were Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom the apostle therefore delivered to Satan, as is found in 1 Timothy 1.

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: Such was Torquatus, of whom is found in the legend of blessed Tiburtius.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Those fish called 'sori' are of this condition, according to Iorath. For they are small by nature, and do not easily grow beyond the size of half a human cubit. Likewise they are of fitting flavor and wholesomeness.
They signify good laymen, humble among others, not exalting themselves, of good edification in themselves and of wholesome exhortation to others.
Such were Fortunatus and Achaicus, of whom is spoken in the last chapter of 1 Corinthians.
Such, too, was the mother of blessed Augustine, as is found in the book of the Confessions.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Those fish commonly called 'oculatae' (large-eyed) are of this condition, according to Iorath. For they are so called because of the notable size of their eyes in proportion to their body, which is not large. This fish is quite broad in proportion to its length, delicate too, and precious, and is judged comparatively wholesome and flavorful.
It signifies a discreet and circumspect man, notably ample in charity, precious in life, and accustomed to divine consolations, wholesome and sweetening in his teaching.
Such was blessed John the Evangelist, as is clear from his Gospel and from his letters, and the Apocalypse, and his legend.
...blessed Ambrose, as he testifies in the book of the Confessions, and as is clear from his legend.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: In the sixty-eighth place, those fish commonly called 'ragiae' (skates or rays) are of this condition, according to Iorath, for they have more breadth, a tail and a beast-like shape, cheap flavor, and a very common value. And so they are food for ruffians and other base persons like them.

They signify lovers of this world, spreading themselves out only in temporal things, having a beast's life and end, lacking edification and virtue, or usefulness; wherefore they are devoured by demons.
Among such were Antiochus the Illustrious, the worst of men, of whom 1 Maccabees 9 speaks; and Herod Agrippa, of whom Acts 12 speaks.
Likewise Simon Magus and Julian the Apostate, of whom is found in the Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: Those fish commonly called 'palamitae,' or 'variati,' or mackerel, are of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For they are beautifully varied in color, elongated in tail, pleasant in flavor, precious in value, quite free of harmful fatness, yet hard to digest, and for that reason held in lesser esteem.

They signify good men, adorned and graced by the variety of holy character and virtues, long-suffering in perseverance, edifying, instructing, or excelling in teaching and counsel, keeping themselves far from temporal things, doing everything with deliberation, and therefore not pleasing to wicked or light men. Among such were Moses and Samuel and the like, as is contained in the canon of the Bible.
Among such were Jerome and Gregory, as is clear from their writings.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the 'columbus' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, having a wholly beast-like shape, it has white flesh but of little flavor, of little value, and of much harm to those who eat it. It is therefore not in use among grave and learned persons.

It signifies certain young men, beautiful in face, beast-like in conduct, ill-pleasing to others in their actions, having little of goodness and very much of wretchedness and iniquity; and so they corrupt those familiar with them, and their doings do not please the wise and discreet.
Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah, sons of David, as is found in 2 and 3 Kings; such too were the sons of Eli the priest, as is found in 1 Kings 2.

Such were those two sons of an emperor, of whom Jerome speaks, in the Lives of the Fathers, who stretched nets in the wilderness for forty miles around, for hunting, and seized a holy old man and tried to compel him to deny the faith.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the salmon is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, being great and noble, it is handsome in appearance, reddish in flesh, delicate and flavorful to the taste, comparatively wholesome, precious in value, moderate in digestibility, famous in reputation, most ingenious in escaping the net. For, with wondrous cunning, laying its tail over its own head and leaping upward, it escapes the ambushes of fishermen with great speed and agility.

It signifies men noble in mind and magnanimous in Christ, gracious in conduct, charitable and fiery in affection, delicate and sweet in unction, or inward consolation, wholesome, in comparison with others, in learning, precious in probity, discreet in deliberation, illustrious in reputation, and most keen-sighted in cunning against demons and tyrants.
Such were the Maccabees, namely Eleazar, the eminent elder, and the seven brothers with their mother, as is found in 2 Maccabees 6 and 7.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Such were those fifteen hundred servants of God under father Pachomius, as Ambrose says, On Paradise.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the red mullet, 'trigla,' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, of short shape, it is reddish and as though suffused with gold, precious in value, delicate in flavor, and has a certain spine on its head.
It signifies those in the Church or in religion who are humble, charitable, discreet, useful, gracious, and jealous in mind.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis De viris illustribus Hieronymi

cit.quote: Such were Timothy and Titus, as is clear in their letters; such were all the illustrious men of whom blessed Jerome makes a book.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Those fish commonly called 'needle-fish,' from their shape, are of this condition, according to Iorath. For they have spines on the head, are elongated, suffused within with a certain fatness, drawn out with a certain greenness, of fitting length, proven in flavor and of rather common wholesomeness.
They signify zealous men, mortified in mind and face against the flesh, suffused with heavenly pleasantness, long-suffering in hope, gracious in conduct, and wholesome in common learning.
Such were Sosthenes the brother and Silas, of whom 1 Corinthians 1 and Acts 15 speak.

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita Epistole Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Such were Dorotheus and Demophilus and Polycarp, to whom blessed Dionysius writes various letters, as to fellow disciples and proven familiars.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the plaice is of this condition, according to Iorath. For it is broader of body, more tender of flesh, whiter in color, precious in value, pleasant in flavor, comparatively praiseworthy in wholesomeness, and is found more useful and pleasant to eat when steeped in wine.

It signifies clerics, or religious, or especially prelates, who, after the likeness of this fish, ought to be found expansive in charity, kind in gentleness, bright with chastity, strong in probity, gracious in edification, wholesome in teaching, and steeped in the wine of the fervor of the grace of the Holy Spirit, that they may be found more praiseworthy and useful in the Church of God.
Such were the apostles and disciples in the primitive Church, as is found in the Acts of the Apostles and in the Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Such were the shepherds after the apostles, as blessed Gregory gives examples of many, in the fourth book of the Dialogues, and blessed Ambrose in the book On Paradise, and blessed Jerome in many places, and the Tripartite History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the sea-locust is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, wholly reddish in color, it is found white in flesh, armed with spines, wholly rough on the outside, hard to digest, with its head or tail much bent back; it has strong and quite piercing strikes.

It signifies a religious man wholly fiery with the love of God, wholly bright with chastity, wholly filled with the zeal of God, wholly rigid with austerity, wholly discreet in deliberation, wholly and perseveringly humble in mind and body, wholly intent upon and fighting against vices and disorders.
Phinehas and Mattathias, as is found in Numbers 25 and 1 Maccabees 2.
Blessed Jerome, as is clear in many ways from his writings and deeds.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the tuna, whence also 'tunny-meat,' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, great of body, filled in the belly with much fat, precious in value, it is found flavorful when eaten, especially if fresh. It has a large head, full of bones, a thick middle, and is covered with scales; salted and transported, it is found useful to many nations; it is somewhat hard to digest, but comparatively not unwholesome.

It signifies good Christian princes in this world who, after its likeness, are magnanimous in mind, in Christ, filled with Christian charity and piety, precious in probity, approved in conduct, fortified above the mind, fruitful and multiplied in affection, fortified and set forth in virtues, useful to all peoples, famous for edification and discretion.
Such were David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, as is found in the books of Kings and Chronicles and Ecclesiasticus.
Such were the emperors Constantine, Theodosius, and Maurice, as is found in the Tripartite History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: Those fish called 'albi,' or 'albelli' (whitefish), are of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For they are so named from their color; they are tasteless and of little value or power; nor are they very good by themselves, without some seasoning.
They signify certain young men or women, comely in face or form, but lacking in action or edification, showing no traces of virtue or goodness, who, left to themselves, are worth nothing at all.
Hamor, son of Shechem, who raped Dinah, the daughter of Jacob; and Dinah herself, who went out to see the women of the region, as is found in both cases in Genesis 34.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the tench is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For it is notably covered with scales, of common shape and color, of common price and flavor equally; its fat and flavor are best around the belly; it has a full, good head, a rather flavorful tongue, at certain times a wholesome fish, at certain times unwholesome.

It signifies common or middling persons in the Church, fittingly furnished with virtues, acceptably received in conduct and edification, sufficiently fed, in their affections, with heavenly sweetness or consolation, endowed with a good magnanimity in the higher part of reason, well-graced in speech, edifying at certain times, and at other times showing some defective traces from their frailty.

Such were nearly all the apostles before the coming of the Holy Spirit; such were nearly all the disciples of the fathers in Egypt, of whom Jerome writes, and also Cassian, in the book of the Conferences of the Fathers.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the seventy-ninth place, that fish commonly called the pike is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, fittingly great of body, and noble among the common fish of lakes, pleasant in color, it has white flesh free of harmful fat; it has an agreeable flavor, a good price, a due wholesomeness, a head or mouth very spiny, and it is thievish and voracious toward lesser fish.
...greedy persecutors of demons and evil men.
The figure of such men was borne by Joab and Abishai, sons of Zeruiah, and Amasa and Abner, soldiers of David, as is found in 2 Kings 2.
Such, too, were those who served as soldiers under the emperor Constantine, as is found in the Tripartite History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That river fish commonly called the bream is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, gracious in color, white in flesh, agreeable in fatness, plump, it is found pleasant in flavor; it is, moreover, of good price and due wholesomeness, and, no less, is well covered with scales.

It signifies nuns, gracious in conduct, bright with chastity, fed on the sweetness of heavenly fatness, especially devoted to edification, upright and discreet, wholesome in exhortation, and fortified with virtues.
Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, as is found in Luke 2.
Such, too, was the mother of blessed Augustine, as is found in the ninth book of the Confessions.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the 'scarpa' (parrotfish) is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, covered with scales good both in color and in flavor, it is commonly pleasant, and also especially fit for frying.

It signifies good widows in the Church, fortified with virtues, gracious in conduct and edification, affectionately devoted to compassion and condescension toward the weak and the afflicted. Among such was the mother of Timothy, and likewise his grandmother, as is suggested in 2 Timothy 1.
Among such, too, was the mother of blessed Gregory, and her friend Tarsilla, as is found in the book of the Dialogues.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the 'alloda' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, being of fitting color, flavor, and price, it is especially suited for roasting.
It signifies good married women who are of beautiful conduct, good edification, good discretion, great charity, and fervent piety toward the weak and the poor.
Such were those women who, still having husbands, followed the Lord, as is found in Luke 8.
Such, too, were the sisters of blessed Ambrose, as is said in his deeds.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the 'scandaua' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For it is very scaly, of quite common flavor, and better suited for frying.
It signifies women abounding in common virtues, edifying in common ways, and especially devoted to compassion for the afflicted.
Mary of Rome, Romans 16; likewise Stephana of Corinth, 1 Corinthians, last chapter.
Among such, too, were Romula and Galla and Tarsilla, of whom blessed Gregory writes in the fourth book of the Dialogues.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the 'lachia' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, white in color and as though partly suffused with gold, milk-white and gracious in appearance and flavorful in taste, it is also precious and quite delicate, and of due wholesomeness.

It signifies virgins in the Church, most chaste in their senses, endowed with evangelical discretion and wisdom, milk-white with holy exhortation, gracious in conduct and sweetening in edification, delicate and outstanding with heavenly anointing, and sound in reputation.

bibl.author: Paulus Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Corinthios prima

cit.quote: Such were the virgins the apostle Paul wished for, 1 Corinthians 7, throughout almost the whole chapter.
Such virgins blessed Ambrose admonishes them to be, in the book On Holy Virginity, throughout.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the 'lichia' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, being great and thick and long, it is of common color, but of better flavor, good price, and good wholesomeness, comparatively.

It signifies the good nobles in the Church who are magnanimous in mind, filled with virtue, long-suffering in hope, of good conduct and great edification, precious in probity, and wholesome in speech in comparison with lesser men.
Such were Fortunatus and Achaicus of Corinth, of whom is written in the last chapter of 1 Corinthians.
Such, too, were the sons of Constantine the Great and of Theodosius, as is found in the Tripartite History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the 'lasca' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, of due proportion and better constitution, it spawns and produces milt abundantly. It is very scaly, flavorful and pleasant, and accepted by all.

It signifies good young women in a monastery or a household who, content with their own limits, are of a lovable constitution; they multiply holy conceptions, abound in the milk of holy teaching, are armed with virtues, are of great edification, and are gracious and acceptable to all.
Such was Ruth, as is found in the book of Ruth.
Rebecca, while she was young; Rachel; Abishag the Shunammite; Sarah, daughter of Raguel, as is found in their respective places: Genesis 24 and 29, and 1 Kings 1, and Tobit 3 and 10.
Such was the mother of Augustine, while she was young, as is found in the ninth book of the Confessions.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: Those fish commonly called sardines are of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, of small shape, they are pleasant in flavor, and accepted by every multitude, and are also of due wholesomeness.
They signify poor and humble religious who, by their edification and exhortation, graciously refresh the souls of the people, and are pleasing in the sight of all men.
Such were the apostles in the primitive Church, as is found in the Acts and in the Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Such were those fifteen hundred servants of God under father Pachomius, as Ambrose says, On Paradise.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Those fish commonly called 'rubiliones' are of this condition, according to Iorath. For, of short shape, they are fittingly flavorful, reddish, covered with small fins and scales, and armed with spines.
They signify the lesser ministers of churches, humbly content with their stipends, of due edification, of twofold charity, fortified with virtues, and armed with the zeal of God.
Such the apostle Paul wished clerics and all servants of God to be, as is found in 2 Corinthians 6: 'in all things let us exhibit ourselves as the ministers of God,' and so on.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Regula pastoralis Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Blessed Gregory also exhorts clerics to be such, in his Pastoral Rule.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Those little fish which the common people call 'lacterini,' or 'calcini,' are of this condition, according to Iorath. For, being of the smallest size, they are pleasant in flavor and wholesome in constitution.
It signifies a man most humble in his own estimation, pleasing to God and men by his edification and wholesome learning.
Such were Peter and Paul, as is clear from their letters and deeds.

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum
Vita sancti Dominici fundatoris ordinis predicatorum

cit.quote: Such, in their own way, were blessed Benedict and blessed Francis and blessed Dominic, as is clear from their legends.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the 'usio' is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to Iorath and many other great authorities. For it is a fish notable in size, beautiful in color, distinguished in nobility, lovable in flavor, honorable in presentation, and durable in preservation.

bibl.author: Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Corinthios secunda

cit.quote: ...fish.

Second, they ought to be gracious in color, that is, in appearance and conduct, adorned with grace, according to that saying, Ecclesiasticus 50: 'as a solid vessel of gold, adorned with every precious stone.'

Third, they ought to be distinguished in nobility, that is, remarkably raised up by the nobility of heavenly teaching, according to that saying, 1 Corinthians 2: 'my speech and my preaching were not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the showing of the Spirit and of power.'

Fourth, they ought to be gracious in flavor, that is, made sweet with a supercelestial sweetness, according to that saying, Colossians 3: 'savor the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth.'

Fifth, they ought to be honorable in presentation, since, set before all persons of the world, or even before few, they ought always to be for the honor of God and of his mystery, according to the pattern of the apostle: 'as long as I am the apostle, I have honored, and will honor, my ministry.'

Sixth, they ought to be durable in preservation, that is, finally persevering and constant in all their goodness and truth and virtue, according to the example of the apostle, Romans 8: 'who shall separate us from the charity of Christ?' and so on. 'For I am sure that neither any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The ram is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to Isidore, book 12, chapter 1.
For first it is a wool-bearing animal. So a prelate ought to be warm, and warming others with divine love: 'our heart is enlarged; as to sons, I say, be you also enlarged.'

For with what zeal of the love of God ought a prelate to burn, after the example of Paul, whom we should imitate, who says, 2 Corinthians 12: 'most gladly will I spend, and be spent myself, for your souls.'
An animal placid in temperament.
So Job ought to be gracious in appearance: 'the light of my countenance did not fall to the ground,' as though it were openly said —
— that, though his face always shone with the cheerfulness that comes of the testimony of a good conscience, yet it never dissolved into any limited mirth, as is found in the Gloss there.
'In the face of the wise man wisdom shines.'
A gentle animal.
So a prelate ought to be mild and gentle, that is, without harshness or tyranny, Galatians, the last chapter: 'you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'Let the prelate hold back the blows, and bring forth the breasts.'
Fourth, as the same Isidore says, it is the leader and prince of the sheep.
So is the shepherd of his subjects, Ecclesiasticus 10: 'in the midst of brethren, their ruler is in honor.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Regula pastoralis Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: For the leadership of a prelate shines forth in outstanding examples and in the marks of holy conduct, as blessed Gregory teaches in the Pastoral Rule.
Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it is stronger than the other sheep, and so their protector.

So a prelate ought to be strong in defending the truth and in guarding the salvation of his subjects, John 10: 'the good shepherd gives his life for his sheep. But the hireling, and he that is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep, and flees.' For the virtue of a prelate is known by his constant defense of evangelical liberty and justice and truth.
It has a worm in its head, roused by whose itching it shakes its head most violently, and strikes hard whatever it meets.

It signifies the zeal of God that a prelate ought to have in his mind, by which, divinely stirred, he fights down all the vices and sins that are opposed to the Gospel, Ecclesiasticus 48: 'Elijah rose up as a fire, and his word burned like a torch.' It is likewise said there, of Elisha: 'in his days he feared not the prince, nor was any man able to overcome him by any word.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: 'Let shepherds be such as to show themselves as John to kings, as Moses to Egyptians, as Phinehas to fornicators, as Elijah to idolaters, as Elisha to the greedy, as Paul to blasphemers and to merchants who deal in Christ.'
Isidore: it is virile in fecundating the ewes.
It signifies, in a prelate, that saying: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'
Chrysostom, on Paul: 'as though Paul had begotten the whole world, so he hastened to bring all men into the kingdom of God, by teaching, by promising, by beseeching.'
Eighth, according to the law, Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14, it is an animal especially clean and fit for sacrifice.
It signifies, in a prelate, the cleanness of evangelical chastity dedicated to the Lord, according to that saying, Luke 12: 'let your loins be girt, and lamps burning in your hands.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily on the same passage: 'for we gird our loins when we restrain the wantonness of the flesh through continence.'
Ninth, it was commonly offered in the law for the sin of the people, Numbers 33 and following, and Leviticus 1, 2, and following.

It signifies that saying of Paul, Acts 20: 'but I fear none of these things, neither do I count my life more precious than myself, so that I may accomplish my course, and the ministry of the word which I received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the Gospel of the grace of God.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'the preacher of the Gospel ought always to be ready to die for the truth.'
Tenth, as is found in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14, since it chews the cud and divides the hoof, it was eaten indifferently by the whole people under the law.

It signifies wisdom and discretion in a prelate, by which all his subjects gladly accept his commands and his admonitions, with edification, Colossians 4: 'let your speech be always seasoned with the salt of grace, that it may give grace to those who hear it.'

For the discretion of a shepherd powerfully draws to itself the devotion of the multitude, according to what is suggested, John 10, in the parable of the shepherd, where the sheep follow him, and so on.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Eleventh, according to Pliny, book 8, whatever veins it bears beneath its tongue, such offspring it produces in its fleece.

It signifies, in a prelate, the inward affections to which outward effects correspond in life, Matthew 12: 'a good man out of a good treasure of his heart brings forth good things; and an evil man, the contrary.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke, and elsewhere: 'affection gives its own name to your work,' and as much as you intend, so much do you do and show.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As Pliny says, book 8, chapter 18: it is natural to it to disdain the lambs and to seek out the old sheep it meets, for it is itself better and more useful in old age.
It signifies, in a prelate, the avoiding of childish and useless, or even wanton, company, Proverbs 13: 'he that walks with the wise shall be wise; a friend of fools shall become like them.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: 'Keep such companions as you will not be shamed by their company; who are adorned with good character, not curled with their attire.'
Thirteenth, as Avicenna says, book 8, sheep naturally fear thunder.
It signifies, in a prelate, a deep reverence for the fear of God, Job 31: 'for I always feared God as waves swelling over me, and I could not bear the weight of it.'
For above all men, shepherds ought to fear God, after the example of Peter and Paul and the other pontiffs, of whom is found in the Ecclesiastical and Tripartite History.
...to sheep.

It signifies, in a prelate, assistance to his subjects, and comfort in times of adversity, and exhortation, now to one, now to another, even to others in fitting times, 2 Timothy 4: 'preach the word, be instant in season, out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and doctrine.'

For, after the example of blessed Martin and Nicholas, a prelate ought to know how to come to the aid of the sick in their time, to assist the needy, to bring help to the wretched, and other such things.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX
Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: The lamb has these properties, or conditions, according to our natural and holy authorities, and especially Isidore, book 12, and Pliny, book 8, chapter 47.

For first, among all the animals of the earth, it is the most innocent and gentle; for it harms no one with tooth or claw, horn or hoof. It signifies Christ made man, who was supremely innocent and most gentle, Exodus 12: 'the lamb shall be without blemish, a male, of one year.'
For no innocence is like the innocence of Christ, that most gentle man, as Pope Leo suggests in the sermon On Palm Sunday.

Second, whatever is found in it is useful; for its skin has various uses, its wool serves for human clothing, its dung for the fruitfulness of the earth, its hooves and horns for medicine. So whatever was in Christ, throughout his whole life, availed for the various benefits of our salvation, 2 Corinthians 5: 'God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.'
Augustine, in many places: 'every action of Christ was an instruction and a direction for the human race.'

...it recognizes its parent's voice among the flock, so that, if it should stray in a great herd, it at once recognizes its mother's voice by her bleating. It signifies Christ, knowing his own and hearing their prayers, 'the eyes of the Lord are upon the just, and his ears unto their prayers,' Psalm 33.
For the Lord knows who are his, as is found in 2 Timothy 2, and is ready with comforts and holy consolations for them, as is suggested in Matthew 6 and John 16.

Fourth, in suckling, it bends its forelegs, and, so that its mother may give it more milk, presses its mother's udder with its head. It signifies a good and pious man, humbly fitting himself to the teaching and character of a prelate: 'obey those who are set over you in the Lord, and be subject to them,' Hebrews, the last chapter.

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: For unless there is a subject, there will be no prelate for him, as Bernard touches on, On Loving God.

Fifth, it rejoices in the company of its own kind; but when solitary, it grieves very much. So the just man exults in the company of the just, but when he lacks it, he is greatly saddened, 1 Corinthians 16: 'I rejoice in the presence of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus,' and so on.
Augustine, to Proba: 'let good men be present; all sad things are lightened.'

Sixth, before the flock it leaps, and, leaping, it plays. It signifies Christ, leaping before his disciples the examples and lessons of the perfections, and rejoicing together at the lessons and works of universal perfection, Song of Songs 2: 'behold he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills.'
For Christ leapt over the mountains, since by perfection he transcended the patriarchs and the great prophets; he skipped over the hills, since he transcended his disciples and all the apostles.

bibl.author: Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Corinthios prima

cit.quote: ...it fears the wolf greatly, and at once takes flight. But afterward, stupefied by fear, it suddenly plants its steps and, no longer daring to flee farther, asks for mercy for itself, not with bleating but rather with a simple look. It signifies a holy man, humanly fearing tribulations and fleeing them as far as he can, but, when they come upon him, placing his affection in God, and, toward God, not with his voice but with his desire, pleading his own innocence, that he may meet his own frailty, according to the teaching of the apostle, 1 Corinthians 10: 'God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able; but will make also with temptation a way to escape, that you may be able to bear it.'

Jerome relates, in the Lives of the Fathers, that Abbot Anthony said, after a most violent temptation: 'where were you, good Jesus?' And he answered: 'I was with you, and I was watching you overcome.'

...it defends itself with horn or tooth, and whether it is stripped of its fleece or its skin, as an innocent animal it stays silent; whether it is led to pasture, or led to sacrifice, it does not murmur or resist, does not groan, but obeys. It signifies Christ in his passion, and a man obedient and patient in his conduct and his end, Jeremiah 11: 'I was like a meek lamb, that is carried to be a victim.'
'He was dumb as a lamb before his shearer, and he opened not his mouth.'
Revelation 14: 'these follow the Lamb wherever he goes.'

Ninth, a lamb conceived in a north wind is better than one conceived in a south wind. It signifies an innocent man, whose holy desire for evangelical chastity is perfected by a gift from heaven, and who is more useful to the Church than one dissolved by worldly prosperity or carnal favor, 2 Timothy 4: 'take Mark' — that is, a man most chaste from his mother's womb — 'and bring him with you' — to preach, supply — 'for he is profitable to me for the ministry.'
For such men are useful to the universal Church.

Tenth, a lamb has such a color in its wool, or fleece, as its parents have in the veins of their tongue; for if the veins were white, the lambs too will be white; if black, the lambs black; if mixed, the lambs mixed.

It signifies a just man, representing in his character and deeds the footsteps of the holy fathers, now in the celibacy of chastity, now in the habit of humility, now in the varied effect of virtue, 1 Corinthians 11: 'be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.'
For we are made conformed to the life of the ancients by the representation of their character and their deeds, as Chrysostom touches on, in On the Praises of Paul.

It has fine and curly hair, folded many times over upon itself. It signifies the discernment of the holy man in thinking, and the manifold quality of his understanding in thought, and, no less, his recognition of his own frailty, in turning back upon himself, Ecclesiasticus 14: 'blessed is the man that shall continue in wisdom, and that shall meditate in his justice, and in his sense shall think of the circumspection of God.'
'My head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights'; and the Gloss: 'the locks are the curly hairs.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'by the name of hairs, or locks, are designated thoughts running now to this, now to that.'

It is dangerous for a lamb to be left alone; for if thunder should come upon it, it easily dies. It signifies that it is safe to live in the congregation of the just, Psalm 110: 'I will praise you, Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the just, and in the congregation,' as though to say, according to Bernard in a certain hymn: 'O how blessed is that pleasantness! With how glorious a light! A shining joyousness, to have fellowship with the saints!'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX
Isaac Iudeus De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: The boar, the wild pig, is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to natural authorities, and especially according to Isidore, book 12, and Pliny, and Avicenna, and Isaac, in his Diets.

...a wild animal, most savage and unmerciful; for it is fierce in solitude, and, for the size of its body, cruel and monstrous. It signifies the cruelty of the devil, or even of the Antichrist: 'the boar out of the wood has laid it,' that is, the soul, 'waste' — that is, the devil, the lurking dragon — 'and a singular wild beast,' that is, the Antichrist, 'has devoured it.'

Second, once castrated, it scarcely becomes gentle, though other animals grow gentle once their testicles are removed. It signifies the pride of the devil, or even of the Antichrist, who, though cut off from those he has led to chastity, is never himself humbled to the love of chastity, so as to cease provoking to lust, 'your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'this is the devil's shamelessness, that he never wishes to blush, even when defeated and openly confounded.'

Third, it is of such ferocity that, despising even death, it thrusts itself fearlessly against the hunter's iron, and gathers its strength even against one resisting it, so as to avenge itself on its adversary. It signifies the presumption of the devil and his demons, or even of the Antichrist, who, despising the death of hellish fire, shamelessly thrust themselves upon temptations against a tempted man who stands firm in the Gospel, and always strive to conquer, though they are found conquered by those they attack, 2 Corinthians 2: 'let us not be deceived by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices.'
Jerome, on Matthew: 'for it would not be safe among so many...'

Fourth, it has two tusks joined in its mouth, strong and sharp, with which it cruelly cuts and mangles all who resist it, or everything that resists it, and which it also uses as a sword for fighting. It signifies the twofold temptation of the devil, or of the Antichrist, with which they wound and mangle most, namely the temptation of avarice and of lust, or of pride and vainglory, Ecclesiasticus 23: 'two kinds abound in sins.'
Ecclesiasticus 50: 'two nations my soul hates.'
'Two kinds seemed to me difficult and dangerous,' namely the two aforesaid temptations.

Fifth, on its right side it has a very hard and thick spot, which it always turns against the hunting-spear of its pursuer, for it uses that bone as a shield to protect itself. It signifies the irremediable obstinacy of the devil and the Antichrist in turning to their own perverse ends, by which they always strive after what is forbidden, and set themselves against every saving effort: 'he wraps his tail together like a cedar. His bones are like pipes of brass.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'for, obstinate in despair of himself, he sets himself against all.'

Sixth, feeling a shield threatening it, sharpening its tusks, it rubs them against a tree, and thus they are more blunted than sharpened. It signifies the wrath of the devil, or of the Antichrist, which he feels when he finds the just prepared not to yield to him, but rather to conquer him, who, even while he helps himself, or strives to help himself, with cunning and devices of temptation, then finds himself, above all, deceived by a holy man: 'round about his teeth is terror; out of his nostrils goes forth smoke, like a pot heated and boiling.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: For the devil's greatest fury arises when he not only fails to conquer, but is himself conquered, as Gregory touches on, in the Moralia.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The donkey, which is also called the ass, is found to have these properties, according to natural authorities, and especially according to Isidore, book 12, Avicenna, Aristotle, and Pliny.

For first, it is a simple animal, subject to human strength and cast down before it. It signifies the simple and humble in the Church, obediently bearing the yoke of the Gospel, according to that saying, Psalm 72: 'I am become as a beast of burden before you; and I am always with you. You have held me by my right hand, and by your will you have conducted me.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Happy indeed is the soul that bows its neck to the yoke of God and continually looks toward paradise, as blessed Ambrose touches on, On Paradise, and Jerome, To the virgin Metrias.

Second, it is a slow and very sluggish animal. It signifies the negligent and lazy in a congregation, gladly working evil, Proverbs 26: 'the slothful man says: there is a lion in the way, a lioness in the roads; I shall be killed in the midst of the streets.'
For as idleness speaks much evil, Ecclesiasticus 33, so lukewarmness, to be vomited out, does worse, Revelation 3.

Third, it is a stupid and forgetful animal. It signifies those deprived of discretion and circumspection in the Church, casting everything behind their back, Ecclesiasticus 21: 'a man of pleasure has heard a wise saying, and it will displease him, and he will cast it behind his back.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: For it is great stupidity for a man to be unwilling to apply himself to the teaching of the wise, as Seneca touches on, to Lucilius.

Fourth, it is an animal content with small and cheap fodder; it even plucks its food among thorns and brambles and thistles. It signifies servants of God, lovers of poverty and austerity, sober and sparing in food and clothing: 'and having food, and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, in a letter to Paulinus: 'to believers the whole world is a treasury of riches.'
...very troublesome to small birds nesting in hedges; for it rubs itself against the hedge, or, plucking, drags it, and, by shaking, makes their eggs fall.

It signifies certain insolent men in the Church, troublesome to the poor and despised, Proverbs 14: 'he that walks in the right way, and fears the Lord, is despised by him that goes by an infamous way.'
For woe to those who do not bear with the little poor and the despised, since they sadden Christ, as is gathered from Luke 17 and Matthew 18.
...like the raven which flies over it so as to destroy its eyes with its beak. Likewise it is an animal hated by nearly all small birds, whose eggs it makes fall generally from their nests in hedges.

It signifies the good and holy in the Church, held in hatred by the devil and his demons, since they thwart their efforts toward evil, Amos: 'they hated him that rebuked in the gate, and abhorred him that spoke perfectly.'
For as the wicked man and his wickedness are hateful to God, Wisdom 14, so the saints, and their sanctity and goodness, are a horror to demons, as is proven in the book On the Praises of Paul.
...the bear seeks to sate itself on his flesh: 'as a roaring lion, and a hungry bear, so is a wicked prince over the poor people.'
But truly, woe once and again to the powers of this world, since their pasture is the poor, as is touched on, Ecclesiasticus 13.

...all venomous things flee from its lung. It signifies the fervent remembrance of Christ's teaching and passion, before which every temptation recoils and yields, 'remember my poverty, and my transgression, the wormwood and the gall. I will be mindful and remember, and my soul shall languish within me.'
The words of Scripture are more powerful than any songs of enchanters against poison.
Origen, On the Passion of Christ: 'so great is the remembrance of Christ's passion, that it overcomes every temptation.'

Ninth, it is an animal most impatient of cold, and so is not found in cold regions, such as Pontus. It signifies the wanton and the petulant, who flee and shudder at evangelical chastity, and so do not enter religious life: 'they said to God, depart from us, we desire not the knowledge of your ways.'
Against which, Ambrose, in the sermon On a Bishop Confessor: 'let us, therefore, resist the manifold evils of this world by chastity and chaste deeds.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The asp has these conditions, or properties, according to our natural and holy authorities, especially Aristotle and Pliny and Isidore, book 12, and Martianus.

For first, the asp is a serpent most deadly in its bite and its venom, called from spraying, since with its bites it sends forth and sprays deadly poisons. It signifies the devil, or the Antichrist, who, by the bites of pestilent temptations, poisons the unwary and spreads sins: 'he will bite like a snake, and will spread poison like a basilisk.'

Augustine, in the sermon On a Single Martyr: 'just as those bitten by the bites of serpents in the wilderness were healed by looking upon the bronze serpent on the pole, so now, whomever the cunning of Satan has bitten, let him look upon Christ hanging on the wood,' and so on.

Second, when the asp begins to suffer the enchanter who calls it out with charms, so as to draw it from its den, if it is unwilling to come out, it presses one ear into the ground, and stops and covers the other with its tail; and so, not hearing those magic words, it does not come out to the enchanter, and does not obey his command.

It signifies those who do not wish to hear the commandments or the words of God, but rather scorn them and rebel, Job 24: 'they have been rebellious to the light; they have not known his ways, nor returned by his paths.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: For it is the height of madness to despise the words of God, as Gregory touches on, in the homily for the Sunday of the Passion.

Third, the limbs struck by it swell, and scarcely regain their health by any remedy, without the amputation of the parts that have been touched. It signifies the incurable poisoning of heresy, and therefore something wholly to be shunned and fled, Titus 3: 'a man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid, knowing that he that is such a one is subverted, and sins, being condemned by his own judgment.'
For there is no greater plague than the crime of heresy, that is, the crime of injured majesty, as the Gloss on Matthew 12 suggests.

...it loves its own mate in a wondrous way. Whence, if one of the pair is killed, the other pursues the killer with an incredible care for vengeance, and, recognizing him alone amid however great a multitude of people, harasses him, striving to overcome every difficulty. It ranges through great distances, nor is it held back except by swift flight, or by rivers and streams, from taking vengeance for the death of its mate. It signifies the wicked, that is, the members of the devil, cherishing one another mutually, and defending one another with care, Job 41: 'the body of Behemoth,' that is, the multitude of the devil, that is, of wicked men, is 'like molten shields, joined together with scales pressing one upon another; one is joined to another, and not so much as any air can come between them.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'the members of the devil so cling together that they agree wholly, out of their vanity, upon the same end.'

Fifth, it cannot see its adversary directly, but only obliquely; wherefore it cannot pursue its enemy by sight, but rather pursues by smell. It signifies wicked men and adversaries of the truth, who cannot look upon good men, the friends of God, but rather seek to harm them: 'they will laugh at the just and despise them; but the Lord will laugh them to scorn.'
'He that walks in the right way, and fears the Lord, is despised by him that goes by an infamous way.'
For it is a very great abuse indeed when a good man is mocked by a wicked one, as is touched on in the Gloss.

The asp does not harm the Africans and the Moors. For they expose to it their own children, born of them, whom they hold suspect; and if they are of their true seed, it does them no harm at all; but if they are illegitimate, they at once die from it. It signifies that the devil cannot harm the friends of God, and true Christians clinging to his grace, but only those who are of his own party through evil will or evil deed, Wisdom 1: 'but by the envy of the devil, death came into the world; and they follow him that are of his side.'
Ambrose, in the sermon for the Sunday of the Passion: 'thus does the devil love his own, as a glutton loves a young pig — to eat it.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'the devil is a weak enemy, who cannot conquer any but the willing.'
For if the tempted man is cautious, he will be stronger than the tempter, as the Gloss on Joshua 1 says.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The spider has these properties, or conditions, according to natural authorities and doctors, especially Avicenna, Aristotle, and Isidore, book 12.
For first, it is very intent on its web, and 'never ceases from its labor, but endures a perpetual expense'; yet at the least breath of wind it loses all its labor.

So it is with human life, which is always intent on children and knowledge and gains, on buildings and honors and various gatherings of temporal goods, and at the least breath of death is frustrated of them all, Isaiah 59: 'they trust in nothing, and speak vanity; they have woven the webs of spiders.'

'You fool! This night do they require your soul of you; and whose shall those things be which you have provided?' For nothing is more foolish than to trust — under God's curse — in the things of this world, as is drawn from Jeremiah 17 and the Gloss on Luke 12: 'he is properly called a fool who does not provide against future dangers.'

Second, it weaves its web out of its own inward substance, so as to catch as its prey the fly, whose moisture is its food. So does human life strive, with its whole affection, to have something in this world, and, when it has labored enough, staking, as it were, its very soul for such a thing, finds nothing but a single fly, that is, some cheap, temporal, momentary thing, on which it spent so great a care, and this very thing it suddenly loses, and finds nothing in its hands but punishment: 'you have chastised man for iniquity, and have made his soul waste away like a spider.'
'Nothing is more wicked than to love money; for such a man sets even his own soul to sale, since, while he lives, he has cast away his innermost parts.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, in the letter to Paulinus: 'the greedy man lacks as much what he has as what he does not have. Even the unbeliever wants for a single coin,' as the same author says there.

Third, the spider foretells clear weather, and then builds its web high and toward the light. But if the coming weather is to be bad, then it does its work in a low and dark place. So it is with the life of man: if it is good, and awaits the time of blessed eternity, it builds in heaven with the brightness of holy edification; but if it is bad, it builds in the lowest part of the world and the depth of hell, in darkness — that is, of sins: 'everyone that does evil hates the light; but he that does the truth, comes to the light, that his works may be manifest, because they are done in God.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: For the just man always tends toward heavenly things, but the sinner always descends toward the lowest, since he savors nothing but infernal things, as Gregory suggests, in the Moralia.

Fourth, a multitude of spiders, or their multiplication, is a sign of a coming flood of rain. So a multitude of sinners, or a multiplication of vanities and vices, is a sure sign of many tribulations that are to come upon the world, Proverbs 18: 'the wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, condemns; but ignominy and reproach follow him.'
'A gathering together of straw is the synagogue of the wicked, and their end is a flame of fire.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: By the frequent evils that come before, the perpetual evils that follow are indicated.

...a spider's web, when not mixed with dusty dirt, checks blood flowing from a wound, and prevents matter or swelling from forming. So the brief and wretched life of man, well considered, checks a man from the habit of sin, and prevents him from hatred, or rancor, and the swelling of pride, Ecclesiasticus 2: 'look, my children, at the generations of men; and know that no one has hoped in the Lord, and been confounded. He has continued in his commandments, and was he ever forsaken?'

For whoever should well consider his own life and the condition of his nature, and always keep it before his eyes, would cease from every sin, as Augustine suggests, in the ninth book of the Confessions.

Sixth, against the bite of a spider the remedy is rennet of a lamb drunk with wine; or to show a spider of the same kind to the one so bitten. So the medicine for a man struck by the poisoned love of this world is the incorporation, or the marrow-deep fashioning within himself, of Christ's passion, together with the wine of fervent devotion toward it; likewise, to show him how badly those have perished who were so struck by the vanity of the world: 'remember my poverty, and my transgression, the wormwood and the gall. I will be mindful and remember, and my soul shall languish within me.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'Happy the soul that always carries the suffering Christ between its breasts.'
The bee is discerned by philosophers and our doctors to have these properties.

For, according to Avicenna and Pliny and Aristotle, Isidore, Ambrose, and Jerome, they first lay down, as the foundation of their work, a certain crust of bitter flavor, and then make another, sweeter one.

So a good man, in the foundation of his life, ought to lay down first the bitterness of his sins, or the reshaping of himself upon Christ's torments, and afterward attach to it the devotion of eternal things, Lamentations 3: 'remember my poverty, and my transgression, the wormwood and the gall. I will be mindful and remember, and my soul shall languish within me. These things I recall to my mind, and therefore I will hope in God.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, in the book On Loving God: 'the passion of Christ rouses us to the love of God, and the remembrance of it compels us to that very love.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Likewise, Bernard, in the same place: 'the love of God toward us cannot be repaid.'

Second, they coat the roof of their hive, throughout, with tears, or drops, or juices of trees having a gummy strength, and so fortify themselves, as best they can, against the greed of other small creatures. So good men fortify and anoint themselves with heavenly devotion and the pious examples of the saints' practices of piety, against the rapacity of hostile temptations, 1 Timothy 4: 'exercise yourself unto godliness. For bodily exercise is profitable to little; but godliness is profitable to all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.'
The Gloss, on the said passage: 'the sum of the Christian religion consists in godliness, which whoever has, even if he suffers the slipperiness of the flesh, will obtain mercy in the end.'

Third, in the time allotted to them for work, whether inside or outside, none is permitted to be idle; for the older ones work within, but the younger ones outside; and when those going out return laden, they are received and unburdened by those who remain. So good men in a congregation ought to do; for none ought to be idle, but all ought to give their labor, in fruitful works within and without, and, working together in works of piety, ought by turns to serve and support one another charitably: 'go to the bee, and consider how chaste a worker she is.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: The love of God can never be idle. For it works great things if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it is no longer love.

...bees gather, from flowers now fresh, now withered, the material from which they compose honey and wax. And when the flowers nearby have been used up, they send scouts to seek out farther pastures. So good men compose their life and their works and their words solely from the graces and consolations of heaven, from gracious character, and from the examples of the holy fathers, and, when the lessons or examples of the present fail them, they turn back to the teaching and life of those who went before: 'stay me up with flowers, compass me about with apples; because I languish with love.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Homilie 'super missus est' sive In laudibus Virginis matris Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'The flower from the root of Jesse, singularly springing forth, loves the flowering homeland.'

Fifth, if night overtakes them on an expedition, they keep watch lying on their backs, so as to protect their wings from dew or rain, so that, morning having come, they may fly more readily to their work, having dry wings. So good men, when they are overtaken by tribulation, keep the wings of their supermental desires and await, patiently and with equanimity, the time when they may pass over to the heavens, 2 Corinthians: 'I am filled with comfort, I exceedingly abound with joy in all our tribulation.'

Augustine, in the Gloss on James 1, 'count it all joy,' and so on: 'do not wonder, brethren, if the wicked flourish in the world and you suffer, for it is not the way of the Christian religion for the good to be exalted in temporal things, but rather brought low. But by the hope of that good toward which you strive, bear patiently all the evils that shall befall you.'

Sixth, they foreknow rains and winds, and then keep themselves under cover, and, when they foreknow that fair weather is coming, they go out in a company to their work, and then some carry back flowers, others water, drop by drop, sucked up in their mouth and in the down of their whole body, to their little cells. So good men, when they perceive the malice of the wicked pressing upon them, wisely and in silence gather themselves within, redeeming the evil days and the evil times. But when they perceive that a heavenly consolation smiles upon them, then they drink it in, with their whole affection, as much as they can, and store it up in the secret places of their minds: 'see, brethren, how you walk circumspectly, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.'
Ambrose, on the letter to the Ephesians: 'they are called evil days on account of evil works; they are called good days on account of good works.'
Bede, in the same place: 'they are called evil days when the wicked reign; they are called good days when the good hold power.'

Seventh, they fill their first cells with little honey, but are wont to fill the last ones very full. So good men grant little consolation to the lower part of reason and to sensuality; but of heavenly sweetness they gain as much as they can for the supermental parts, Romans 8: 'ourselves also, having the first-fruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption of the sons of God, the redemption of our body. For the Spirit himself gives testimony to our spirit that we are the sons of God.'
For the spirit of holy devotion proves the sons of light.

Eighth, wondrous is their obedience toward their king. For when the whole swarm goes forth, it is gathered around him, and, as it were, surrounded and enclosed and fortified by them on every side; and wherever he pitches camp, there all take their stand, and keep him alone free from labor; and, seeing him, the whole army is roused, but, losing him, the whole swarm scatters. And if any bee should stray, or, weary, fall behind, it follows its companions by scent. So good men are obedient to the higher part of reason, as to the king of the whole soul and body; and all their powers, and all their desires and thoughts, serve it, and take their stand where it takes its stand, that is, with their intention and their act, where it fixes itself — namely, in heaven — and they withdraw it alone from temporal occupations, so that it may be free for eternal things alone; and, that part considered, together with its acts, the whole army of thoughts and desires is roused to good and renewed for the better. And if that part should fall from its good state, the whole soul scatters and falls from the unchangeable good. And if any power of the soul should stray from God, or, wearied by sins, should cease from the communion of the Church's holy unity, it follows, by the scent of holy examples and heavenly inspirations, the imitation of the good, with its affections, and is restored to the way and the company of the elect, Proverbs 20: 'the king that sits on the throne of judgment, scatters away all evil by his look.'
Proverbs 21: 'as the divisions of waters, so is the heart of the king in the hand of the Lord; whithersoever he will he shall turn it.'
Psalm: 'your wife as a fruitful vine, on the sides of your house.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: Chrysostom, on Matthew, homily 47: 'the soul of the poor man is not subject to involuntary passions, but has thoughts as its servants. It shines like gold, blooms like a rose, and gleams like a pearl. For there no thief comes, no moth; but it lives on earth as an angel. It is not subject to demons, nor does it wait upon kings. It does not fight alongside men, but alongside angels. It has its treasure not on earth but in heaven.'

Ninth, it is a many-footed and small animal among all living creatures. So good men are multiplied in holy affections and heavenly desires, and humble in their own estimation: 'our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged.'
The Gloss on 1 Kings 2: 'if you rejoice in Jesus, your heart is enlarged.'
'We are today humble in all the earth,' and so on.

Tenth, it is an animal endowed with great skill and ingenuity and magnanimity in its work, although small in body. So good men are perceptive and skillful in doing the works of God, although they seem contemptible in outward habit, yet are effective in deed, Ecclesiasticus 10: 'the bee is small among flying things, but her fruit has the chiefest sweetness.'

2 Corinthians 10: 'his bodily presence,' they say, 'is weak, and his speech contemptible; but his letters are weighty and strong. Let such a one think this, that such as we are in word, by letters, when absent, such also we will be indeed, when present.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, in a letter to Paulinus: 'John, a rustic, a fisherman, unlearned. And whence that voice, I ask: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God? This, the learned Plato never knew; this, the eloquent Demosthenes was ignorant of.'
The ox is known to have these properties, according to natural and our doctors.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni
Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni
Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX
Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: For, according to Gregory, on Ezekiel and in the Moralia, and Isidore, book 12, and Pliny, book 8, and many others, first, toward its companions, 'it is of exceptional devotion. For one seeks out the other with whom it has been accustomed to draw the plow by the neck, and, by frequent lowing, testifies its dutiful affection,' when it does not happen to find it quickly.

It signifies, in a prelate, a dutiful affection and condescension toward the household of the faith, Galatians: 'while we have time, let us work good to all men, but especially to those who are of the household of the faith.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'Hold back the blows, bring forth the breasts.'

Second, alone among all animals it feeds while walking backward. It signifies a prelate, after Christ's example, humbly drawing himself back from the honors and favors of the world, Philippians 2: 'in humility, let each esteem others better than themselves. For let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Dominici fundatoris ordinis predicatorum

cit.quote: It is said, in the legend of blessed Dominic, that he so trampled underfoot the world and the world's glory that, walking with Peter with dry feet upon the sea, he would not fix the print of his foot in it at all.

Third, it grows fat from a washing of warm water. It signifies a prelate who is affectionately fed and spiritually refreshed by the use of heavenly wisdom, or the fervent grace of the Spirit, Jeremiah 15: 'your words were found, and I ate them, and your word was to me a joy and gladness of my heart, for your name has been invoked upon me, Lord God of hosts.'
Ambrose, in the gloss on 1 Kings 1, chapter 2: 'if you rejoice in Jesus, your heart is enlarged.'

Fourth, when oxen are yoked together by the horns of their heads they can bear more labor than when they are coupled by the neck. It signifies the concord of prelates and subjects, by which, when present, all things are done in the strength of charity, and, when absent, all things collapse, 1 Thessalonians 4: 'we beseech you, brethren, to know them who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you, that you esteem them more abundantly in charity, for their work's sake; and have peace with them.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Commentarii Hieronymi in Evangelium Matthei

cit.quote: As by concord small things grow, so by discord the greatest things collapse.

Fifth, it is a gentle and clean animal. It signifies, in a prelate, kindness and cleanness: 'be kind to one another'; and below: 'but fornication and all uncleanness, let it not so much as be named among you, as becomes saints.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On Loving God: 'for holy men, all flesh is an instrument for good work.'

Sixth, the ox tills the fields and renders them fit for the fruits of fatness. It signifies, in a prelate, diligence toward his subjects for the bringing forth of spiritual fruits, Ecclesiasticus 7: 'you have cattle, take care of them; you have children, instruct them.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul, as if he were the common father of the whole world, surpassed all bodily parents in the love of souls.'

...the ox greatly refreshes and comforts with its own flesh. It signifies, in a prelate, various forms of assistance, comforting the weak among his subjects, 2 Corinthians 11: 'who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul was bitten and thoroughly torn within when he saw any perishing.'
Eighth, it is a mature and slow animal. It signifies, in a prelate, maturity and gravity in his undertakings, 1 Corinthians 14: 'let all things be done decently, and according to order, among you.'
'Walk with wisdom toward them that are outside, redeeming the time.'
The Philosopher, in the Ethics: 'one ought indeed to deliberate slowly, but to act swiftly.'

Ninth, it is deceived by a certain small creature called 'burestus,' resembling a beetle.
