For this creature deceives the ox among the grasses in this way: it places and hides itself among the grasses the ox loves, and the ox, unwarily devouring it while cropping its beloved grass, is at once invaded by this creature in its liver, which greatly inflames it, and, suddenly, with the greatest torment, at last it bursts and comes out. It signifies that, in prelates, pleasure and concupiscence frequently hide themselves under the appearance and cloak of necessity, and inflame toward evil, and so kill the soul and torment the conscience, Ecclesiasticus 18: 'go not after your lusts, but turn away from your own will. If you give to your soul her desires, she will make you a joy to your enemies.'

An example is given by Cassian, in the book of the Conferences of the Fathers, of the servant boy of a holy father, who, out of the desire of gluttony, stole bread every day, and, eating it secretly, showed himself as fasting; on account of which, having become a joy to the devil, had he not been brought to contrition by his father's preaching, he would have perished forever, and, as far as it depended on him, would have brought shame upon the wilderness and its inhabitants.
The buffalo has these conditions, or properties, according to natural and holy authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX
Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: For, according to Isidore, book 12, and Pliny, book 28, and many others, first, it is like the ox itself.

It signifies the feigned, or the hypocrite, who outwardly puts on the appearance of a mature and good man, Matthew 23: 'woe to you, hypocrites, who are like to whited sepulchers, which outwardly appear to men beautiful, but within are full of filthiness and iniquity.'

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore De meditatione Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: The reason so few advance is this: that all have their eye turned outward, toward the appearance of the work, and not inward, toward the profit of virtue.

Second, it is so untamed an animal that, out of ferocity, it accepts the yoke only under a strong hand, whenever such a thing happens at all. It signifies a proud and stiff-necked man, Isaiah 48: 'I know that you are hard, and your neck is an iron sinew.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De sancta virginitate Augustini

cit.quote: No rest of the soul is found otherwise than in a tumor of pride quietly digested.

...an animal of great strength; whence it cannot be brought under the yoke except by an iron ring fixed in its nostrils, by which it is led about. It signifies those swollen with worldly philosophy, who cannot be drawn to the yoke of the Gospel, or the love of heavenly wisdom, unless they submit to the spirit of humility and poverty. We have a great example of this in Dionysius and in Paul: 'I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little ones.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Augustine, On the Spirit and the Soul: 'nothing is more excellent, for a blessed life, than to be turned within oneself, and be made a stranger to desires.'

Fourth, it has few and sparse hairs. It signifies, in a good man, the fewness and sparseness of the thoughts of the old man: 'when I was a child, I thought as a child, I understood as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'by the name of hairs are designated the thoughts of the old life.'

Fifth, it has its forehead surrounded with very strong horns. It signifies, in a good man, the face of the soul fortified, against hostile assaults and temptations, with the arms of the virtues, according to the pattern of the apostle: 'put on the armor of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day, and to stand perfect in all things.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: Such was blessed Martin, who used to say, as is found in his Life: 'I, protected not by shield or helmet but by the sign of the cross, will penetrate the enemy's ranks safely.'

Sixth, its flesh is useful not only for food, but also for medicine, in many trials. It signifies a good man, and his pious conduct, useful for all things, 2 Timothy, the last chapter: 'take Mark, and bring him with you; for he is profitable to me for the ministry.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On Loving God: 'for holy men, all flesh is an instrument for good work.'

Seventh, buffalo-oxen hate and pursue everything red, or ruddy. They signify wicked men, holding hatred for holy and grave men, and pursuing works of charity, Proverbs 14: 'he that walks in the right way, and fears the Lord, is despised by him that goes by an infamous way.'
Chrysostom, in the third sermon for the third Sunday in Lent: 'the wicked cannot bear to see what is good. The degenerate do not wish the better man to live,' and so on.

Eighth, this beast is of such cruelty that, after it has killed a man by falling heavily upon him with its knees, or hocks, against his belly, suspecting that he might still be alive, it puts its ears and nostrils to smell whether he, now dead, still breathes, unwilling to spare his life in any way. It signifies the devil who, even after he has cast a soul into mortal sin, in no way ceases, but even to the end of that life watches its heel and lies in wait for the man's whole life, lest he come to possess eternal life, according to that saying: 'your adversary the devil,' and so on.
It was said to the devil: 'you shall lie in wait for his heel.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: As one who neither slumbers nor sleeps, who fights against Israel.
The basilisk has these properties, according to the philosophers and doctors.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For, according to Isidore, book 12, chapter 4, and Pliny, first, it is the king of serpents.

It signifies the devil, or even the Antichrist, who reign over earthly, serpent-like men, or those who scorn the decrees of God: 'he beholds every high thing; he is king over all the children of pride.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily for the first Sunday in Lent: 'surely the devil is the head of all the wicked. Is not Pilate a member of the devil?'

Second, seeing it, other serpents flee and fear. It signifies the devil, or the Antichrist, from whose sight and temptations good men recoil, Jeremiah: 'flee out of the midst of Babylon, my people, and let every one save his own soul.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, in the book On Paradise: 'demons are to be fled, vices and sins are to be fled.'
...a living bird, it.

It signifies the devil and the Antichrist, killing souls, even the souls of contemplatives, with their offers and their attractions, unless they are wary, 1 Peter 5: 'your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour,' and so on.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily On a Single Martyr: 'we who have come to the contest of faith take up a struggle against evil spirits.'
...a weasel.
It signifies that the devil and the Antichrist are to be overcome and confuted only by the humble, James 4: 'God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De sancta virginitate Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, in the book On Holy Virginity: 'no rest of the soul is found otherwise than in a tumor of pride quietly digested.'

Fifth, it is half a foot in size, marked with white spots. It signifies the brevity, or smallness, of the power of the devil, or the Antichrist, over those who do not consent to them, and the outward show of pleasing things which, at first sight, they offer to those they tempt, 1 Corinthians 10: 'God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able; but will make also with temptation a way to escape, that you may be able to bear it.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'the enemy is weak, who cannot conquer any but the willing.'

Sixth, burned to ash it loses its malice, though it remains irremediably poisonous as long as it lives. It signifies the devil and the Antichrist, whose malice will cease, after their humiliation, in the abyss of hell, though they exercise it now, up to the judgment of the great day: 'the devil, who seduced them, was cast into the pool of fire and brimstone, where the beast also is; and the false prophets shall be tormented, forever and ever.'
The Gloss on the letter of James: 'wherever the devil goes, he carries with him the torments of flames, that is, bitter remorse and the shackles of prisons.'
...for the elect, concerning the humbling of the devil and the Antichrist: 'for the sake of the elect, those days shall be shortened.'
Daniel 12: 'at that time your people shall be saved, everyone,' and so on.
The camel is known to have these properties, according to the philosophers and doctors, especially Aristotle, Isidore, and Pliny.

For first, it is a gentle animal, appointed for men to carry their burdens. It signifies the just man, and his life, in gentleness of character and the exercise of the virtues, Psalm 72: 'I am become as a beast of burden before you; and I am always with you. You have held my hand, and by your will you have conducted me.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De diversis questionibus octoginta tribus

cit.quote: Augustine, in the book of 83 Questions: 'the prouder a man is, the more he is made subject to baser things.'

Second, it bends its knees when it is loaded by men. It signifies the just man, and his life, in every reverence before God, and in every patience toward his neighbor: 'bear one another's burdens, and so you shall fulfill the law of Christ.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De diversis questionibus octoginta tribus

cit.quote: Augustine, in the book of 83 Questions: 'nothing so proves a man a friend as the bearing of a friend's burden.'
Third, it moves its right foot before its left.

It signifies the affection of the just man, tending first and chiefly toward divine and eternal things, according to the pattern given: 'seek first the kingdom of God, and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you.'

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore De meditatione Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: Hugh, in the book On Meditation: 'an affection is then called good when it is directed at what it ought to be, and in the manner it ought to be.'

Fourth, it does not mate with its mother, or the like, but rather kills one that deceives it into this, and is stronger for having every mating denied to itself. It signifies a zealous lover of chastity, who is thereby made more virtuous against every hostile assault, Proverbs 30: 'a cock girt about the loins, and a ram; and there is no king that can resist him.'
Ambrose, in the sermon On a Bishop Confessor: 'let us, therefore, resist the manifold evils of this world by chastity and chaste deeds.'

Fifth, it is solitary in the mountains at the time of love. It signifies the just man, at the time of prayer and devotion, going about eternal things and transcending heavenly things, Song of Songs 2: 'I will rise, and will go about the city, in the streets and the broad ways, I will seek him whom my soul loves.'
He truly ascends to God who, entering within and penetrating himself, transcends himself.
...the just man, continuing in the desires of the blessed life, and, after the manner of the apostle, rejoicing in tribulation, Philippians 1: 'I desire to be dissolved, and to be with Christ.'
'And not only so, but we also glory in tribulations.'
It is read of blessed Francis that he cried out that he willingly wished to suffer evils for Christ.

Seventh, it lives fifty, and sometimes a hundred, years. It signifies the just man, long-sufferingly persevering in the service of God, Matthew 10: 'he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved.'
None is crowned, except he that has striven lawfully.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily On a Single Martyr: 'let the greatness of the rewards delight the mind, then, but let it not be deterred by the struggle of the labors.'

Eighth, it is an animal most hot by nature, and therefore naturally lean. It signifies the just man, greatly warmed by divine grace, and therefore mortified in his senses, 2 Corinthians 4: 'we who live are always delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus may be made manifest in our mortal flesh.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Better is the iniquity of a man who withdraws necessities from the body and afflicts it, than a woman who does it good — that is, one who is dissolved by carnal action and satisfies the body in every way.
The chameleon is discerned to have these properties, according to the philosophers and doctors, especially Aristotle, Isidore, and Pliny.

For first, it is a small creature, sprinkled with a diverse variety of colors, whose little body changes, with the easiest turning, to match the various colors it sees, nor is any other animal found whose body so takes on the change of opposite colors. It signifies hypocrites, wrapping themselves about with every color of sanctity, and representing in themselves the graces of all men, Matthew 23: 'woe to you, hypocrites, who are like to whited sepulchers, which outwardly appear to men beautiful, but within are full of dead men's bones.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'feigned fairness is not fairness, but a doubled iniquity.'

Second, it shines like a star and changes colors. It signifies the worldly man, variously flourishing in the world and showing himself off in different ways, yet in the end losing everything: 'he comes forth like a flower, and is destroyed, and flees as a shadow, and never continues in the same state.'
Blessed Cecilia used to say, as is found in her legend: 'the power of man is like a wineskin filled with wind, which, if a single needle should prick it, is at once deflated and bent low.'
Third, it is a timid animal, and of little blood. It signifies a man who has a worldly fear, and no courage of spirit toward eternal things, Proverbs 28: 'he that fears man shall quickly fall.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On Loving God: 'the spirit was given to man for this, that it might always go before the sense of the flesh.'

Fourth, it has sharp and curved claws. It signifies robbers and thieves, and all who lay hands on the goods of others: 'in the dark they dig through houses, as in the day they had agreed among themselves,' Job 24.
Augustine, in his sermons: 'while other vices grow old in a man, avarice alone grows young.'

...a creature made of pig and monkey. It signifies actors and their base performances: 'man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to senseless beasts, and made like to them.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Commentarii Hieronymi in prophetas minores

cit.quote: Mimes are unworthy of the Gospel's support.
...in the air. It signifies the worldly man, rejoicing in vanity alone; against which it is said, Psalm 23: 'he that has not taken his soul in vain, he shall receive a blessing from the Lord.'
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'that alone is to be loved which cannot be lost while it is loved.'

...it feigns itself gentle, though it is cruel. It signifies the deceitful and the cunning, being one thing and pretending another: 'there is one that is hindered from sinning through poverty, and if he find opportunity to do evil, he will do it,' Ecclesiasticus 19.
The son of lying, cruelest of the Antichrist in soul, will show himself to the world as gentle.
Eighth, its power and effort is chiefly directed against hawks; for it draws down to itself hawks that fly near it, and offers them, willingly, to be torn apart by other animals.

It signifies the zeal and effort of the devil, especially against the hawk-like — those who, seeking the heights and rejoicing at the prey taken from hostile assaults, he gladly draws to himself, and, if he can, exposes to be tormented by his demons, Job 39, where it can be said to the devil: 'is it by your wisdom that the hawk grows feathers,' that is, the contemplative man always progresses in virtue, 'spreading his wings,' that is, his desires, 'toward the south' — that is, toward the renewal of the grace of the Holy Spirit — as though it were said: 'not by you, but by me, since you always strive for the contrary.'
The roe deer has these properties, according to the philosophers and doctors.
For, according to Aristotle, Isidore, and Pliny, first it is a wild goat, named from cropping shoots.

It signifies students of theology, solitary from the occupations of the world, according to the pattern given, Ecclesiasticus 28: 'the wisdom of a scribe comes by his time of leisure. Run before to your house, and there take your pleasure, and think over your own devices.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Augustine, On the Spirit and the Soul: nothing is more excellent, for a blessed life, than to be turned within oneself, and be made a stranger to desires.

Second, it sees most sharply. It signifies those who contemplate and understand divine things, 2 Corinthians 3: 'but we, beholding the glory of the Lord with open face, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De diversis questionibus octoginta tribus

cit.quote: Augustine, in the book of 83 Questions: 'it belongs to the mind alone to know, but not to the mind alone to love.'
...roes, to the fawns of the deer, at Bethel.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: He truly ascends to God who, entering within, transcends himself in mind toward God.

Fourth, it is most swift in running. It signifies a man freed from the world and virtuous in the Gospel, Proverbs 22: 'have you seen a man swift in his work? He shall stand before kings, and shall not be before men of low degree.'
The Philosopher, in the Ethics: 'one ought indeed to deliberate slowly, but to act swiftly' — that is, virtuously.

Fifth, it is lightest in leaping. It signifies the agility of spirit in a good man for fleeing and escaping hostile temptations and the importunity of thoughts, Song of Songs 2: 'behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills.'
Proverbs 11: 'he that avoids snares shall be secure.'

Sixth, it is tender and most wholesome as food. It signifies, in a learned theologian, a gracious and fruitful teaching and preaching, 2 Timothy 3: 'all Scripture, inspired of God, is profitable,' and so on, 'that the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work.'
Bernard: 'for holy men, all flesh is an instrument for good work.'
Seneca: 'he that comes to a philosopher should carry away something good with him each day.'

...for by sight, taste, and smell, it discerns among the grasses and the little branches of trees, whose tender tips it eats and crops. It signifies the spiritual man, skillfully discerning all things, and finding consolation only in heavenly things, salutary to himself and his soul, Philippians 3: 'I count all things to be but loss, for the excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord; for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them as dung, that I may gain Christ.'

Jerome, to the virgin Metrias: 'happy is that conscience, and blessed the virginity, in whose heart, besides the love of Christ, who is wisdom, chastity, patience, and justice, no other love dwells, nor does it ever sigh at the remembrance of a man.'

Eighth, its milk, when drunk, cures the languishing leopard of the force of its languor. It signifies that, by drinking the teaching of our humanity and redemption, spiritual languors are healed in the proud: 'I have given you milk to drink, not meat.'

Augustine, in the seventh book of the Confessions: 'your Word, God, was made flesh, that your wisdom, by which you made all things, might give milk to our infancy, and that we, seeing your divinity brought low before our feet, might fall down, prostrate before it; and that it, rising, might lift us up.'
The roebuck is discerned by the saints and philosophers to have these properties.
For, according to Aristotle, Isidore, and Pliny, first it is like a fawn of the deer.
It signifies an evangelical man, conforming himself in all things to Christ, the Son of the patriarchs and kings according to the flesh, John 12: 'if any man minister to me, let him follow me.'
For every Christian's action ought always to consist in the imitation of Christ, according to the sentence of blessed Augustine.
Second, they have wisdom; for when they are wounded, they seek out pennyroyal and eat it, so as to draw out from their body the arrows fixed within them.

It signifies the wisdom of the saints who, in the dangers of temptations, run back for their remedy to Jesus Christ, Romans 7: 'unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God, by Jesus Christ,' and so on.
The Gloss on Nehemiah, chapter 8: 'prayer is the one refuge against all enemies and all plagues.'

...its flesh is relieved of excess moisture, and is made more tender and digestible, and the heaviness of flavor and smell is removed. It signifies a holy man, always moving and applying himself to divine things, and, by the constant practice of good works, always advancing, useful to himself and to others, Ecclesiasticus 33: 'in all your works be quick, and no infirmity shall come to you.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Celestial Hierarchy: 'the mobile spirits of the seraphim are always carried about divine things.'

Fourth, feeding by grace, it tends from high places to yet higher ones. It signifies, in a perfect man, the daily increase of supermental ascents and the progress of supercelestial consolations, 2 Corinthians 5: 'for whether we be transported in mind, it is to God; or whether we be sober, it is for you; for the charity of Christ presses us.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Dionysius, at the end of the Celestial Hierarchy: 'holy men are frequently made participants in supercelestial delights, through godlike advents of illuminations.'
Fifth, it chews the cud and divides the hoof. It signifies, in the elect, holy discretion, Matthew 10: 'be you wise as serpents.'
The knowledge of the saints is wisdom and prudence.

...it defends itself with claw, horn, and tooth. Whence, when it is pursued in the open fields, fleeing to the mountains, it seeks the heights. It signifies, in evangelical men, resolution against lust, which they know can be overcome only by flight, 1 Corinthians 6: 'flee fornication.'
Augustine, on the letters of Paul: 'lust is a thing that is overcome by flight alone.' And so its battle is not to be sought by holy men, but fled.

Seventh, among wholesome and harmful herbs it discerns and distinguishes by scent, and gladly feeds on aromatic herbs. It signifies the life of the saints, avoiding above all the examples of the wicked, and eagerly hungering after the sweet-smelling works of the ancient fathers, and daily refreshing themselves with them: 'you are like a roe, and a young hart, upon the mountains of aromatical spices.'
'Lord Jesus Christ, I give you thanks, that you have separated me from all pollution, and have always illumined my soul; for your fragrance has stirred up in me eternal desires.'
The goat is known to have these conditions, or properties, according to the philosophers and saints, and especially Aristotle, Isidore, and Pliny.

For first, it always tends upward, so as to crop and take the tops of the leaves, or the sweet little branches it prefers. It signifies the just man, always seeking the higher things and hungering after eternal consolations, Philippians 3: 'forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before, I press toward the mark, of the prize of the supernal calling. If by any means I may attain, in which also I am attained by Christ Jesus.'
As though Paul already lived among the incorporeal powers themselves, so, by the constant intention of his mind, already possessing heaven, he wholly despised all earthly things.
Second, it is very prolific. It signifies, in the just man, the fruitfulness of good works, 1 Corinthians 15: 'the grace of God in me has not been void, but I have labored more abundantly than all.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On Loving God: 'for holy men, all flesh is an instrument for good work.'

...it is said to breathe through its ears, and not through its nostrils. It signifies, in the just man, attention and intention toward heavenly things: 'he was caught up into paradise, and heard secret words which it is not granted to man to utter.'
It is also said, in the legend of blessed Martin, of blessed Severinus, archbishop of Cologne, that at the death of blessed Martin he heard voices singing in harmony on high.
Fourth, it is rarely without fever. It signifies that the just man is rarely without some defect: 'for in many things we all offend.'
'We are all become as one unclean, and all our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman.'
Ambrose, treating the words of Isaiah 59: 'our goodness, compared to the goodness of God, is found injustice and uncleanness.'

Fifth, it sees no less by night than by day. It signifies, in the just man, prudence and circumspection, with equanimity, in adversity as much as in prosperity, Ephesians 5: 'see how you walk circumspectly, not as unwise, but as wise.'

'What we have chosen must be kept, and we must walk as it were among scorpions and serpents, so that, with loins girded and feet shod and staves in hand, we may make our journey through the deserts of this world and through its poisons, and may be able to come to the sweet waters of the Jordan, and enter the promised land, and ascend to the house of God.'
Sixth, in many regions it has milk without having conceived. It signifies those who have teaching without life; against which, Acts 1: 'Jesus began to do and to teach.'
Gregory: 'when a man's life is despised, it follows that his preaching too is condemned.'

...they graze in the pastures facing one another. It signifies students of the sacred page, or those refreshing themselves on the word of God in preaching, applauding one another in mutual congratulation in Christ, Psalm 127: 'your children as olive plants, round about your table.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis Enarrationes in Psalmos Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, on the Psalms: 'the table of God is holy Scripture, from which the elect of God are refreshed.'
The dog is known to have these conditions, or properties, according to the philosophers and doctors, especially Aristotle, Pliny, and Isidore.
...a dog.
It signifies the preacher of the Gospel, who ought to excel in much sense and much cunning, 1 Corinthians 2: 'but we have the mind of Christ; and we speak wisdom among the perfect.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'the preacher ought to know what, to whom, how, when, and where he speaks. If any one of these should be lacking, his speech will not be fitting.'
Second, it recognizes its own name.
It signifies the preacher humbly recognizing his own condition, Revelation 2: 'be mindful, therefore, from whence you have fallen; and do penance, and do the first works.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus De copia verborum

cit.quote: Death, moreover, ought to be before the eyes as much of the young man as of the old.

Third, it is found to be of great memory; for after many years, finding its master again, it knows him, and, its master lost, over very long distances of land, it knows how to return alone to its master's house. It signifies the preacher, from whose memory the praise and meditation of God ought never to cease, Tobit 4: 'keep God in mind, and let all your counsels rest in him.'
Psalm 18: 'the meditation of my heart, always in your sight.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: The remembrance of Christ's passion compels one to the love of God.
Cecilia, who always carried the Gospel of Christ in her breast.

We have found that dogs have fought for their masters against robbers, and we have heard that, weakened by wounds, they drove off birds of prey and wild beasts from their masters, and we have read that they compelled a murderer, by tearing and barking, to confess his master's crime. We have found also that two hundred dogs brought back King Garamantus from exile, and fought with wondrous boldness against those who resisted them. Likewise the dog of Jason of Sicily refused to take food after its master was killed, and so was consumed alike by grief and by starvation. We have read too that a dog defended Celon, a senator of the city of Piacenza, when he was set upon by armed men, and was not wounded before its master was slain. So the dog of Titius Sabinus abandoned him neither in death nor in prison, but, giving forth mournful howls, remained with him dead; and when someone threw food to it, it carried the food to the mouth of the dead man, and, when the corpse was dragged into the Tiber, leaping in, it swam within the river to support the body, while a crowd ran up to witness the animal's faithfulness.

It signifies, in a preacher of the truth, faith, zeal, and constancy for the honor of Christ and the Gospel, even to martyrdom, Ecclesiasticus 4: 'strive for justice for your soul, and contend even unto death for justice, and God will fight for you against your enemies.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Nothing pleases God so much as zeal for souls.

Fifth, its ferocity is soothed when a man sits down humbly before it. It signifies that divine wrath ceases at the humbling of the mind, James 4: 'God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'We will run after you, good Jesus, altogether because of the gentleness that is preached in you, hearing that you do not spurn the poor man, do not shrink from the sinner, did not shrink from the thief confessing,' and so on.
...for by wind and scent it pursues wild beasts fleeing even through the waters, and, catching their tracks, betrays the hidden lairs of beasts with its barking and its snout.

It signifies, in a preacher of the truth, skill and diligence against the adversaries of the faith, and the confutation of their pestilent wiles and inventions, 2 Timothy 4: 'reprove, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and doctrine'; and below: 'but watch you, labor in all things, do the work of an evangelist.'
Bede, treating that same word: 'the work of an evangelist is to labor for the truth and to live according to the Gospel.'

...it runs for its master's prey. It signifies, in a preacher, readiness for the salvation of souls and for gaining them, after the example of the apostle: 'most gladly will I spend, and be spent myself, for your souls.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'let your love be strong and steadfast, yielding to no terrors, succumbing to no labors.'

Eighth, it guards its master's dwellings and possessions. It signifies, in a preacher and in a prelate, diligence in the care of churches and their sacraments and sacramentals: 'my daily instance, the solicitude for all the churches.'
Chrysostom, in the book On the Praises of Paul: 'no one, as Paul did, governed the people entrusted to him — indeed, the whole world.'

Ninth, from a tiger and a dog is born a dog so strong that it overcomes a lion and an elephant, as Alexander the Great found in the dog sent to him by the king of Albania, which first, in his presence, crushed a lion, and then, an elephant having been brought, seeing the beast, with the hair bristling over its whole body, first gave out a great bark, and then, by skillful fighting, so afflicted the elephant that it was forced to fall to the ground.

It signifies, in a prelate or a preacher, boldness and strength of mind against tyrants, victorious in the defense of ecclesiastical liberty, after the example of Peter and Paul against Simon Magus, and of Prisca and Aquila, the last chapter of Romans, who laid down their own necks for the soul of Paul.
The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep. But the hireling, and he that is not the shepherd, sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep, and flees.
Paul, as though incorporeal, scorned labors and dangers, and, as though already possessing heaven, despised all worldly things.

Tenth, a dog breeds sooner, if it is a greyhound, than others. It signifies a preacher, eager for eternal things, more quickly and more abundantly begetting sons for God in the Church: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'

Chrysostom: 'as though Paul had begotten the whole world, so he hastened to bring all men into the kingdom of God, by teaching, by promising, by judging, by begging, now praying for them, now even beseeching them.'

Eleventh, the best offspring is the one the mother first carries to the den, and which is the last to begin to see. It signifies Paul, whom the Lord drew into his fold among the first in the primitive Church, and who yet saw God last of all, 1 Corinthians 15: 'I am the least of the apostles,' and so on, 'but by the grace of God I am what I am,' and so on.
'I obtained mercy, that in me first Christ might show forth all patience, for the instruction of them,' and so on.
'But last of all, as by one born out of due time, he was seen also by me.'
I marvel at the power of God, I wonder at the spirit of Paul, since he strove to show himself such, since he prepared himself to be capable of so great a grace.

...a greyhound can beget more when it is in labor than when at rest. It signifies a prelate or preacher, truly eager for heavenly things, who, the more vigorously he exercises his office, the greater the influence he receives from God for the multiplying of the faithful, grace assisting him then more than when he is idle, 1 Kings 3: 'and Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and not one of his words fell to the ground.'
The Ordinary Gloss, there: 'empty words fall to the ground, to be reckoned as nothing, and trampled underfoot by the sight of all.'

...a sick dog eats the root of a certain herb, so as to vomit, and so heals itself. For the dog first showed vomiting — that is, medicines and purgations — for, filled with harmful food, it eats grass and, thus freed by vomiting.

It signifies, in the sinner, the recourse to penance and confession, by which remedies they obtain the remission of sin and the recovery of the soul's health, Psalm 31: 'I said: I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord,' and so on.
Augustine: 'penance is a certain best and perfect thing, calling back every defect to what is perfect.'
The Gloss on Matthew 3, 'do penance,' and so on: 'the first virtue is to kill the old man through penance.'
The deer has these conditions, or properties, according to our holy authorities and the philosophers.
For, according to Aristotle, Isidore, Pliny, and Gregory, first, it is fecund, and, in its fecundity, very honest and modest.

It signifies the just man, abounding in good works, and excelling in modesty and brightness of character, 1 Timothy, the last chapter: 'follow after justice, godliness, faith, charity, patience, mildness.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily for Pentecost: 'the love of God can never be idle. For it works great things if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it is no longer love.'

Second, it feeds more gladly and eagerly on aromatic plants. It signifies the just man, seeking pastures in the fragrant pleasantness of the ever-green paradise, Song of Songs, the last chapter: 'be like to a roe, and a young hart, upon the mountains of aromatical spices.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'He who does not sense your fragrance, Jesus, is either dead or foul-smelling.'
...of the deer.
Christ willingly taught and prayed on a mountain, that he might teach the faithful, by his example, to be lifted up toward heavenly things.

Fourth, it is carried, by a wondrous desire, to the drink of the living fountain. It signifies the just man sighing, from the heart, for the enjoyment of God, Psalm 41: 'my soul has thirsted after the strong living God,' and so on; and it goes before, there: 'as the hart pants after the fountains of water, so my soul,' and so on.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in his homilies: 'he desires little the heavenly homeland who does not seek it daily with tears.'
Fifth, with ears raised and sharp it wonders at the sound of pipes, and listens.

It signifies the just man, intent, above the mind, upon the harmonies of heaven, and wondrously hungering after the angelic praises in heaven, Job 38: 'where were you, when the morning stars praised me together, and all the sons of God made a joyful melody?'
It is written and sung of blessed Francis: 'praising, he taught praise; praise was always at hand with him — praise, I say, that saves.'

Sixth, it is the enemy of the serpent. For if it finds one, it kills it, and after its victory seeks a mountain where it may refresh itself. It signifies the just man, an enemy and adversary of the devil, the world, and the flesh, each of which, once overcome, he rises up toward God, giving thanks and resting in him, Joshua 1: 'every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon shall be yours.'
The Gloss, there: 'if I shall be able to conquer the devil, and so bring it about that I crush him under my feet, I shall accordingly hold his place in heaven.'
Seventh, in crossing the sea, or the deep, they serve one another in a wondrous manner.

They signify just men who, especially in tribulations and infirmities, serve one another out of the love of charity, 2 Timothy 1: 'the Lord give mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me, and has not been ashamed of my chain.'
Augustine: 'let good men be present; all sad things are lightened and softened.'
...it shakes out arrows fixed in it by feeding on the herb dittany.

It signifies the just man, overcoming every temptation and tribulation by the power of the suffering Christ, Hebrews 12: 'think diligently upon him that endured such opposition from sinners against himself, that you be not wearied, fainting in your minds.'
Whomever the cunning of Satan has bitten, let him look upon Christ hanging on the wood.

Ninth, when it feels itself failing in spirit through old age, it draws serpents out from their dens with the breath of its nostrils, and, overcoming their deadliness, is restored by feeding on them, and so is renewed.

It signifies penance, which draws mortal sin out of the heart and renews the soul in every virtue, Acts 2: 'do penance, and be baptized every one of you in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, for the remission of your sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De vera et falsa penitentia Pseudo Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, On Penance: 'penance is a certain best and perfect thing, which calls back every defect to what is perfect.'

Tenth, its tears, gathered, and its heart-bone, given as a drink, are of great strength for the disorders of the heart. It signifies that Christ's tears, on the cross, avail those who gather them affectionately in their heart, against every defect that man can suffer spiritually, by the power of him who wept, Hebrews 5: 'who, in the days of his flesh, with a strong cry and tears, offering up prayers and supplications to him that was able to save him from death, was heard for his reverence.'
Origen, in his homilies: 'so great is the remembrance of Christ's passion, that by it one can overcome all adversities.'

Eleventh, by night it seeks its pastures. It signifies the just man, in the time of greatest tribulation, seeking out God and his consolations, Psalm 76: 'in the day of my trouble I sought God, with my hands; and I was not deceived.' Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul, confined in prison, dwelt in heaven.'

...serpents flee from the smell of its burnt horn. It signifies that the fragrance of a holy man's virtue and good life puts evil men and demons to flight, 2 Timothy, the last chapter: 'Demas has left me, loving this world, and has gone to Thessalonica; Crescens into Galatia, Titus into Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'the garments of Paul were a terror to demons.'

Thirteenth, its horns, carried or kept close, are said to hinder conception. Whether this is literally true or false, it is most certain, mystically, that the powers of the soul of a just man, trusting in the goodness of God and resting upon him, hinder every malice and wickedness of the devil, and his every effort: 'or will you have proof of him that speaks in me, Christ?'
It is written, in the book of Illustrious Men, of blessed Ignatius, that he was accustomed to say: 'let all the torments of the devil come upon me, only that I may enjoy Christ.'

Fourteenth, its rennet heals the bites of serpents. It signifies, in the just man, the heartfelt transformation of Christ's passion, overcoming every displeasure and prick humanly inflicted upon him, Galatians, the last chapter: 'God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ; by whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world.'
It was told to Constantine the Great by an angel, as is found in the Tripartite History: 'in this sign,' namely of the cross, 'you shall conquer.'

...he found deer of such an age, and covered and marked them with collars. It signifies, in the just man, the perseverance and justice by which he is worthy of praise and glory and honor, James 1: 'blessed is the man that endures temptation, for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life,' and so on.
A crown is given to the victors.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The beaver, as Isidore says, book 12, is a wondrous beast which lives with the four-footed animals and walks upon the land, but swims beneath the waters and dwells among swimming creatures, like a fish.

And it is called 'castor' from castrating, as the same Isidore says. For its testicles are useful for medicine, on account of which, when it senses the hunter, it castrates itself, biting off its own virile parts.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: These animals, as Pliny says, book 11, chapter 13, build for themselves houses and dens on the outermost banks of waters and rivers, prepared with wondrous craftsmanship. They live together in a group, and love their own kind. Gathering together, too, they cut down wood from the forest with their teeth, and, serving one another in a wondrous way, carry and lead it, backward and from the side, to their hiding places; and one of them, lying on its back at times, has the wood piled between its haunches and on its belly, and, thus loaded, is dragged by the others to the appointed dens, where they unload it of the wood, and so they build their hiding places, upper and lower, so that when the river floods, they may stand in the upper part, but when it recedes, in the lower part of their own channel. It is always necessary for them, moreover, to keep their tails in the water, since their tails are, by nature, fish-like; for otherwise they would quickly spoil.

These animals signify evangelical preachers and perfect religious who, out of love for the salvation of their neighbors, spend their days among the people, but by night dwell in the waters of holy Scripture, or in the tears of heavenly devotion and the anxious sighs and groans of supernal piety. They are also such great lovers of evangelical chastity that they castrate themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and to avoid the universal snare and evil incitement of demons; and, after the likeness of these animals, they live in charity and fraternal unity, and pursue those of the household of the faith with all the affection they can, and, with one desire and one intention, do all things, and provide for one another mutually against every future danger to themselves.

bibl.author: Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Corinthios secunda

cit.quote: Their tail, no less — that is, their persevering, firm, and holy purpose — they continually keep in the waters, that is, in the mysteries of holy Scripture and its examples and its tearful devotions, lest their sense should be corrupted, in any way, from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus, according to that saying of the apostle, 2 Corinthians 11.
...Christ, Luke 21: 'and Jesus was, in the daytime, teaching in the temple; but at night, going out, he lodged in the mount that is called Olivet.'
As to the second point, Matthew 19: 'there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. He that can take it, let him take it.'
As to the third point, Ephesians 4: 'that you walk worthy of the vocation in which you are called, with all humility and mildness, supporting one another in charity.'
As to the fourth point, Matthew 10: 'he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved.'
And concerning this last point, Augustine says, in the letter to Marcellinus, that a man ought to take more care not to lose his patience than to lose any possession.
The dromedary has these properties, or conditions, according to the philosophers and the saints.

For, according to Aristotle, Isidore, Papias, Gregory, and Pliny, first it is a kind of camel, of smaller stature than the camel, but of far swifter course, on account of the length of its stride. For it can travel a hundred miles and more in a single day.

It signifies a humble preacher, expanded in the strides of charity, and, spreading it simply, advancing more in the Church, and directing others more strongly toward eternal things, 1 Corinthians 15: 'I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me has not been void, but I have labored more abundantly than all.'

Chrysostom, in the book On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul, like a winged bird, flew about the whole world, teaching, and, as though incorporeal, scorned labors and dangers, and, as though already possessing heaven, appeared so to all.'

Second, it is castrated in its youth, so as to be fitter for the course, and lest it be held back from its course by desire, stirred by females. It signifies a religious man, or preacher, of good disposition from childhood, cherishing the yoke of the Gospel and celibacy of life, so that, freed from desires, he may always proceed on his journey toward God, Lamentations 3: 'it is good for a man, when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He shall sit solitary, and hold his peace, because he has lifted himself above himself.'

It is read of blessed Nicholas, in his Life: having simply passed his childhood years at home, like the patriarch Jacob, he began, as a youth of good disposition, and did not, as that age is wont, embrace the wantonness of the world, but now, accompanying his parents' footsteps, now alone, kept to the thresholds of churches, unveiling to God the covering of his desire.

Third, it chews the cud, like the ox and the camel. It signifies discretion of teaching in the preacher, Ecclesiasticus 21: 'the heart of fools is in their mouth; but the words of the just shall be weighed in a balance.'
Bede, on Ecclesiasticus: 'a word ought first to pass through the file, and only afterward come to the tongue.'

Fourth, it is the hottest animal in its natural constitution; whence the strength of its heat consumes in them their oiliness and fatness, and does not allow them to be burdened with a mass of flesh. It signifies, in the preacher or religious, the fruitfulness of the love of Christ, consuming in them all pleasure and wantonness, and not allowing them to be entangled or wrapped up in any earthliness, 1 Corinthians 9: 'I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection; lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a reprobate.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De divinis nominibus Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Divine Names, chapter 4: 'divine love is ecstatic, not allowing lovers to belong to themselves, but rather to those they love.'
Whence the apostle Paul, being made subject to the seizure of divine love: 'I live,' he says, 'now not I; but Christ lives in me.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'he through whom...' is altogether wholly to be loved by me.'

Fifth, it is a light animal, on account of the paucity of its food; for it is not an animal of great eating, but is content with little food, only in the evening. It signifies, in the preacher and the religious, sparingness of life and temperance of diet, 1 Timothy, the last chapter: 'and having food, and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content.' 1 Timothy 5: 'use a little wine for your stomach's sake, and your frequent infirmities.'

'You had not yet known my life. Bread alone, with olives, and rarely also with vegetables, is my usual food. As for clothing, this that you see is a tunic with a cloak. And having this, I require nothing else; this is enough for me, since my mind aspires not to these present things, but to those that are eternal.'
The dragon is found to have these properties, or conditions, from the philosophers and the saints.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Of serpents, Isidore, book 12, it is the greatest of all; often drawn out of caverns, it is carried into the air, and the air above is stirred up because of it, and the sea swells up against its venom.

It signifies the devil, the head of all the wicked, and his temptation and pride, Job 41: 'he is king over all the children of pride. Out of his nostrils goes forth smoke. He makes the deep sea boil like a pot, and he sets it as when ointments boil.'
Augustine, in the sermon On a Single Martyr: 'the devil is a lion and a dragon. A lion for his onslaught; a dragon for his ambushes. A lion rages openly; a dragon lies in wait secretly.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as Isidore says, book 12, it is crested, with a small horn, and draws breath through narrow pipes; it raises its tongue, and has sharp, serrated teeth.

It signifies the devil, of small power but great boasting and greatest malice, Job 41: 'behold, his hope shall fail him, and he shall be cast down in the sight of all. He shall esteem iron as straw, and brass as rotten wood. His heart shall be as hard as a stone, and as firm as a smith's anvil.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory: 'the enemy is weak, who cannot conquer any but the willing.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: Blessed Martin used to say, at the hour of his death, as is found in his Life: 'why do you stand here, bloody beast? You shall find nothing deadly in me.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Third, according to Isidore, book 12, its power lies not in its teeth, but in its tail.

It signifies the devil, always lying in wait for the heel of death, and always acting with treachery, Job 40: 'he wraps his tail together like a cedar; the sinews of his testicles are wrapped together. He sleeps under the shadow, in the covert of the reed.'
He lies in wait, that he may catch the poor man; to catch the poor man, while he draws him to himself.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Commentarii Hieronymi in Evangelium Matthei

cit.quote: For human life would not be safe amid so many snares of the enemy, were it not defended and supported by the protection of the holy angels.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fourth, as Isidore says, book 12, it needs no poison to bring death to anyone, but whomsoever it binds with its tail, it kills. From this not even the elephant is safe, for all the greatness of its body; for, lurking along the paths by which elephants walk, it binds and entangles their legs with its tail, and, choking them, destroys and kills them; but not without paying for it, since it is itself crushed by the elephant's fall.

It signifies, in the devil, the most cunning entrapment and entangling of souls, to his own damnation, Revelation 12: 'the dragon stood before the woman who was ready to be delivered, that, when she should be delivered, he might devour her son.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: The devil, in his infernal presumption, is so bold that he thinks he can deceive even the greatest members of the Church, and swallow and devour them with himself into hell.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fifth, as Pliny says, book 9, chapter 14: a dragon of ten cubits in size is born among the Ethiopians. They are accustomed, ten or eleven together, to intertwine their tails with one another, and, with their heads raised, to sail like ships across the sea and rivers, seeking better feeding grounds.

These things signify the joining together of the greater demons and tyrants and heretics with one another, and their care and eagerness for the killing and devouring of simple souls, Psalm 11: 'the wicked walk round about.'

bibl.author: Gregorius IX papa Decretales Gregorii IX

cit.quote: Having indeed different faces, but tails bound together to one another, since out of vanity they agree upon the very same end.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis In Hieremiam prophetam Hieronymi

cit.quote: 'They have drawn in the wind like dragons.' It is an animal so very thirsty that it can scarcely be satisfied even in water.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis In Hieremiam prophetam Hieronymi

cit.quote: It also opens its mouth against the wind, so as to temper its own heat, according to Jerome, in the passage cited above.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: But most of all, according to Isidore, book 12, chapter 14, it desires the blood of the elephant, by whose great coldness it may cool its own burning heat.

It signifies that the devil cannot be satisfied by our evils, and that he desires most of all the blood of more perfect souls and those of greater virtue, Job 40: 'he will swallow up a river' — that is, the multitude of ordinary just men, according to Bernard — 'and not wonder; he trusts that the Jordan may run into his mouth' — that is, the abundant number of the perfect and of the greater elect.
The horse has these conditions, according to the philosophers and the ancient authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it has a hollow foot, and 'with its pressed hoof it hollows the earth,' which the other animals scarcely do at all.
It signifies the just man, having a humble affection and a contempt for earthly things, Matthew: 'learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart. Take my yoke upon you.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: The yoke of Christ is humility and poverty.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, it sounds with its feet, as Isidore says, book 12.

It signifies a good man, affectionately intent on the preaching of the Gospel, or the edification of his neighbor, after the example of the apostle, 2 Corinthians 13: 'or will you have proof of him that speaks in me, Christ?'
Romans 15: 'from Jerusalem round about, even unto Illyricum, I have replenished the Gospel of Christ.'

Who would not marvel that, from Paul's tongue, the speech that leapt forth put death to flight, dissolved sins, illumined the darkness of blindness, and, by a wondrous change, turned earth into heaven?

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As Isidore says, book 12, it exults in the open fields.
It signifies a holy man rejoicing in the breadth of charity, 2 Corinthians 6: 'our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged.'
'Rejoice in the Lord, and exult, you just; and glory, all you right of heart.'
Ambrose, in the gloss on 1 Kings 2: 'if you rejoice in Jesus, your heart is enlarged.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fourth, it is roused to battle by the sound of a trumpet, as Isidore says, book 12.
It signifies the just man roused, by the word of Christ preaching the Gospel, to triumph over vices, Job 39: 'the horse, when he hears the trumpet, says: ha, ha; and goes forth to meet armed men.'
Origen: 'the soul is roused, by the words of Scripture, against all the assaults of demons.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fifth, roused by the voice, it is provoked to running, as Isidore says, book 12.

It signifies a good man, always more kindled to what is good, and to progress toward what is better, by the encouragement of his fellow companions, 2 Corinthians 5: 'but we are confident, and have a good will to be absent rather from the body, and to be present with the Lord. And therefore we labor, whether absent or present, to please him.'
Hebrews 3: 'exhort one another every day, whilst it is called today; that none of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.'
They showed the elephants the blood of grapes and mulberries, that they might excite them to fight.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As Isidore says, book 12, it rejoices when it has conquered its enemies in war, whom it knows and recognizes so well that it attacks them with its bites.

It signifies, in a good man, joy at the victory over temptations, or hostile assaults, James 1: 'count it all joy, my brethren, when you shall fall into diverse temptations; for blessed is the man that endures temptation, for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life.'
The Ordinary Gloss, there: 'the wicked have nothing in heaven, and you have nothing in the world. Therefore, by the hope of that good toward which you strive, overcome whatever befalls you.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As Isidore says, book 12, it recognizes its own master, having forgotten its gentleness, if it should be changed for another.

It signifies a good man, knowing Christ alone, and caring nothing for any other master, Philippians 3: 'I count all things to be but loss, for the excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord,' and so on.

Blessed Eugenia the virgin: 'let those like you have your riches; it delights us to beg with Christ.' Thus she spoke to Melania, who was urging her and promising her much, so as to bend her to her lust, thinking her to be a man.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: ...it weeps at the death of its master, and permits no one to mount it but its own master.

It signifies the just man, of such faith and love toward Christ that he affectionately mourns his passion and death, as though it were always set before him, and wishes to carry nothing else in his mind: 'remember my poverty, and my transgression, the wormwood and the gall. I will be mindful and remember, and my soul shall languish within me.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, in the book On Loving God: 'Christ willingly dwells in the soul that meditates on his passion.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Ninth, according to Pliny, book 7, chapter 44: it shrinks from mating with its mother, especially among the thirsty; for horses have a certain awareness of kinship.

Whence Aristotle tells, in book 8: 'the king of the north,' he says, 'had a beautiful mare, which bore a beautiful colt, and wished to draw offspring from that horse and its mother, and it was arranged that the horse should mount its mother, its face being covered. And when its mother's face was uncovered after the mating, it recognized her, and the horse fled and threw itself from a height for grief, and died.'
It signifies a good man who loves supremely the modesty of chastity, Luke 12: 'let your loins be girt.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: For we gird our loins when we restrain the wantonness of the flesh through continence.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Tenth, according to Pliny, book 7 and the chapter cited above: in a herd it walks more gladly with its sister than with its mother.

It signifies that the holy man wishes rather to dwell with his sister, the wisdom of heaven, than with his mother, the desire of the flesh, Proverbs 7: 'say to wisdom: you are my sister; and call prudence your friend.'
The Amorite, that is, the love of the world, and the Hittite, that is, the concupiscence of the flesh.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Pliny, book 7, chapter 44: it delights at the sound of music and the blast of the trumpet.

It signifies the just man who, at the sound of heavenly praise and the words of Scripture, conceives and feels a great consolation, Ephesians 5: 'be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual canticles, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.'
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'those voices flowed into my ears, and the truth was distilled into my heart, and tears flowed, and it was well with me in them.'
The Gloss on the title of the Psalms: 'a hymn is the praise of God with a song.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Twelfth, according to Pliny, the book cited above: that horse is judged more useful which, in drinking, plunges its nostrils more deeply, and such a one is not burdened, in running, by the carrying of urine.

It signifies, among good men, that man is more praiseworthy who more eagerly grasps the divine mysteries, and drinks more deeply of the draughts of wisdom, Job 28: 'wisdom is drawn out of hidden things' — that is, the knowledge and savor of heaven, out of the secret mysteries of the Scriptures.
Thirteenth, as Aristotle says, book 8: the older it is, the whiter its teeth are.

It signifies a good man who, the longer he lives, shines forth the more by examples and lessons; against which, Isaiah 65: 'the child of a hundred years shall be accursed, and the sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed.'
Proverbs 22: 'a young man, according to his way, even when he is old, will not depart from it.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: The Greek history relates: 'Alexander the Great, king and ruler of the world, could not, in his conduct, be free of the vices with which, as a boy, he had been infected by his tutor Leonides. For the emulation of evils is prone to evil.'
Fourteenth, as Aristotle says, book 5: the male lives 25 years and begets from the third year.

It signifies a preacher who, long, and from his youth or early manhood, advances in the office of preaching and begets children for God, 1 Timothy 4: 'command this, and teach. Let no man despise your youth; but be an example to the faithful, in word, in conduct, in gravity, in chastity.'
It is good for a man, when he has borne the yoke from his youth.
It is said of blessed Jerome, in his Life, that he received the garment of Christ as a boy in Rome.
...a horse recognizes the neighing of one who wishes to fight against it.
It signifies a holy man, knowing the efforts of the devil, or the flesh, or the world, rising up against him, 2 Corinthians 2: 'for we are not ignorant of the devices of Satan.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: The just man is always found girded against temptations.
...animals.

It signifies holy men, singularly desiring the multiplication of the faithful and of good men in the Church, Tobit 13: 'I shall be blessed if there shall be a remnant of my seed, to see the glory of Jerusalem.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul strove to draw all men to Christ.'
Elephants are known to have these conditions, or properties.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, they are the greatest in size, and surpass all four-footed animals in bulk and height.

They signify the Pope and the cardinals, greatest in the dignity of their authority and chief in the care of the universal administration of the churches; whence not undeservedly that saying is understood of them: 'you shall make them princes over all the earth'; and that other saying: 'the princes of the people are gathered together with the God of Abraham; for the strong gods of the earth are exceedingly exalted.'
Dionysius, in his answer to the Architect: 'a higher order receives more of the light.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: Chrysostom, on Matthew: 'the Son gave to Peter, everywhere on earth, that which belongs to the Father and to the Son himself, and gave to a mortal man the authority of all things that are in heaven, giving him the keys, so that he might enlarge the Church everywhere on earth.'
The same author also says, on John: 'he confines James, locally, to one place; but he made Peter master and teacher everywhere on earth.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX
Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Second, as Isidore says, book 12, and Pliny, book 8, chapter 1, among all other animals they are of the greatest virtue and probity, of vast size, industry, memory, and understanding, so that such probity is scarcely found even in men. For they carry wooden towers, overthrow battle-lines, do not fear weapons, and, with their foreheads and trunks, tear down tall palm trees, and so eat their fruit. At every new moon they gather together in herds, and wash and bathe themselves in a river, and so return to their own place. They always make their young go before them, and guard them with diligent care, and instruct them wondrously. When they are ill, they gather certain herbs wholesome for them, and, before they use them, lift them, with heads thrown back, toward heaven, and, with a certain religious feeling, ask for help from the divine powers. They recognize their own king, and bow before him out of reverence. Likewise, when hunters attack them for the sake of their ivory tusks, they break off those tusks that are sought from them, so as to be left in peace.

They signify the Pope and the cardinals, most virtuous and upright among all the elect of God. For they bear the towers of all the virtues of the universal Church; they overthrow the battle-lines of unbelievers and the adversaries of the Gospel; they do not fear the arms of tyrants or the threats of the insolent; by life and teaching, by vigor and diligence, they surpass, conquer, and triumph over the kingdoms of the earth; they are always renewed toward better things; they multiply and nourish sons for God, and draw all men to God. In their tribulations they have refuge and recourse to the eternal God. They recognize their king, Jesus Christ, and honor God alone.

Whence one of the apostles said, of such men, in the person of Peter and his fellow apostles, 2 Corinthians 10: 'for walking in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty to God unto the pulling down of fortifications, destroying counsels, and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every understanding unto the obedience of Christ; and having in readiness to revenge all disobedience, when your obedience shall be fulfilled.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, On Consideration, to Eugenius: 'let shepherds be upright in judgment, provident in counsel, diligent in disposing, strenuous in acting.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: They are always enemies to dragons. For the dragon thirsts for the elephant's blood, since it is most cold, so as to cool its own great heat and burning. Likewise, their bones, when burned, put serpents and all venomous things to flight.

They signify the Pope and the cardinals, always opposing and being enemies to the devil and his members, who lie in wait for the blood of faithful souls to fulfill their own most wicked desire and intent, whose sentences and letters, powerful and strong, put to flight heresies and poisonous and deadly schisms throughout the whole world, just as the relics and garments of the apostles put to flight demons and demonic arguments and temptations, and every infirmity and death and plague, 2 Corinthians 2: 'for we are not ignorant of the devices of Satan'; and below: 'but thanks be to God, who always triumphs us in Christ Jesus, and manifests the odor of his knowledge by us in every place; for we are the good odor of Christ unto God, in them that are saved, and in them that perish.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'do you wish to know the gifts of God? The garments of Paul were a terror to demons.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As Pliny says, book 8, chapter 6, and Solinus: they are of wondrous modesty; for they know no adultery, and never fight over females; and when they contract impurity, they wash themselves in living water, and do not return to the herd before their washing. Likewise, if one is overcome by another, the defeated one flees the voice of the victor.

They signify, in the Pope and the cardinals, the celibacy of evangelical chastity and universal cleanness before God and the angels and all their neighbors, or subjects, 2 Corinthians 6: 'giving no offense to any man, that our ministry be not blamed; but in all things let us exhibit ourselves as the ministers of God, in much patience, in chastity, in sweetness, in the Holy Spirit.'

Jerome, to the virgin Metrias: 'happy is that conscience, and blessed the virginity, in whose heart, besides Christ, who is wisdom, chastity, justice, patience, and the other virtues, no other love dwells, nor does it ever sigh at the remembrance of a man, nor desire to see one whom, once seen, it would be unwilling to let go.'
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: only the celibacy of Ambrose seemed to me a hard thing.

Fifth, they are naturally gentle, because they lack gall, according to the Philosopher, book 14 of Animals. Yet they accidentally become fierce when they are too greatly provoked, or made drunk with wine, so as to be sharpened for battle.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Likewise, according to Pliny, book 8, chapter 5, and Aristotle, book 14, chapter 5: when they find a man wandering in the wilderness, they leave the path so as not to frighten him, and stand still, and gradually go before him, showing him the way; and if another wild beast should come, they defend him.

They signify, in the Pope and the cardinals, an affectionate love and piety for the guidance and salvation of all wandering souls, James, the last chapter: 'if any of you shall err from the truth, and one convert him, he must know that he who causes a sinner to be converted from the error of his way, shall save his soul from death, and shall cover a multitude of sins.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Nothing pleases God so much as zeal for souls.

As is said in the ordinary and prose Physiologus, they are caught and taken by two naked virgins with loosened hair, singing loudly and delightfully in the wilderness; for they come to lick their breasts, and so are held fast.

It signifies, in the Pope and the cardinals, the denial of familiarity and affection to all but the honest and chaste, the poor and those who praise and venerate God, 2 Corinthians 13: 'for we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.'
'In the midst of brethren, their ruler is in honor, and his eyes are upon those that fear God.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Keep such companions as you will not be shamed by their company.
...when they are weary and wish to sleep, they lean against a very great palm tree, and so rest.

They signify, in the Pope and the cardinals, in persecutions and weariness, recourse and clinging to the cross of Christ, upon which, resting, they triumphantly find rest in Christ, Song of Songs 7: 'I said: I will go up into the palm tree, and will take hold of its fruit.'

Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'woe to the bold soul, which hoped that, having withdrawn from you, it would have something better; turn and turn about, on this side and that, and behold, all is hard, and you alone are rest.'
Our heart is restless until it rests in you.
Eighth, it lives longer than all other animals, as Aristotle sets forth, book 18.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For it lives three hundred years, as Isidore says, book 12, and this because of its constitution, by which it resembles the continent; for it mates rarely. For it is necessary for it to carry its young for two years, on account of the great size of the offspring conceived, which cannot be perfected or completed in a shorter time.
And after it gives birth, the female rests for three years, as Aristotle says, book 5.

These things signify, in the Pope and the cardinals, equanimity and long-suffering perseverance in all wisdom and goodness and truth and holiness, Matthew 10 and 22: 'he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily On a Single Martyr: 'let the greatness of the rewards delight the mind, then, but let it not be deterred by the struggle of the labors.'
He that strives in the contest is not crowned, unless he has striven lawfully.

Ninth, as Solinus relates, when by some chance they fight, they have no small care for their companions; for they receive the weary and the wounded into their midst, and protect and defend them more than themselves.

They signify, in the Pope and the cardinals, mercy and compassion toward the weak and sinners and all wretched persons, 2 Corinthians 11: 'who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?'

The Gloss, there: 'who is weak in any virtue, and I am not weak, compassionating him? Who is scandalized, apostatizing from the faith or holy conduct, and I am not on fire?' — that is, wholly with the fire of the zeal of God — as though he said, 'I grieve for him just as for myself.'

Tenth, according to Aristotle, book 1, and Avicenna: the elephant's trunk is so strong and long that it uses it in place of a hand, and by it takes its food and drink, and brings it to its mouth, which indeed no other animal does.

It signifies, in the Pope and the cardinals, the vigor of supreme discretion, by which ecclesiastical power advances, and the refreshment of souls, and their progress, proceeds and grows strong. Song of Songs 7 says of the Church: 'your nose is as the tower of Lebanon, that looks toward Damascus.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Regula pastoralis Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Pastoral Rule: 'discretion and wisdom are themselves the strength and vigor of the Church and of souls.'
Eleventh, as it is said, book 8: it is more domesticated and obedient, or tractable, than all wild animals, having a better understanding.

It signifies that the Pope and the cardinals are more obedient than other men toward the God of heaven, and more tractable to the friends of Christ; whence Peter said, Acts 5: 'we ought to obey God, rather than men.'

bibl.author: Paulus Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Corinthios secunda

cit.quote: Not us, but Paul; 2 Corinthians 4: 'for we preach not ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord; and ourselves your servants through Jesus.'
And again, 1 Corinthians 9: 'I became all things to all men, that I might save all.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, to prelates: 'bring forth the breasts, pastors; hold back the blows.'
Twelfth, their tongue is very small in proportion to their body, and appears within, and is rarely seen outside, except when it licks after food and drink.

It signifies, in the Pope and the cardinals, virtue more in life than in word, and authority more in deed than in outward show, 2 Corinthians 2: 'for the kingdom of God is not in speech, but in power.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul did nothing without purpose, but all things with just cause and reasonable ground; for he did everything with much deliberation.'
The kid has these conditions, or properties, according to the natural philosophers.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, according to Isidore, book 12, it is small and fat and pleasant in flavor.

It signifies the suffering Christ, for the effective increase of our humility and devotion, of the abundant and interior, or spiritual, refreshment of our consolation, 1 Peter 2: 'he himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, by whose stripe we were healed.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis
