cit.quote: Bernard, in the person of Christ: 'I laid down my soul, that I might join you to myself.'

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: Second, as Isaac says, in his Diets, for one recovering from illness, and generally for all others, its flesh is better and more suited to digestion; for its natural dryness is tempered by the moisture of its youth.

It signifies that especially the little ones and the humble are taken up by the Lord, or take up the Lord within themselves, Psalm 114: 'the Lord keeps little ones; I was humbled, and he delivered me.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Homilie 'super missus est' sive In laudibus Virginis matris Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on 'He was sent': 'be humble, that you too, after Mary's example, may find the grace of God.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily on the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar: 'for the water flows from the swelling of the hill down to the humility of the valley.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As Pliny says, book 8, it has very sharp sight, and a simple but sidelong gaze.

It signifies a good youth, sharp in wit, lovable and cautious in company, Wisdom 8: 'though I be young, I shall be found of a quick understanding in judgment, and shall be admired in the sight of the mighty, and the faces of princes shall wonder at me.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'the angelic creature, with an unblinking gaze of mind, beholds the vast abyss of the divine judgments,' and so on.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fourth, as Pliny says, book 8, it recognizes its parent by its bleating, and seeks it.

It signifies the prudence and circumspection of the just, always attending and intent upon the Father of all, Wisdom 10: 'he gave him the knowledge of the saints'; the Gloss: 'that is, to converse prudently in knowing.'
Proverbs 9: 'the knowledge of the saints is prudence.'
'Blessed is the man that shall continue in wisdom, and that shall meditate in his justice, and in his sense shall think of the circumspection of God.'

Fifth, its liver is said to heal the failing evening sight of those who are called night-blind, as the same author says. It signifies that the love of God enlightens those ignorant of the truth, John 8: 'you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.'
Anselm, in the Proslogion: 'surely we shall know only as much as we shall love, and as much as we shall love, so much shall we rejoice.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As Pliny says, book 28, chapter 10: the skins of kids heal poisonous bites if bound on warm. Their burnt hairs, too, drive off serpents. Their fresh skin is also used for wounds. Their blood, too, avails against poisons; their rennet, too, avails against a defect from drinking, and against the ill effects of drinking bull's blood.

All these things signify that the footsteps, the remembrances, the reconstructions, and the invocations of the suffering Christ avail against every danger and in every crisis, Hebrews 12: 'think diligently upon him that endured such opposition from sinners against himself, that you be not wearied, fainting in your minds.'
Augustine, in the sermon On a Single Martyr: 'whomever the cunning of Satan has bitten, let him look upon Christ hanging on the wood.'
...an animal fat and fleshy within, but shaggy and lean without.
It signifies a religious man, despised outwardly, but filled inwardly with divine consolation, Song of Songs 1: 'I am black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem; therefore has the king loved me.'
Bernard, in his sermons: 'many see our crosses, who do not see our anointings.'
Eighth, as the same author says, in the same book, it is a peaceable and harmless animal, chewing the cud, and clean, fit for the sacrifices of the ancients.
It signifies innocence, kindness, discretion, and devotion, according to that saying, Psalm 36: 'keep innocence, and behold equity; for there are remnants for the peaceable man.'
Augustine, in the City of God: 'it belongs to the office of the innocent not only to harm no one, but also to restrain others from sin.'
Ninth, as is found in the same book, it especially loves to eat the leaves of the ivy and of similar shrubs.

It signifies, in the just man, an eager feeding on the holy Scriptures, ever-green with everlasting pleasantness and excelling in supermental height, Job 38: 'he looks round about the mountains of his pasture, and seeks out everything that is green.'

Augustine, speaking of himself and his mother, in the book of the Confessions: 'we touched the region of your everlasting abundance, of the ever-green pleasantness of paradise, where you feed Israel forever with the food of truth.'
...a wanton, skipping, and playful animal.
It signifies young men or old men, always frivolous and dissolute, wasting their time, Proverbs 18: 'he that is loose and slack in his work, is brother to him that wastes his own works.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: Against which, it is said of blessed Francis, in his legend, that he did not, however, go among wanton young men after the wantonness of the flesh, nor, like greedy merchants, hope in money and treasures.
The ant has these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.
For first, according to Ovid's Metamorphoses, the ant, 'formica,' is so named as it were 'ferens micas,' that is, bearing the grains of meal which it gathers.
It signifies those who gather the sentences of the Scriptures and fashion, or store, them in the habit of memory.
This was signified by Ruth 2, when she said: 'I will go into the field, and glean the ears of corn that escape the hands of the reapers.'
This field is holy Scripture; the reapers are the doctors; the gatherers of the ears of corn, that is, of the sentences, are the disciples.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as Isidore says, book 12, it cuts off the ends of the grains it has gathered, and strips them of their husks, lest they sprout.
It signifies, in a good man, caution against vainglory in good deeds, Matthew 6: 'take heed that you do not your justice before men, to be seen by them.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily On the Treasure Hidden in a Field: 'let the work be done in the open, but let the intention remain hidden.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Isidore, book 12; for it provides for itself against the future, gathering in summer for winter.

It signifies a good man who labors in the present for the life to come, or in his youth for his old age, Proverbs 6: 'go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, which, having no guide, nor master, nor captain, provides her food in the summer.'

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore De tribus diebus Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: The ant, gathering grain in summer for winter, and the spider, weaving its web from its own inward substance so as to catch prey, are witnesses to the wisdom of God.
Psalm 127: 'for you shall eat the labors of your hands: blessed are you, and it shall be well with you.'
'The goods you have not gathered in your youth, how shall you find them in your old age?'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Nepotian: 'a new vessel long retains alike the flavor and the smell with which it was first steeped.'
What the new vessel takes in, the old one savors.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fourth, it gathers wheat and does not trouble itself with barley, as Isidore says, book 12.

It signifies a spiritual man, gathering merits for eternal goods, not for perishing, transitory ones, Matthew 13: 'gather up the cockle, and bind it into bundles to burn; but the wheat gather into my barn.'
The pure grain, the grain threshed of chaff, enters the barns of the highest King.
And, of blessed Dominic: 'from the threshing-floor of poverty, he is stored in the barn of heaven.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fifth, as Isidore says, book 12, when rain falls upon the wheat it has heaped up, the ant casts it all out and exposes it to the sun.
It signifies a good man who, when tribulation comes upon him, spreads out his merits before God, so as thereby to move God and turn away his wrath.
So did the afflicted Hezekiah, Isaiah 38: 'I beseech you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth, and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is pleasing before you.'
The Gloss, there: 'happy is the conscience that, in the day of evils, remembers its good deeds.'

Sixth, the grains they gather they skillfully store away in more secret little chambers, lest they be seized by birds or scattered by wind. It signifies that a good man fortifies and girds himself against every danger, and preserves his merits from demons and tribulations, Luke 21: 'take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness, and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly. For as a snare shall it come upon all that sit upon the face of the whole earth.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: 'For darts strike less that are foreseen as coming, and we bear the world's evils more tolerably if we are fortified against them by the shield of foresight.'
As Solinus says: they make hidden and straight paths to the houses they inhabit, and the wiser ones always stand along those paths, lest the foolish stray or wander from them.
They signify the straight paths of the just, given for the direction of the weak, Hosea, the last chapter: 'the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them.'
Psalm 1: 'the Lord knows the way of the just.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As Pliny says, book 11, chapter 31: they share their labors with one another.
They signify good men serving one another mutually, out of charity, 1 Peter 4: 'as every man has received grace, ministering the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Martin, in his Life, that he took turns serving his own servant.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Ninth, as Pliny, book 11, chapter 31: they carry burdens greater than their own bodies; for they make up for the smallness of their body by the greatness of their strength.

They signify holy men bearing and enduring more, and greater, displeasing things than their nature, or condition, or constitution, would be known able to bear, Galatians, the last chapter: 'bear one another's burdens, and so you shall fulfill the law of Christ.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: The just man knows how to overlook injuries, to bear with the defects of others, so that, by conquering himself, he may seize the kingdom of heaven.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Tenth, as Pliny says, in the same place: they diligently gather up scattered grains, lest they be lost, and divide the larger grains at the entrance, so as to bring them more easily into their storehouses. For they have care, reckoning, and memory concerning their own commonwealth.

These things signify the care and diligence that good and holy men have, without ceasing, for progress in common and in particular, 2 Peter 1: 'and you, employing all care, minister in your faith. Labor the more, that by good works you may make sure your calling and election.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'nothing so brings forth the imitation of Christ and of Paul as that a man's good should profit the common good.'
No good thing is enjoyed pleasantly without a companion.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Eleventh, as Pliny says above: at the full moon they work at night; at the new moon they cease from labor.

It signifies the diligence and opportunity that scholars, too, ought to have in studying or earning merit, carefully, at every place and time, Ecclesiastes 9: 'whatsoever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly'; and there, 11: 'in the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand cease, for you know not which shall rather spring up, this or that; and if both together, it shall be the better.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Nepotian: 'let holy reading never be laid down from your hands.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Twelfth, according to Pliny, above: they have a fixed time given them for mutual recognition, and then the greatest gathering occurs, and a certain meeting and diligent inquiry among those they encounter, by way of the worn and cleared paths they have chosen for themselves.

They signify, by this, the showing of charity that ought to be had by clerics and religious in councils, chapters, assemblies, and visitations, 2 Corinthians 8: 'show, therefore, before the face of the churches, that showing of your charity.'
Whence blessed Francis says, in his Rule: 'and wherever the brothers may be, and find one another, let them show themselves to be as members of the household toward each other.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Thirteenth, according to Isidore, book 12, chapter 3, a certain kind of them, of great size, in Ethiopia, dig up golden spiders with their feet, and guard them lest anyone take them away; and, seizing intruders, they pursue them to their death — so great is their fierceness in the love of gold.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Pliny also states, book 11, chapter 32, that in India there are ants of the greatest size, and horned, which guard gems and gold with a wondrous greed. But the Indians steal from them, chiefly in the summertime, when the ants hide themselves in heaps on account of the excessive heat.

They signify great lovers and greedy seekers of money, who nevertheless must necessarily lose it all, Ecclesiastes 2: 'but to the sinner God has given vexation, and superfluous care, to heap up and to gather together, and to give it to him whom God has pleased.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: Chrysostom, on Matthew, homily 47: 'if you wish to see the soul of one who loves gold, you will find it, like a garment gnawed by ten thousand worms, pierced through everywhere with cares.'
As Aristotle says, book 8: they have a sense of smell, as bees also do; for they hate everything foul-smelling.
It signifies the discretion of the saints, by which they flee from everything unlawful, 2 Peter 1: 'fleeing the corruption of that concupiscence which is in the world.'
Gregory, in the Dialogues: 'holy men have this property: that, so as to be far from what is unlawful, they often cut themselves off even from what is lawful.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As Pliny says, book 8: their eggs are medicinal in many cases, and even they themselves, devoured by sick bears, heal them.
It signifies that whatever is in holy men is of profit to the spiritually weak, toward their salvation, Matthew 5: 'you are the salt of the earth. You are the light of the world.'
2 Timothy 3: 'that the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work.'
'I am made all things to all men, that I might save all.'
The ant-lion has these conditions.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is both ant and lion.

It signifies an evangelical man who is humble in his own estimation, but magnanimous and manly in overthrowing his enemies and purging out vices, 1 Maccabees 3: 'he was made like a lion in his works, and like a lion's whelp roaring for his prey.'
...sheep among wolves. Be you therefore wise as serpents, and simple as doves. But beware of men.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a small animal, troublesome to ants; for, secretly entering their storehouses, it eats the ants' grain, and so, by taking away their food, is the cause of the death of the simple ants in the cold.

It signifies the lesser officials of the Church who burden the poor and spare the rich, James 2: 'but you have dishonored the poor man. Doth not God choose the poor? Judgment without mercy shall be to him that has not done mercy.'
It is read of Decius, in the Tripartite History, that he held the poor in hatred, and it went ill for him.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Third, as Isidore says, book 12, it is devoured by other animals, like the ant, nor can it defend itself by its own strength.

It signifies that one who seizes what belongs to others, and does violence to others, is in the end devoured by demons, or by hell, Job 15: 'fire shall devour the tabernacles of those who gladly receive bribes.'
Job 20: 'a fire that is not kindled shall devour him; he shall be afflicted, left in his own tabernacle.'
Griffins have these properties, according to the authorities and natural philosophers.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a feathered and four-footed animal, born in the Hyperborean mountains.

It signifies the rich of this world, feathered with worldly pride and power, having their affections given over to avarice, vainglory, gluttony, and lust, 1 Timothy, the last chapter: 'for the desire of money is the root of all evils, which some, coveting, have erred from the faith. For they that will become rich fall into temptation, and into the snare of the devil, and into many unprofitable and hurtful desires.'
Augustine, treating that saying, 'make unto you friends,' and so on: 'every rich man is either an unjust man or the heir of an unjust man.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, in every part of the body, except the wings, they are lions; only in their head do they resemble eagles.
They signify a powerful worldly man, glorying and priding himself everywhere in his nobility and his kindred, yet, in some fashion, striving at least to seem to please God and to tend toward him.

Such was Antiochus, 2 Maccabees 9, who, judged by God for the loftiness of his mind and the boasting of his words, when he had come to the very end, said: 'it is right to be subject to God, and that a mortal man should not think himself equal to God.' But this wicked man was praying to a God from whom he was not to obtain mercy.

Gregory, in the Dialogues, of a certain king of the Spains: 'because he did not have the root of piety, and greatly provoked God, though he wished to be converted, he did not deserve to attain to salvation.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: ...they are most fiercely hostile to horses, and tear living men to pieces.
It is so hostile to the horse, as Hugh says, that it snatches it up into the air, together with an armed rider, as the Gloss also says, on Deuteronomy 14.

They signify tyrants who oppress the just and prelates by opportunity, and yet lift them up to eternal things, Wisdom 5: 'these are they whom we had sometime in derision, and for a parable of reproach. We fools esteemed their life madness. Behold how they are numbered among the children of God,' and so on.
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul counted tyrants breathing forth fury as mere gnats.'
Blessed Vincent, to the tyrant Dacian, when he was lifted up on the rack by him: 'I am borne up on high, and, set higher, I look down on the lowest things of the world.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As Isidore says, book 12, chapter 3: they guard the mountains in which there are precious stones, such as emeralds and jaspers, and do not permit them to be taken away from there.

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: They signify the assaults of demons and the pestilent persuasions of wicked men, drawing men back from the counsels of the Gospel and of religious life, in which, as in a state of perfection, are the precious stones of the virtues, of graces, of character, and of the holy Scriptures, Tobit 13: 'all its walls round about shall be of precious stone' — that is, of holy religion, in which regular observance flourishes, according to blessed Bernard, on the Song of Songs, there: 'cursed shall they be who have despised you. But you shall rejoice in your children, since they shall all be blessed and gathered together to the Lord.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As Isidore says, book 12: they have claws so great and so wide that cups are made from them, which are set upon the tables of kings.

They signify, in this, the affectionate lovers of this world and its plunderers, finally destined for food, or devouring, by the devil and his angels, as the obstinate are, Revelation 19: 'come, birds' — that is, demons — 'gather yourselves together to the great supper of God, that you may eat the flesh of kings, and of tribunes, and of mighty men, and of horses, and of them that sit on them.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'by the name of a claw is designated the end of any given thing.'
The he-goat is known to have these conditions, or properties.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is 'a wanton and lustful animal, always burning for mating, whose eyes, from lust, look sideways; whence also it took its name.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For the corners of the eyes are called 'hirci,' as the same author says, in the same place.

It signifies the lustful man, hindered by this from the right and true knowledge of spiritual good and the pursuit of wisdom, Wisdom 1: 'for the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Augustine, On the Spirit and the Soul: 'bodily delight hinders the knowledge of spiritual good.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, its nature 'is so hot that it softens and breaks the adamant stone, which neither fire nor iron can tame, by its own hot blood.'

It signifies the efficacy of the blood of goats and bulls or calves, which sanctifies the unclean to the cleansing of the flesh; how much more shall the blood of Christ cleanse our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God?
O the abundant redemption in God! For it was not a drop of blood, but a flood, that flowed out through the five parts of his body.

The wild goat is so called since it always strives to crop the tops of trees. It signifies a young religious, or another of good disposition, who is eager to attain the wisdom and perfection of the ancient fathers, according to the counsel of the wise man: 'my son, from your youth receive instruction, and even to your grey hairs you shall find wisdom.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Martin, in his Life, that 'from nearly his first years, the sacred infancy of the illustrious boy breathed rather of divine service.'
Fourth, as Aristotle says, book 7, the he-goat begins to breed after one year, and the offspring that is first born is thicker and fatter than what is born afterward.

It signifies a good man who, acting fervently from his youth, begets sons for God in the Church more useful than others do in their old age, 1 Timothy 4: 'let no man despise your youth; but be an example to the faithful, in word, in conduct, in gravity, in chastity.'
An example is found in blessed Bernard, in his Life, who acted so fervently in his youth that he brought his whole noble household to God together with himself.
Fifth, as the same Aristotle says, in the same place: the fatter they are, the less their seed.

It signifies the gluttonous and the sensual, unfit for good examples or edifying speech, Jude 2: 'these are spots in their banquets, feasting together, feeding themselves, clouds without water' — that is, without heavenly grace or teaching.

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: Sixth, as Isaac says, in his Diets: the flesh of he-goats, among all the flesh of cattle, is the worst and hardest, especially when the he-goat is decrepit.
It signifies that carnality in old men is especially to be abhorred and detested, 1 Kings 11: 'and when he was now old, his heart was turned away by women.'
'My soul hates three sorts of persons, and I am greatly grieved at their life: a poor man that is proud, a rich man that is a liar, and an old man that is a fool, and doting.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Seventh, as Pliny says, book 28: Democritus is said to have never been without a fever.
It signifies that the lustful man is never without the fever of carnal desire: 'a hot soul is like a burning fire; it shall not be quenched till it devour something.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke, concerning the fever-companions of Simon: 'lust is more inflaming than fever, and more gravely casts down and inflames.'
Eighth, as Isidore says: its blood, with ivy, wondrously dissolves a stone in the kidneys and the bladder.
It signifies that Christ's passion and the example of his humility dissolve every hardness in affection and in thought, 1 John 1: 'the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin.'
Bernard, On the Passion of Christ: 'you pass through the narrow opening of the passion, that you may offer a wide entrance to the members who follow you.'

Ninth, as the same author says: its burnt horn puts serpents to flight, and heals fistulas and cancers and other ulcerous diseases; it also corrodes and cures polyps. Its liver, too, avails against the bite of a rabid dog. Its gall, too, clears the sight, and corrodes cloth and web. Its urine, too, mixed with gall, removes freckles.

It signifies that the devout and actual remembrance of the passion of all Christ's members hanging on the cross avails, infallibly and universally, for spiritual remedies, Tobit 5: 'take out the entrails of this fish' — that is, chew over and turn again in your mind the bitter condition of the suffering Christ — 'and the heart, and the gall, and the liver' — that is, with what purpose, or desire, with what bitterness, and out of what charity he suffered — 'keep for yourself' — that is, commend to eternal memory; for these things are necessary — supply, for one who wishes to be saved — 'for all spiritual remedies, usefully' — that is, universally and infallibly.
The hedgehog has these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a spiny animal, with rough and sharp spines.

It signifies the rich of this world, affectionate, that is, lovers of riches, hemmed in and surrounded, on account of them, by cares as though by pricking thorns, Luke 8: 'that which fell among thorns, are they who have heard, and, going their way, are choked with the cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and yield no fruit.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: If you wish to see the soul of one who loves gold, you will find it, like a garment gnawed by ten thousand worms, pierced through everywhere, rotting, and full of rust.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it has a hide surrounded on every side by spines, within which it shuts itself, and by which it protects and defends itself.

It signifies quarrelsome men who, when they are rebuked, always excuse themselves with barbed contention; against which, 1 Corinthians 11: 'if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor the Church of God.'
But the servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be mild toward all men.

An example is found in the Dialogues of blessed Gregory, of a young monk of the monastery of Saint Gregory who was incorrigible, and was given over to a dragon to be devoured, but, by the prayers of his brothers, was, by God's mercy, wondrously delivered.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: ...for it climbs into a vine, or another fruit-bearing tree, and pulls off the grapes, and knocks down the fruit; and when the fruit has fallen to the ground, it rolls itself over the fruit, so that it may be pierced on its spines, and so carries food to its young.

It signifies the wisdom and industry of worldly men, gathering and seeking temporal goods for their children with every subtlety and cunning, Luke 16: 'the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light.'
'They are wise to do evils, but to do good they have no knowledge.'
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'woe to the desires of this world, woe again, and woe a third time.'
Fourth, as Aristotle says, book 3, it is proper to it to have little flesh.
It signifies a religious man austere with himself, having little of worldly consolation, 1 Corinthians 4: 'even until this hour we both hunger and thirst, and are naked.'
'We are made poor, but not destitute.'
The Gloss, there, of blessed Ambrose: 'sometimes we come to such need that the necessities of life are lacking, but we are not destitute, since at last God feeds and refreshes us.'

An example is found in blessed Eugenia, who said to Melania, a very wealthy citizen, who invited her with gifts to lust, believing her to be a man: 'let those like you have your riches; it delights us to beg with Christ.'
Fifth, the hedgehog, as Aristotle says, in book 19 of Animals, has a small body and many spines larger than its body.
It signifies those who are great in riches and small in virtues, Haggai 1: 'you have sown much, and brought in little; and he that has earned wages, put them into a bag with holes.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Nepotian: 'the emulation of evils is prone, and those whose virtues you cannot imitate, you quickly imitate in their vices.'
Sixth, as Aristotle sets forth, book 8: the hedgehog knows, fears, and flees the north and south winds; whence it makes a hole to which it flees when it senses such winds are coming.

It signifies a religious man, holy and of austere life by his own will, and providently withdrawing from the devil's temptations and from the favors of the world, and taking refuge in the hole of the crucified one's side, Jeremiah 48: 'leave the cities, and dwell in the rock, you inhabitants of Moab; and be like a dove that makes her nest in the mouth of the hole's edge.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'the remembrance of Christ's passion protects against the temptations of the devil and the assaults of every vice.'
Seventh, as Aristotle says, book 17: it has as many stomachs as it has teeth.

According to the spiritual understanding, it signifies that the devil has as many receptacles for the eternal punishments of the sins incorporated into himself as he has strong wiles for the various vices and desires of such sins, Deuteronomy 25: 'according to the measure of the sin, shall the measure of the stripes be.'
'Render to Babylon according to her works. As much as she has glorified herself, and lived in delicacies, so much torment and sorrow give to her.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis Epistola Augustini ad Orosium contra Priscillianistas et Origenistas

cit.quote: Augustine, to Orosius: 'there are four deaths of the sinner: namely, mortal sin, the most bitter bodily death, the death of the soul in hell, and the continual death of the body after the resurrection.'
The hyrax, which is also called the rock-badger, is found to have these properties, or conditions.
...a small and spiny animal, dwelling in caverns, like the hedgehog.
It signifies the religious: 'the highest hills are a refuge for the harts, the rock for the hyraxes.'

Bernard, in the sermon On the Nativity of Blessed John: 'John leaves the world, knows no parents or homeland, dwells in the wilderness, and fixes his supermental gaze on the summit of the blessed Godhead alone.'
...of camels, the locust and wild honey, John of Judea.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Second, as Pliny relates, book 8, chapter 38: besides and beyond the fruits which it carries fixed on its spines and on its back into the hollows of trees, it always carries one in its mouth.

It signifies an eager gatherer of temporal riches, laboring at it continually with mind and body and tongue alike, and storing it up in a fallible treasury, Ecclesiastes 4: 'considering, I found also another vanity under the sun: there is but one, and he has not a second, no child, nor brother, and yet he ceases not to labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with riches; neither does he reflect, saying: for whom do I labor, and defraud my soul of good things? In this also is vanity, and a most evil vexation.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, in the book On the Duties of Ministers: 'riches lend no support at all toward a blessed life.'

Which the Lord clearly demonstrated in the Gospel, when he said: 'blessed are the poor'; and 'woe to you rich'; and 'that which fell among thorns, are they who, going their way, are choked with the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and yield no fruit.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Third, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 38: when it is hunted, it rolls itself into the shape of a ball, so that it cannot be seized because of its spines. But when it despairs of being able to escape, it emits from itself a maddening and poisonous urine, and that urine first harms itself, if its back or spine is evenly sprinkled with it. For, by such a flow, the little spines of its back are easily plucked out, and so it does not know that it is thereby more easily caught; whence it proposed to harm others more easily.

It signifies those cunning according to the world, helping themselves, even to the last, with malice and sometimes with impatience and injury, yet in the end doing prejudice only to themselves: 'the paths of their steps are entangled, they shall walk in vain, and shall perish.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De diversis questionibus octoginta tribus

cit.quote: Augustine, book 83 Questions: 'the prouder a man is, the more he is made subject to baser things.'
Alas, my daughter, you have deceived me, and you yourself are deceived.

...the hedgehog, if, after it has loaded itself with fruits and grapes, a fruit should fall from its spines, by some chance, out of indignation shakes everything off its back, and, so as to load itself again, is accustomed to return to the tree.

It signifies the many who, on account of anger, lose themselves and many good things, and afterward wish to recover them and cannot, Proverbs 29: 'he that is easily stirred up to indignation, shall be more prone to sin.'
Ecclesiastes 9: 'he that sins in one point, shall lose many good things.'
The young bullock, or heifer, is found to have these properties, or conditions.

For first, as Isidore says, a young bullock, or heifer, is a young cow fit to be subjected to the yoke, for tilling the earth. Or it is called 'iuuencus' because in ancient times it was sacrificed to Jove, as the same author says.

It signifies novices in religious life, young men fit for regular exercises and ready for heavenly devotions, Proverbs 28: 'he that tills his land, shall be satisfied with bread; but he that follows idleness is very foolish.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, in the book On God: 'for holy men, all flesh is an instrument for good work.'

Second, according to the same author, it is a wanton and lustful animal, and therefore it is pressed and restrained by a stronger yoke, and pricked also with a goad, so that it may be more strictly compelled to follow the ox rightly.

It signifies that gentle and dissolute young men are to be tamed and subjected to a stricter discipline, and, by the goad of correction, brought back to the right course of life, Proverbs 13: 'he that spares the rod, hates his son.'
He that loves his son, continues to give him correction, that he may rejoice in his latter end.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De diversis questionibus octoginta tribus

cit.quote: Augustine, book 83 Questions: 'beasts abstain from pleasant things on account of blows; how much more should men.'
Third, according to the same author, it is fattened in the pastures, so that, led to the slaughterhouse, it may be killed for the various uses of men.
It signifies those who are fattened by riches and delights, to their own harm, 1 Timothy, the last chapter: 'they that will become rich fall into temptation, and into the snare of the devil.'
Augustine, treating that saying of Luke: 'every rich man is either an unjust man or the heir of an unjust man.'

bibl.author: Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Timotheum secunda

cit.quote: Fourth, they have flesh better and warmer and more tender and firmer than suckling calves, and this is because they have been weaned from milk. It signifies young men of good disposition in religious life, fit for every good thing and for every advancement in the Church, according to the pattern of the apostle, 2 Timothy 3: 'that the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De diversis questionibus octoginta tribus

cit.quote: Augustine, book 83 Questions: 'better is he who is good by his own will.'
The lion is found to have these 42 properties and conditions, of which 34 are noble and are worthily approved for those in positions of principality, but eight are base, badly used by the noble.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12: 'leon' in Greek, 'rex' in Latin; for it is the king of all beasts.
It signifies Christ made man, ruling in his mind over every kind of the beasts of the earth: 'they shall be at peace with you; and you shall know that your tent has peace.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis Questiones Augustini in Heptateucum

cit.quote: As, in Noah's ark, all the animals were tamed, so, in Christ's body and heart, all movements were pacified.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as Isidore says, in the same place, it has its strength in its chest and its firmness in its head.

So Christ made man had the gathering-together of holy habits in his heart, and the constancy of a holy will in his reason: 'who was predestined the Son of God in power, according to the spirit of sanctification.'
Hugh, and Anselm likewise, in the book Why God Became Man: 'whatever the Son of God has by nature, that assumed man had by grace.'
...to hunters.

So Christ made man, out of a habit of humility, lowered his eyes, so as to confound the proud demons and elated men, and to gain for himself the name of glory, Philippians 2: 'he humbled himself; for which cause God also has exalted him, and has given him a name which is above all names, that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Altogether, because of the gentleness that is preached in you, Jesus, we will run after you, good Jesus, knowing that you do not spurn the poor.
Fourth, as the same Isidore says, when it sleeps, its eyes keep watch.
So Christ made man slept, at times, in body, but continually kept watch in mind, Song of Songs 5: 'I sleep, and my heart wakes.'

He was, indeed, by day teaching in the temple, but by night, going out, he lodged in the mount that is called Olivet. And all the people came early in the morning — that is, hastened at dawn — to him, to hear him.
Fifth, as the same Isidore says, when it walks, it covers its own tracks, lest hunters should find them.

So Christ made man observed, with every caution, that demons or evil thoughts should not detect his secret desires, John 2: 'but Jesus did not trust himself to them, for that he knew all men, and because he needed not that any should give testimony of man, for he knew what was in man.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De divinatione demonum Augustini

cit.quote: Demons, wondrously and invisibly penetrating the hearts of men through certain imagined visions, mingle themselves with their thoughts.
Which is to be understood, not that they know secret thoughts, but that they conjecture them, as the same Augustine states in the second book of the Retractations.
As the same Isidore says, after three days it rouses, with its roar, its cub, born dead, and sleeping.

So Christ, by the power of his divinity, raised, after three days, his own body, sleeping in the tomb, Psalm 3: 'I have slept, and taken my rest; and I have risen up, because the Lord has protected me.'
Pope Leo: 'Christ rose again, his divine power raising him within three days.'
The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered.

Seventh, as the same Isidore says, it cannot become angry against a man without harm to itself; rather, 'it spares the prostrate, and permits captives it meets to return home'; it scarcely, or rarely, or never touches infants, and rages only against women.

So Christ harmed no one, spared all, came to the aid of all, cherished the innocent, and shudders at and punishes the effeminate, Matthew 11: 'come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.'
Exodus 32: 'I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will be clement to him on whom it shall please me. But I will visit this sin of theirs also, in the day of vengeance.'
The Lord is sweet and upright; sweet to the pious, upright to the impious.
Eighth, as Isidore says, it appears most glorious especially in dangers. For it sits in the open fields when it suffers persecution from hunters or dogs, and does not hide itself.

So Christ, in his passion, did not hide himself; rather, he offered himself to those who wished to seize him, and, when he was believed dead and in peril, then, above all, after his resurrection, he appeared glorious, Revelation 1: 'fear not; I am the first and the last, and alive, and was dead; and behold, I am living for ever and ever.'
Augustine, in the sermon On a Single Martyr: 'what strength has the devil against the death of God, who hung the serpent upon the wood?'

Ninth, as Isidore says, it fears nothing but the creaking of wheels and fire, a white cock — on account of a certain stone resembling chalcedony that is within it — likewise its crest and its crowing, and the leopard-snake, a very small animal, poisonous to it above all others, and, when it hears a dog being beaten. So the just man fears nothing but the strife and quarrels of the wicked, and an evil death, which is signified by the creaking of wheels, and hell, which is signified by fire, and Christ preaching the Gospel, signified by the white cock, by reason of the cleanness and virginal chastity signified by the stone of the white cock. He also fears the cock's authority and preaching, signified by its crest and its crowing; likewise the pleasure of the body, signified by the small animal contrary to the lion by its venom.

Likewise, when he hears that others are struck by the just judgment of God in the present life, which is signified by the beating of a dog offending its master, Ecclesiasticus 18: 'a wise man fears in all things, and, in the days of sins, he shall beware of slothfulness.'
The just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread.
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'there was one thing to be dreaded and feared by Paul, namely, offense to God, and nothing else at all. Beyond this, he counted nothing else among sad things.'
As Isidore says, it is ashamed to eat prey that it has caught alone.
So the just man is generous to all with the graces granted to him, 1 Peter 4: 'as every man has received grace, ministering the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'nothing so brings forth the imitation of Christ and of Paul as that a man's good should profit the common good.'
Eleventh, as Pliny says, it is a grateful animal, recognizing and loving one who has done it good.

So the good man is grateful to God, and, for his benefits, recognizes and loves him as his own benefactor, 1 Timothy 1: 'I give thanks to him who has strengthened me, for that he has counted me faithful, putting me in the ministry.'
'By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me has not been void.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis De contemptu mundi Bernardi Morlanensis

cit.quote: As there is no moment in which a man does not partake of God's goodness, so there ought to be no moment in which he does not hold him in memory and thanksgiving.
As Isidore says, it hides itself on the highest mountains, and from there contemplates its prey, which, when it sees, it roars from the greatest height.

So the holy man, like an eagle, gathers himself within, above the mind, and, contemplating from there the food of blessed eternity, or the pastures of the ever-green paradise's everlasting pleasantness, is carried by the greatest desire, and sighs toward them, Job 39: 'does the eagle mount up at your command,' that is, a man translated into the supernal mind, 'and make her nest in high places? She abides among the rocks, and dwells among craggy flints. From thence she looks at her prey, and her eyes behold afar off.'
Chrysostom: 'Paul, confined in prison, dwelt in heaven,' as though he already lived among the very virtues.
Thirteenth, as Isidore says, in every wound it inflicts, even without tooth or tongue, it draws blood.

So the holy man, in every struggle against temptations, puts forward Christ's passion, by whose power he triumphs over his enemies, Lamentations 3: 'remember my poverty, and my transgression, the wormwood and the gall. I will be mindful and remember, and my soul shall languish within me. These things I recall to my mind, and therefore I will hope in God.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Sententiarum libri III Isidori Hispalensis

cit.quote: However much bitterness earthly adversity may bring us, we bear nothing, if we recall how much the gallows drank for us, which invites us to heaven.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'let us render,' and so on.
Fourteenth, as Pliny and Isidore say, other animals are terrified at its voice, and stand still, and it makes a circle around them with its tail, which they dare not cross.

So the holy man, by the thundering of conscience, subjects to reason all brutish and carnal impulses, and, by the voice of prayer, or the power of preaching, terrifies demons and checks their temptations, and, by the insistent perseverance of grace and the final holiness of his life, compels the flesh and the world and the devil to obey him, Proverbs 20: 'as the roaring of a lion, so also is the wrath of a king,' as though it were said: as the lion terrifies all animals by its roar, so he who rules powerfully over the senses subdues them to himself; Proverbs 20: 'the king that sits on the throne of judgment, scatters away all evil by his look.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis De contemptu mundi Bernardi Morlanensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On the Contempt of the World: 'it is not fitting that the handmaid should rule, or the mistress serve.'
Fifteenth, as Isidore says, it always suffers a quartan fever.

So the holy man is always humbled by the condition of his own frailty, and, from the vexations of the world and the assaults of the flesh and the devil, always suffers temptations for the preservation and crowning of his own virtues, James 1: 'blessed is the man that endures temptation, for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life.'
Augustine, in the gloss on the opening of James, 'count it all joy,' and so on: 'it is not the way of the Christian religion for the good to be exalted in temporal things, but rather brought low.'
Sixteenth, as Pliny says, its fat is wholly opposed to poisons, so that whoever is anointed with it does not fear the bites of wild beasts or reptiles.

So the true devotion of holy men toward God, and likewise the consolation, or anointing, of the Holy Spirit, is in no way agreeable to sins and vices, but rather wholly opposed to them, 2 Corinthians, the last chapter: 'for we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On Loving God: 'for holy men, all flesh is an instrument for good work, and is found useful for all things.'
As Isidore says, when it is wounded, by a wondrous discernment it recognizes who first touched it, and, however great the multitude, attacks that striker first.

So the holy man attends to nothing but the tempter, the devil, and, when he perceives that he is somehow being tempted by him, wondrously attacks him, notwithstanding the multitude of other demons aiding the tempter and abetting his temptation toward evil, acting with the greatest care so that never again, over this or that temptation, will the devil or his infernal ministers dare to return to him, Psalm 100: 'in the morning I put to death all the wicked of the land, that I might cut off all the workers of iniquity from the city of the Lord.'
Augustine, and it is found in the Ordinary Gloss: 'in the morning, that is, at the very beginning of the temptation.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Eustochium

cit.quote: Jerome, to Eustochium: 'since it is impossible that the movement of the marrow's heat should not somehow rush into a man's senses, that man is praised, that man is proclaimed blessed, who, as soon as he begins to think, kills the thoughts and dashes them against the rock. But the rock was Christ.'
As Pliny says, its fat, mixed with rose oil, preserves the fairness and brightness of the skin of the face.

So the grace of Jesus Christ, joined to the remembrance of the cross, preserves the brightness of life and the fairness of chastity, or conscience, from the stains of defect and vice, Ephesians 2: 'but God, who is rich in mercy, for his exceeding charity with which he loved us, has quickened us together in Christ, by whose grace you are saved.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: No understanding understands anything without the influence of eternal light.
Nineteenth, as Isidore says, its gall, mixed with water, sharpens the clarity of the eyes. It is also of benefit against epilepsy and falling sickness.

So, for holy men, the bitterness of the suffering Christ, considered like a fish, clarifies the eyes of contemplation upon him, and helps against every carnal or spiritual desire and disease, Tobit 6: 'take out the entrails of this fish' — that is, chew over and subtly consider the suffering Christ — 'and the heart, and the gall, and the liver' — that is, the intention with which he suffered, and the bitterness which he suffered, and the charity in which he suffered — 'keep for yourself' — that is, commend to perpetual memory; for these things are necessary for remedies, usefully — that is, availing for every medicine of salvation.
Twentieth, as Pliny says, its heart, taken in food, cures a quartan fever.

It signifies that the love of Christ's goodness, deeply set within the soul, drives out from the mind the four greater vices of the world, namely pride, avarice, lust, and vainglory, Romans 7: 'for the law of the spirit of life, in Christ Jesus, has delivered me from the law of sin and of death.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, in the book On Loving God: 'nothing is more just, nothing more fruitful, than to love God. The cause of loving God is God himself; but the manner is to love without measure.'
Twenty-first, as Pliny says, its skin drives away hemorrhoids, if one sits upon it.

It signifies that the consideration of Christ's life and of his examples drives away and restrains the abuses of the five senses, if it is carried through to imitation. For hemorrhoids are a flowing of blood from the five veins of the anus.
1 Corinthians 10: 'be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.'
Augustine, in many places: every action of Christ is our instruction.
The merits of Christ have become our own, since they were accomplished in our flesh.
Twenty-second, as Pliny says, an anointing with the fat of its kidneys, and an anointing with its dung, drive off wolves from the man so anointed.

Of this sort, it signifies that the examples of Christ's chastity and humility, once received in deed and rooted in the heart, drive off demons and every enemy from the soul, and give peace, Matthew 11: 'learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet' — that is, of chastity — 'and my burden light' — that is, of holy humility.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De vera religione Augustini

cit.quote: Those who have learned from the Lord to be humble profit more by praying and meditating than by reading and hearing.
Twenty-third, as Pliny says, once it has eaten its fill, it goes two or three days without food.
It signifies a good man content with his own necessity, and requiring nothing more, Proverbs 13: 'the just eats and fills his soul; but the belly of the wicked is never to be filled.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Nepotian: 'born in a poor house and a rustic hut, I who could scarcely satisfy my hunger with millet-bread, now disdain fine wheat flour and honey.'

Twenty-fourth, as Pliny says, the leopard recognizes the mating of the lioness by scent alone, and, when it has caught her, at once punishes her, and rises wholly to the punishment of the adulterer, unless she first washes herself in a living river.

It signifies that the holy man at once discerns and recognizes any defilement of his flesh or soul with the world, and rises up in zeal against it, unless the body voluntarily undergoes punishment, and so purges and washes away the fault with a river of tears, 1 Maccabees 2: 'Phinehas, in his zeal for the law, received the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.'

It is written of blessed Nicholas, in his Life: though from the time of his boyhood he shuddered at the company of women, he nonetheless fled from it as from a kind of plague. The fame of his goodness, too, grew daily, carrying the praise of Nicholas everywhere.
Twenty-fifth, as Pliny says, it lives a very long time, which is shown by the wearing down of its teeth.
It signifies that the holy man perseveres long-sufferingly in what is good, that is, even unto death, Revelation 2: 'be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.'
By the hope of that good toward which you strive, bear whatever befalls you on the way.
Twenty-sixth, according to Aristotle, book 18: it has many fissures in its paws, and therefore produces blind cubs.

It signifies that the holy man has many outreachings of supermental desires toward God, and therefore does his works hidden from the world, as far as his pious intention allows, Ecclesiasticus 24: 'I have stretched out my branches as the terebinth, and my branches are branches of honor and grace.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily On the Treasure of the Gospel: 'let good works be done in the open, in such a way that the intention remains hidden.'
Twenty-seventh, as Aristotle says, in the book cited above: it has serrated teeth, and therefore produces imperfect offspring.

It signifies a powerful man in the world, divided in his household or his charge or his power, and therefore not bringing forth deeds worthy of praise, Luke 11: 'every kingdom divided against itself shall be brought to desolation, and house upon house shall fall.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Commentarii Hieronymi in Evangelium Matthei

cit.quote: As by concord small things grow, so by discord the greatest things collapse.
As Aristotle sets forth, in the book cited above: passing through rougher ground, it draws its claws back within its paw and hides them, lest they be harmed or blunted.

It signifies the holy man of God, who knows how to pass by, by dissembling, at a time when things are displeasing to him, and to attend to and keep the ends of perseverance in what is good, lest he be in any way hindered or delayed from the path he has taken toward his God, Proverbs 12: 'he that dissembles an injury is wise.'
'Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. Be you therefore wise as serpents, and simple as doves.'
Augustine, in his sermons: 'tribulations do indeed burn, but for the good, not unto their consumption, but unto their purging. Tribulation is like a plaster: now it burns you, now it heals you.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Twenty-ninth, as Pliny says, book 8: its tail is the index of its mind, as the ears are for horses. For when it grows angry, it first beats the ground with its tail; then, as its anger grows, it strikes and lashes its own back with it.

It signifies the holy man, always chastising his own flesh out of zeal for God and perseverance, 1 Corinthians 9: 'I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection; lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a reprobate.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily on 'This is my commandment': 'behold, they tame the flesh of God, they strengthen the spirit, they preach their eternal homeland with voice and character.'

Thirtieth, as Avicenna says, book 17, chapter 1: it is an animal eager and gluttonous for food, and therefore devours its food without chewing, and does not cast out its dung except once every two or three days, and that dung is dry, without moisture, and very foul-smelling.

It signifies the belly, according to the world, of those given over to the voracity of gluttony, and therefore called by a certain infamy, Philippians 3: 'whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.'
Bernard, in his sermons: 'the pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the breadth of two fingers.'
Jerome: 'man fell not on account of a haunch of meat, but on account of an apple.'
Thirty-first, as the same Avicenna says, when its belly is opened, an evil humor comes out, and it has a foul and infectious breath.

It signifies a notorious sinner coming to confession, Joshua 7: 'Joshua said to Achan,' that infamous and openly transgressing man: 'my son, confess, and give glory to God, and tell me what you have done; hide it not.' But he said: 'indeed I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel.'
Ambrose, in the sermon for Saint Peter's Chains: 'tears wash away the sin which shame keeps us from confessing with the voice.'

Thirty-second, as Aristotle and Avicenna say: it becomes rabid, like a dog, and then has a deadly and poisonous bite. It is also a cruel and furious animal, beating itself out of indignation, roaring for anger and gnashing its teeth, especially when it is hungry. And, lying in wait for animals passing by so as to seize them, it leaps suddenly upon them as they come out of dens and caves to pasture, and cruelly tears them apart and kills them with claw and tooth. It crushes and breaks their flesh, bones, and hide, and, once broken, devours them piece by piece. And if it should see anyone coming against it, to snatch away the prey it has seized, it embraces its prey, and gnashes its teeth, and beats the ground with its tail. And if the man draws near, it leaps upon him, and, once he is overcome, returns to its prey. It first drinks and licks the blood of the animal it has killed, and then, tearing the rest apart, divides it limb from limb, devours it, and swallows it.

All these things signify the rabidness, the wrath, the fury, the cruelty, and the impiety of the devil and of the tyrants of this world, and of the unbelieving powerful men of the world, and of heretics, toward the souls, or persons, of the poor of Christ and the Christian people, 1 Peter: 'your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour.'
The lion's prey is the wild ass in the wilderness; so too the poor are the pasture of the rich, and so on.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily on 'This is my commandment,' of God: 'the elect of God can be killed, but they cannot be bent.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul counted tyrants and peoples breathing fury as mere gnats.'
Thirty-third, as Aristotle says, book 2, and likewise Avicenna: it always moves its right foot first, and afterward its left.

It signifies that the affection of the just man is moved principally toward divine things, and afterward toward what is necessary for human life, according to the pattern of the Lord, Matthew 6: 'seek first the kingdom of God, and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Celestial Hierarchy: 'the mobility of the angels is always carried about and within divine things.'
Thirty-fourth, as Aristotle says, there: it has a neck that is, as it were, immobile and very rigid.
It signifies the extension and hardness of pride and obstinacy in a powerful worldly man, Job 15: 'he has run against God with his neck erect, and is armed with a fat neck.'
Job 40: 'strength remains in his neck' — that is, obstinacy and hardness.

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Against which, Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'learn modesty from Christ,' and so on.
Thirty-fifth, as Aristotle says, there: it has little marrow in its bones.

It signifies the hypocrite, or the rich man according to the world, who, although he seems to have much outwardly, in substance or in appearance, yet has little, or nothing, within his soul, of the grace of God and saving virtue, Haggai 1: 'you have sown much, and brought in little; and he that has earned wages, put them into a bag with holes.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis De contemptu mundi Bernardi Morlanensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On the Contempt of the World: 'they seek God through these outward things, forsaking their inward parts, in which the inward God is. Therefore one must return from outward things to inward, and from inward things to what is above.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Thirty-sixth, as Pliny says, book 8, its bones are so hard that fire comes out from their collision.

It signifies iron-hard obstinacy in a worldly powerful man, upon whom, once cast out of the present life by death, the fire of hell follows, Job 20: 'he shall flee from the iron weapons, and shall fall upon a bow of brass. A fire that is not kindled shall devour him; he shall be afflicted, left in his own tabernacle.'
Blessed Andrew said to Aegeas the proconsul: 'run for yourself, wretch, while you can, lest you wish it when you cannot. Everlasting destruction awaits you, the straw of an eternal fire.'
Thirty-seventh, as Isidore says: when someone throws a weapon against it and does not touch it, it strikes down the one throwing the weapon, but in no way wounds or harms him.
It signifies a spiritual man who scorns to render evil for evil, Romans 12: 'not rendering evil for evil, but, on the contrary, blessing.'
Jerome, in his letters: there was a philosopher who, though he committed everything else to memory, alone forgot injuries.
Do not remember every injury of your neighbor, and do nothing in the works of injury.
...a claw.

It signifies a religious man helping himself, against hostile assaults, with the strictness of abstinence and the goads of austerity, 2 Corinthians 10: 'for walking in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Francis, in his Life, that he compelled the flesh to serve the spirit outright.
As Aristotle says, it is of the greatest heat.

It signifies a worldly man, greatly given to lust and very much intent on carnality, Ecclesiasticus 23: 'a hot soul is like a burning fire, it will not be satisfied till it devour something. All bread is sweet to a fornicator; he will not be weary till he die.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis Adversus quinque hereses seu Contra quinque hostium genera

cit.quote: Augustine, Against Five Heresies: 'if to pleasure, and pleasure, how shall the lovers of pleasures be able to excuse themselves, so as not to be judged persecutors of Christ? They are guilty of Christ's death, and, if not as its authors, then as despisers of so great a sacrament.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fortieth, as Dioscorides and Pliny say, book 18: since its flesh is excessive in heat, it is harmful to eat.

It signifies that a man excessive in wantonness harms others by his bad example, 1 Corinthians 5: 'it is absolutely heard that there is fornication among you,' and so on; 'purge out therefore the old leaven,' and so on; and it goes before: 'know you not that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Those who burn with zeal for justice most vehemently abhor and pursue every impurity of the flesh.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Forty-first, as Pliny says, book 8: in giving birth, its cub tears its mother's womb, and therefore the lioness does not often give birth, but the longer she lives, the more, through the succession of years, she becomes sterile.

It signifies the affliction that holy men bear, for God and the Church, in making, preserving, and nourishing their spiritual children, Galatians 4: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'
Chrysostom, on Paul: 'as though Paul had begotten the whole world. So he was wholly torn within when he saw converts perishing.'

Forty-second, as Jerome touches on, Judges 16, on that word 'shut up in prison, they made him grind': the lion is caught thus. A double pit is made, one right beside the other. In the second, a cage or chest is placed, which closes easily as soon as it is touched. A lamb or a sheep is placed in the first pit, into which the lion leaps when it is hungry, desiring the little sheep. But seeing that it cannot break out of the pit, it is ashamed at being deceived, and, wishing to enter the second pit so as to hide there out of shame, it falls into the trap, or cage, prepared there, which, after its entry, at once closes and no longer permits it to go out, but it is drawn out, captured and chained, into a cage outside the pit, until it is tamed.

These things signify the cunning devices and the subtle and manifold malices of the devil and his demons for ensnaring the souls of the greater members of the Church, and making them fall from sin to sin, even to their final death: 'the shadows cover his shadow; the willows of the brook shall compass him about. He will swallow up a river, and not wonder; he trusts that the Jordan may run into his mouth.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo, in the sermon On the Circumcision: 'the devil knows to whom he should offer the incitements of lust, to whom he should apply the poison of envy, to whom he should press the enticements of gluttony,' and so on; 'he has very many among them whom he has bound to himself so tightly that he makes use of their wits and their tongues for the deception of others.'
The lioness has, besides those of the lion, these special conditions, or properties.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Aristotle and Pliny say, and Isidore relates, book 12, it is a very lustful beast; for it is always eager for mating.

It signifies wanton and unchaste women; Ecclesiasticus 26 says of a woman of this sort: 'as a thirsty traveler will open his mouth, and drink of any water near him, so shall she sit against every post, and open her quiver against every arrow, till she fail.'
Aphrodisia, who, as is read in the Passion of blessed Agatha, being herself most wicked, had nine daughters most base for the defilement of chaste souls, and of blessed Agatha.
Second, as the same Aristotle and Pliny and Isidore say, it is more cruel than the lion, especially when it has offspring.

It signifies the mind of the greedy rich man, or the usurer, savage and cruel toward the poor, especially when he has heirs, Job 15: 'he has conceived sorrow, and has brought forth iniquity, and his womb prepares deceits.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, in the book On the Duties of Ministers: 'riches lend no support at all toward a blessed life. Which the Lord clearly demonstrated in the Gospel, when he said: blessed are the poor; and woe to you rich, who have your consolation here.'
Third, as the same Aristotle and Pliny and Isidore say, it exposes itself to death for its young, and does not fear the hunters' spears in their defense.
It signifies a good prelate in the Church who, for the salvation of his subjects, or spiritual children, and for the defense —
— of the Church's liberty and of his evangelical sheep, exposes himself to death, John 10: 'the good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.'
Ecclesiasticus 4: 'strive for justice for your soul, and contend even unto death for justice, and God will fight for you against your enemies.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Nothing pleases God so much as zeal for souls and their salvation.
Fourth, as Pliny and Aristotle say, its young are born unformed, and at first small in size, like weasels.

It signifies that the Church renders her children despised, in outward humility, at the beginning of their conversion, but, as they progress, causes them to advance in shining virtues, 1 Corinthians 4: 'we are fools for Christ's sake, but you are wise in Christ.'
We are humbled, but not cast down.

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Francis, in his Life, that at the time of his conversion he was first founded in the humility of Christ, and so conceived the spirit of evangelical holiness.

Fifth, as Aristotle and Pliny and Isidore say, it produces more young the first time, or in the first year, than in the following ones; for, because of the sharpness of her young's claws, her womb is injured, and so she becomes sterile year by year.

It signifies those who are more upright in youth than in old age, or better at the beginning than at the end, Galatians 3: 'are you so foolish, that, whereas you began in the Spirit, you now are made perfect by the flesh?'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Nepotian: 'for the emulation of evils comes more readily to him, and the vices of those whose virtues he cannot attain, he quickly imitates.'
Sixth, out of the heat of her lust, she mates with a leopard, and, so as not to be caught by her own lion, who senses the foul mingling by scent, she at once washes herself in a river.

It signifies the sinful soul which, recognizing that it is befouled by sin and has departed from its eternal bridegroom, runs with tears to penance and is washed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, according to that saying, Psalm 6: 'every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears.'
Ambrose, in the sermon for Saint Peter's Chains: 'tears wash away sin.'
The leopard is proven to have these properties, according to the authorities and natural doctors.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a most savage beast, born of the adultery of the lioness and the panther.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Commentarii Hieronymi in Ezechielem

cit.quote: It signifies the generation of evils, caused by their mother, concupiscence, and by the devil who works upon it, Ezekiel 16: 'your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite'; 'the father is the devil, the mother is evil concupiscence,' according to Jerome, in the original.
...an animal very headlong, and it thirsts for blood.

It signifies a fickle man, excessive in anger: 'do not quarrel with an angry man, and go not into the desert with a bold man; for blood is as nothing in his sight, and where there is no help, he will overthrow you.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De divinis nominibus Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Divine Names: 'the furious, the contentious, and the wrathful seek a peace which they do not know how to find.'
Third, as Aristotle says, the female is more cruel than the male.
It signifies that a woman's anger and malice is worse than a man's, Ecclesiasticus 25: 'all malice is short to the malice of a woman.'
Origen, On the Canaanite Woman: 'woman is the head of sin, a weapon of the devil, the corruption of the ancient law, the expulsion from paradise.'
Fourth, as Isidore says, it has a varied color, like the panther.
It signifies hypocrites and the double-minded, Ecclesiasticus 2: 'woe to the double heart, and to wicked lips, and to the hands that do evil, and to the sinner who goes upon the earth two ways.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'feigned fairness is a doubled iniquity.'

Fifth, as Aristotle says, it pursues its prey by leaping, not by running; and if it does not catch its prey on the third or fourth leap, out of indignation it stops, and, as though defeated, turns back.

It signifies the devil, who tempts souls by assault so as to ensnare them, and who, if he does not succeed after many attacks, withdraws in confusion, and halts his advance, Luke 4: 'and all the temptation being ended, the devil departed from him for a time.'
The Gloss on Tobit, chapter 6: 'the devil stood over the arm of the cross, considering in Christ whether he had any stain of sin, and, knowing that he had none at all, withdrew, utterly cast down.'
Sixth, as Aristotle says, its body, with its tail and feet, resembles the lion's, but in its head it imitates the shape of the panther.

It signifies the hypocrite, or a man made up, showing by every gesture and habit the appearance of an upright man, but never departing, in his intention, from the devil, his head, Jeremiah 4: 'they are wise to do evils, but to do good they have no knowledge.'
The feather of the ostrich is like the feathers of the stork and the hawk; she is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: He whose portion is God ought to care for nothing but God.

It is wondrously hateful to the male lion. Whence, being smaller of body, and fearing the lion, it makes an underground pit with two openings, one through which it enters, the other through which it goes out. This pit, moreover, is very wide at each opening, but narrower in the middle. So, when the lion comes, it at once plunges into the pit, into which the lion, coming after it with force, enters, thinking to triumph over the leopard there. But, on account of the size of its body, it cannot pass freely through the middle of the pit, where it is narrower. The leopard, knowing this, and that the lion is stuck there in the narrow place, at once leaves the pit, and, entering again through the opposite opening, attacks the lion from behind with bites and claws, and so the leopard often obtains victory over the lion by cunning, not by strength.

It signifies that wicked men frequently accomplish by cunning and malice, against the good and upright, and especially against prelates, what they cannot accomplish by power: 'if the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots, you also may be able to do well, when you have learned evil.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: You may see the wicked walking apart, meeting together and sitting side by side, and soon loosening their bold tongues into detestable whispering. One is joined to another, nor does any breath come between them, so great is their lust for detracting or for hearing one who detracts. They enter into familiarities for the sake of cursing, concordant for discord. They contract among themselves the most hostile friendships, and, with an equal affection of shared malignity, a hateful conference is celebrated; this was once carried on between Herod and Pilate, who were made friends on the day of the Lord's death, Luke 23.
Eighth, as Pliny says, when it is sick, it drinks the blood of a wild goat, and so recovers from its ailments.

It signifies that spiritual infirmities are cured by a draught of affectionate devotion to the sprinkling of Christ's blood on the cross, Hebrews 12: 'laying aside every weight, and the sin which surrounds us, let us look toward the author and finisher of faith, Jesus, who, having joy set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame.'
