Ninth, as Aristotle and Avicenna say, when it eats something poisonous, it then seeks out human excrement and eats it. And therefore hunters hang such dung over a tree, and, when the leopard comes to the tree, it leaps up so as to take it, and meanwhile the hunters kill it.

It signifies that demons capture men by riches, which they present to themselves as a comfort for all their needs and infirmities, Luke 8: 'going their way, they are choked with the pleasures and riches of life, and yield no fruit.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, in the book On the Duties of Ministers: 'riches lend no support at all toward a blessed life.'
The hare has these conditions, or properties, according to the common authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The hare, as it were 'levipes' (light-foot), since it runs swiftly.
It signifies a religious man, proceeding toward God with unhindered desire and affection and action, Psalm 118: 'I ran the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Francis, in his Life, that by an ordered progress he came from the lowest things to the highest.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it is a timid and unwarlike animal.
It signifies a religious man fearing God and innocent, or gentle, Proverbs 28: 'blessed is the man that is always fearful; but he that is hardened in mind shall fall into evil.'
Augustine, in the City of God: 'it belongs to the office of the innocent not only to bring evil upon no one, but also to restrain others from sin.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Third, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, its sight is weak, like the other animals that do not close their eyelids when sleeping.

It signifies an evangelical man, walking simply and without curiosity about the deeds of others, according to that pattern, Ecclesiasticus 11: 'about the thing that concerns you not, never contend, and sit not in the judgment of sinners, my son, lest your acts be manifold.'
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'a curious race of men, eager to know the life of others, slothful to know their own.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fourth, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, its hearing is best, above all, when its ears are raised. For it has very long and flexible ears, with which it defends its eyes from the harassment of gnats and flies.

It signifies attentive hearers of holy teaching, whose persevering listening defends them against the temptations of demons and the harassments of carnal pleasures, Proverbs 8: 'blessed is the man that hears me, and that watches daily at my gates.'
He that shall hear me shall rest without terror, and shall enjoy abundance, the fear of evils being removed.
The words of Scripture are more powerful than any songs of enchanters against poison.

Fifth, as Aristotle says, book 3: the hare's feet are hairy underneath, which is more rarely found in other animals. For it has, under its feet, a great shagginess of hair, so that the hairs of its foot may protect the fleshy part from injury, in running over rough ground.

It signifies the affection of a religious man, filled with holy thoughts, by which, in his manner of life, he is protected from evils, Proverbs 21: 'the thoughts of the strong are always in abundance, but every slothful man is always in want.'
It is read of blessed Anthony of the Order of Friars Minor that he committed what he had read so tenaciously to memory that his memory served him in place of books.

Sixth, as the same author says, in the same place: its hind legs are longer than its forelegs. This was necessary for it to lift its body easily in running, when it flees uphill. Whence it is caught with more difficulty going uphill than going downhill. And this happens because of the shortness of its joints.

It signifies a religious man, helping himself, like a roe or a young hart, at every season, and always girding himself with great vigor toward better things, and hastening toward higher things, and fleeing the dangers of the world: 'flee, my beloved, and be like to a roe, and to a young hart, upon the mountains of Bethel.'
Augustine, in the tenth book of the Confessions: 'terrified by my sins, and weighed down by the mass of my misery, I had turned this over in my heart, and had considered flight into solitude.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: ...hares are said to bear young without a mother.

It signifies that religious men have supermental conceptions, without worldly concupiscence, Tobit 4: 'keep God in mind, and beware lest at any time you consent to sin, and neglect the commandments of the Lord our God. And let all your counsels rest in him.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Dominici fundatoris ordinis predicatorum

cit.quote: It is read of blessed Dominic, in his Life, that, giving himself wholly to the pursuit of every perfection, he occupied himself with holy meditations, and devoted himself, without ceasing, to reading and prayer.
Eighth, as the same Pliny says, it is an animal useful both for food and for clothing, and for manifold medicine.

For its rennet avails against poison, its brain against a trembling of the head, its blood soothes pain in the eyes, and, as Aristotle says, rennet is not found in any animal in both jaws except in the hare.
And the older its rennet is, the better, as Pliny says.

bibl.author: Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Timotheum secunda

cit.quote: These things signify that whatever is in a good religious is useful to the Church and to fraternal edification, according to the pattern of the apostle, 2 Timothy 3: 'that the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, in the book On Loving God: 'for holy men, all flesh is an instrument for good work.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris
Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The lynx, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 39, and Isidore, book 12, is first so named because it is placed in the kind and number of wolves.
It signifies the hypocrite or the heretic, named wolves in the Gospel, Matthew 7: 'beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly are ravening wolves.'
For the heretic in a parish, the hypocrite in a household, are wolves in the flock; and so rightly to be guarded against.

Second, as the same Pliny and Isidore say, it is a beast like the wolf, having its back marked with spots. It signifies that the hypocrite or the heretic is made like the devil, full of vices and sins, and marked with stains, Proverbs 6: 'an apostate man, an unprofitable man, walks with a perverse mouth,' contriving evil with a perverse heart.
Men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith, going forward to worse, erring, and sending others into error.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'feigned fairness is not fairness, but a doubled iniquity.'
Dionysius, in his answer to the Architect: 'he sins doubly who, after sinning, justifies himself.'
Third, as the same Pliny and Isidore say, it sees most keenly.
It signifies the hypocrite or the heretic, judging good men and their deeds, Proverbs 14: 'he that walks in the right way, and fears the Lord, is despised by him that goes by an infamous way.'
Chrysostom, in the sermon for the Beheading of the Baptist: 'Herod, you commit adultery, and John goes to prison.'

As the same Pliny and Isidore say, there, it is of an accursed nature. For, knowing that its urine turns into a precious gem, called 'ligurius,' envying and grieving that it should pass into human use, it hides its voided urine under the earth. But there it hardens into stone all the more quickly, as the two aforesaid authors state.

It signifies a wicked and grudging man, who, seeing that he could do great good to others, both spiritually and temporally, does not wish to, but rather does the contrary; but God always compensates, by another way, for that man's evil will, with the fruit of souls, Ecclesiasticus 14: 'there is no reason in the possessions of a covetous and grasping man, and what shall gold do to an envious man? He that is evil to himself, to whom shall he be good?'
'Cursed be his portion on the earth, and let not his name be celebrated in the streets.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus De copia verborum

cit.quote: Seneca, On the Four Virtues: 'nothing better can be wished for the greedy man than that he should live long.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, in the letter to Paulinus: 'the greedy man lacks as much what he has as what he does not have; to the believer the whole world is a treasury of riches; even the unbeliever wants for a single coin.'

Nothing so brings forth the imitation of Christ and of Paul as that a man's good should profit the common good, and provide more useful things for all. Which the apostle well understood, when he said: 'be imitators of me, as I also am'; and 'be imitators.'
The wolf is known to have these properties, or conditions.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, the wolf, 'lupus,' is so called as it were 'lepos,' since its strength, like that of the lion, is in its feet.
It signifies the devil, the Antichrist, a tyrant, or a robber-man, whose effort and strength is extended chiefly and above all to subverting the outermost and weakest members of the Church.

Whence Mother Church complains of those lost to such wolves, Job 30: 'they have destroyed my feet, and have oppressed me with their paths as with waves. They have marred my paths, they have lain in wait for me, and have prevailed.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: by the name of the wolf is designated any robber, and the devil.
Second, as Isidore says, it is rapacious and eager for blood. For, in the madness of its rapacity, it slaughters whomever it finds.

It signifies the devil, or the greedy man, with excessive voracity and ravenous desire, intent and eager for the death and impoverishment of men, Job 41: 'out of his mouth,' that is, the devil's, or the usurer's, and men of this kind, according to...

Gregory: 'lamps,' that is, burnings toward evil, 'proceed, like torches of fire kindled' — evil desires. 'Out of his nostrils goes forth smoke' — of pride, like a heated and boiling pot. 'His breath,' that is, his instigation, 'kindles coals' — that is, inflames desires in the soul.
If the wolf senses that it has been noticed by a man, it lays aside the boldness of its ferocity.

It signifies that the devil, or his great member, when they perceive that their cunning and their effort to harm are foreknown and discerned, are restrained and tempered from their malice by holy men, and confounded in their wickedness, 2 Corinthians 2: 'for I also, if I have pardoned anything, for your sakes have I done it in the person of Christ, that we be not circumvented by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices.'

Blessed Jerome gives an example, in the Lives of the Fathers, of a certain young man who, having the will to serve God, and perceiving himself drawn back by demons, at once stripped himself and cast away everything, and ran naked to the monastery, confounding the demons.
As Isidore says, wolves mate no more than twelve days in the year; they endure hunger for a long time, and, after long fasts, devour greatly.
They signify greedy hypocrites and double-minded men who, for the sake of the purpose of gaining what they intend, actually withdraw themselves from the pleasures and comforts of the flesh.

But once they have obtained, or achieved, their vows, they run to wantonness and pleasures, and repay and apply to themselves ten times what they abstained from, Matthew 7: 'they come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you shall know them.'

Since, once they have obtained what they intended, as though desperate of not achieving it, they show afterward, by an evil life, what they had before pretended by a feigned purpose and a simulated abstinence.
Fifth, as Aristotle says, book 6, wolves are very fierce at the time of mating, and she-wolves, when they have cubs, are worse still, as female dogs also are.

It signifies the lustful, burning with an evilly inflamed love, and, at the time of such burning and evil inflammation, especially consuming and destroying the inward parts of souls, and greatly harming others by their foul-smelling examples, Ecclesiasticus 23: 'a hot soul is like a burning fire; it will not be quenched till it devour something. All bread is sweet to a fornicator; he will not be satisfied, transgressing even unto the end.'
A fire that devours even to destruction, and roots out all the increase.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: By the name of this fire, consuming all things, rooting out all things, is understood the lust, or wantonness, of the unclean flesh, and the foulness of a defiling wantonness, as the Gloss there also touches on.
Wolves have serrated teeth, and eat flesh more eagerly; nor do they eat herbs except when they are sick, and then they eat only a little, for medicine.

They signify gluttons, eating voraciously, who never know how to restrain themselves from the satieties and pleasures of gluttony unless they are compelled by being overtaken by illness, Philippians 3: 'for many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.'
Bernard, in his letters: 'the pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the breadth of two fingers.'
Aristotle, book 8: when they go out or flee, they carry their young with them, and, when they come out of their dens, they eat and chew oregano, so as to sharpen their teeth.

They signify the devil and the wicked man, raising up their own kind and making them like themselves, and always sharpening and girding themselves for evils, Matthew 23: 'woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you go round about the sea and the land to make one proselyte; and when he is made, you make him the child of hell twofold more than yourselves.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily for the fourth Sunday of Advent: 'from poisonous parents, poisonous children are born.'
As the same Aristotle says, there, the wolf greatly loves to play, and, if it can seize some child, it plays with it at length, and in the end kills it.

It signifies the devil, gladly playing, or rather mocking, offering various delights for a long time to pure souls, and, after long deceptions, spiritually destroying and devouring them, Job 40: 'all the beasts of the field play there.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'the beasts of the field,' that is, of the world, 'are demons, who play there, since, continually flitting through the air, they run about to contentions.'
Ninth, as Homer says, in the book On the Battles and Cunning of Beasts, the wolf is very watchful, and fears fire.
It signifies the devil and every man who is his great member, eager for all evils, and yet fearing the torments of hell's fire, James 2: 'the demons also believe and tremble.'
As a roaring lion, he goes about, seeking whom he may devour.

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: That madness which afflicts men: to thirst for the wormwood of vices, to follow the shipwreck of this world, to bear the misfortune of a slipping life, to endure the divine tyranny of the impious, and not rather to fly to the happiness of the saints and the fellowship of angels.

Tenth, as the author of the Properties says: if a wolf is stoned, it first considers the one throwing the stone, and, if that stone has hurt it, it will kill him. But if it does not hurt it, should it catch him, it will not harm him much, but only a little, and, as though out of anger, lets him go.

It signifies furious and wrathful men, watching those who assail them or their property by word or deed, and avenging themselves, as far as they can, out of affection, remaining, in the end, in the curse of the soul, Ecclesiasticus 27: 'anger and fury are both of them abominable, and the sinful man shall be subject to them.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus De copia verborum

cit.quote: Against which, Seneca, On the Four Virtues: 'the remedy for every sorrow is patience.'
A noble kind of conquering is patience. He conquers who suffers. If you wish to conquer, learn to suffer.

Eleventh, as Aristotle says, book 7, wolves, the older they are, the worse they are, and harm men, since they cannot hunt beasts because of their age; and their fangs are weakened, and their old age is known by their teeth, since these become worn down in old age.

They signify the long life of the perverse, always growing and persevering in malignity, in evil word and evil example, Daniel 13: 'you that are grown old in evil days, now your sins have come, which you have committed formerly.'
'The sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Nepotian: 'the emulation of evils is prone,' and so on.
...the inward parts of wolves are very weak, and easily undergo corruption when they are wounded.

They signify that demons and wicked men are very weak, and of no real power in spiritual and internal things, and are therefore easily overcome and shamefully confuted by holy men, Ecclesiastes 9: 'better is a living dog' — that is, a preacher of the word who is manly and prudent and zealous — 'than a dead lion' — that is, the devil, or any powerful man, deprived by himself of every real power.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'the enemy is weak, who cannot conquer any but the willing.'
His wisdom — that is, the holy man's — has struck down the proud.
...of wolves, of the dog.

They signify, in this, actors and certain others who defame good men when they do not give them what they want, Micah 3: 'they bite with their teeth. And if any man gives not something in their mouth, they sanctify a war against him.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: A cursed tongue strikes charity in all.
Fourteenth, as the same Aristotle says, there, they have great strength in the neck and the head.

They signify the tyrants of this world, showing their power in the loftiness of their pride and the ostentation of worldly dignity, or preeminence, Job 15: 'he has run against God with his neck erect, and is armed with a fat neck. The wicked man is proud all his days, and the number of the years of his tyranny is uncertain.'
Against which, Augustine, to Proba, on praying to God: 'a man's mind is not sound unless it prefers eternal things to temporal ones.'
A very voracious animal, as Aristotle says, book 8, it has its greatest vigor in its mouth, or jaws.
It signifies a man powerful for curses and revilings, and insatiable for money, Psalm 10: 'whose mouth is full of cursing, and of bitterness; their throat is an open sepulcher.'
Augustine, in his sermons: 'while other vices grow old in a man, avarice alone grows young again.'

As Avicenna says, book 7: 'there are some of them that naturally have an appetite for eating fish; and they eat the cheap ones that fishermen cast out from their nets, and, when they find nothing of the fishermen's leavings to eat, go to the nets and tear them apart.'

They signify demons and wicked men lying in wait, in great and small goods, for active men and women given to works of piety and beset by the tribulations of this world, and, when they cannot harm them spiritually, striving, as far as they can, to harm them temporally, Habakkuk 1: 'why, Lord, do you look upon them that do unjust things, and hold your peace when the wicked man devours the man that is more just than himself? And you make men as the fishes of the sea, and as the creeping things that have no ruler.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo, in the sermon On the Circumcision: 'the ancient enemy does not cease to spread the snares of souls, but seeks occasions of harm wherever he sees each one more eagerly occupied. He knows to whom he should apply the heats of lust, to whom he should press the incitements of deceit,' and so on.
Seventeenth, as the Physiologus says, in no month can it bend its neck, except in May, when thunder occurs.

It signifies that the proud man cannot be better humbled and turned back toward God than by the delights of eternal comforts or refreshments, which are represented by the flowers and roses of May, and by the threats of the torments of hell, which are signified by thunder, Ezekiel 2: 'the hand of the Lord was sent to me, in which was a book rolled up; and he spread it before me; and there were written in it lamentations, and a canticle, and woe.'

For the preacher compels souls to enter the Lord's supper, both by the allurements of rewards, and by the threats of torments, Revelation 10: 'and when the seven thunders had uttered their voices, I was about to write; and these seven thunders are nothing else than the universal rebukings of the universal abuses of smell, hearing, taste, touch, sight, movement, and generation, according to the incitements of the seven capital vices.'

Eighteenth, as the same author says, its cunning is such that it does not seize its prey near the place where it nourishes its young, but hunts then from a distance. This it does lest those who seek what was taken from them should, by that means, happen to find the place of its young and take them away.

It signifies the cunning of demons and wicked men who, so as to do more deadly harm, sometimes give peace to their familiars or neighbors, so that they may trust them and not detect their malice, according to that saying, Psalm 27: 'who speak peace with their neighbor, but evils are in their hearts.'
When he shall speak low, do not trust him, for there are seven mischiefs in his heart.
Thus it is said of the devil, that he is a lion and a dragon: a lion for his onslaught, a dragon for his ambushes.

Nineteenth, as the same author says, when it goes by night to a sheepfold for the sake of prey, so that its dogs may not sense the smell, it goes against the wind; and if, by some chance, its foot, in treading on something, has made a noise, it punishes that very foot with a dire bite.
It signifies the devil, and every wicked man, fearing and being wary of holy men, zealots for souls, when they wish to destroy other simple ones from the Church.

And when something happens to them, through incaution, by which they are detected, they greatly reprove and afflict themselves, Psalm 10: 'he lies in wait in secret, like a lion in his den. He lies in wait, that he may catch the poor man; to catch the poor man, while he draws him to himself.'
Do you wish to know the gifts of God? The garments of Paul were a terror to demons.
Twentieth, as Solinus says, its eyes shine at night like lamps.

It signifies that the devil, and every strong member of his, exercises his subtlety and cunning above all in the darkness of malice and error, Luke 22: 'but this is your hour, and the power of darkness.'
Every one that does evil hates the light, and comes not to the light, that his works may not be reproved.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De divinatione demonum Augustini

cit.quote: Demons, by the subtlety of their knowledge, or the sharpness of their perception, by the swiftness of their movement, by long experience, sometimes learn men's dispositions, not only when spoken aloud but even when only conceived in the mind — understand this only as a kind of conjecture — with wondrous ease, for the most part; they even receive the power to send diseases, and, by corrupting the very air, to make it diseased; they can also, if it is permitted, penetrate the bodies of men who do not turn themselves away.
Twenty-first, as the same Solinus says, it carries, in its tail, an appearance that excites love, which it tears out with its teeth when it fears being caught.

It signifies that the devil and his members always show, at the end of their temptations and actions, strong and fiery desires around the love of worldly things, which nevertheless they sometimes lay aside, especially when they fear being conquered or detected by the saints, 2 Corinthians 11: 'for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. It is no wonder, then, if his ministers also transform themselves as the ministers of justice, whose end shall be according to their works.'
Job 41: 'out of his nostrils goes forth smoke; out of his mouth go forth lamps, like torches of fire kindled. His breath kindles coals.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: since his very suggestion stirs up and inflames desires.
Twenty-second, as the same author says, it fears stones greatly. Whence, if someone strikes two stones together, the wolf loses its boldness, and yields, if the sound of the stones reaches its ears.

It signifies that the devil is terrified at the wounds of Christ, signified in Scripture under the name of stones, once rubbed together in the heart of a devoted man, and by them is cast down, and struck dumb, and utterly destroyed, 1 Kings 17: 'David took the staff which he always had in his hands, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and went forth against the Philistine, and slew him with a sling and a stone.' This David is any holy man who, feeling the Philistine, that is, the devil, rising up against him, takes up the staff of Christ's cross, and chooses for himself five smooth stones from the brook, that is, the five wounds of the crucified one, or of his passion, and goes forth against the devil, and overcomes him.
Origen, in his sermons: 'so great is the power of the diligent meditation on Christ's passion, that, if it is continually held in memory, no desire, no malice of sin or of demons, can overcome it.'
Twenty-third, as the same author says, its cubs are born blind, whom it most tenderly loves and nourishes.

It signifies heretics, making their sons and disciples deprived of the light of truth, and nourishing them most tenderly in every blindness and depravity, 2 Corinthians 4: 'and if our Gospel is also hid, it is hid to them that are lost, in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers, that the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should not shine unto them.'
The Gloss on Matthew 12, on that saying, 'every sin,' and so on: 'heretical depravity casts down into the lowest of all vices.'

...that it may more easily seize goats cropping leaves, it hides itself, lurking beneath leaves and grasses; and it deceives sheep more by cunning than by power. And if it should sometimes prevail, if it is permitted, it strangles and kills the whole flock, and buries and hides underground the part of the prey it cannot devour, and, when it is hungry, runs back to it.
It infects, with its bite, the sheep it kills, and, as Isidore says, a garment made from such wool becomes very full of lice.

These things signify the manifold malice of demons and wicked men, striving for the death and infection of souls, and for a singular, private love, and for their universal corruption, Ecclesiasticus 11: 'beware of the pestilent man, for he devises evils, lest perhaps he bring upon you a perpetual disgrace. Receive a stranger in, and he shall turn you aside into a whirlwind, and shall estrange you from your own family.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Commentarii Hieronymi in Evangelium Matthei

cit.quote: Jerome, on Matthew: 'we ought not even to have names in common with unbelievers.'

Twenty-fifth, as Aristotle says, in its whole kind, the nature of wolves is opposed to the nature of sheep, so much so that even a lute-string made from the intestines of a wolf, joined to strings made from the intestines of sheep, destroys and corrupts them, just as an eagle's feather, joined to a dove's feathers, wears them away and corrodes them, if they are left together in one place for a long time, as the same author says.

It signifies that the nature of demons and wicked men, even in the smallest things, is opposed and contrary to, and harmful to, the good, and especially to the simple and humble of the Gospel, Ecclesiasticus 13: 'the wild ass is the lion's prey in the desert; so also the poor are devoured by the rich. What fellowship has a holy man with a dog? Or what good part has the rich man with the poor?'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De divinis nominibus Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Divine Names: 'a multitude of demons is the cause of all evils, both to themselves and to others.'
The mule is discerned to have these properties, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: For first, as Pliny says, book 7, chapter 44, it is born, against nature, of a mare and a donkey.
It signifies the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.
...of donkeys, and their flux is as the flux of horses.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: By the name of the horse is sometimes understood the slippery life of the wicked, and by the name of the donkey the immoderate wantonness of lust.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Second, as the same Pliny says, there, it is a sterile animal, and yet fit for labor. For nothing is generated by its seed, because of the excess of coldness dominating within it.
It signifies certain prelates, eunuchs, worn out, or with their testicles removed and their organ cut off, in the church of the Lord.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Regula pastoralis Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Pastoral Rule: 'he who cannot beget children ought not to be set over the Church.'
Third, as Aristotle says, book 7, the more it drinks water, the more its food profits it.

It signifies an eager and diligent hearer of holy Scripture, greatly profiting in spirit and being nourished in the grace of God: 'blessed is the man that hears me, and that watches daily at my gates, and waits at the posts of my door. He that shall find me, shall find life, and shall have salvation from the Lord.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Celestial Hierarchy: 'but you, good child, made divine in divine teaching, be separated from the unclean.'
Fourth, as Aristotle says, book 16, it does not smell the urine of mules, as other beasts with hooves do. For the blood their nature needs comes out with the overflow of the bladder.

It signifies an illegitimate man, good by virtue, not an imitator of his father's or mother's crimes, nor going after their foul and bloody desires, according to the pattern of the wise man, Ecclesiasticus 18: 'a wise man fears in all things, and, in the days of sins, he shall beware of slothfulness. Go not after your lusts, but turn away from your own will. If you give to your soul her desires, she will make you a joy to your enemies.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, On the Duties of Ministers, and in the Decretum: 'not by nature, but by his own conduct, does each man gain dignity for himself.'

bibl.author: Isaac Iudeus De dietis universalibus et particularibus Isaac Israeli

cit.quote: Fifth, according to Isaac, on the donkey: its flesh is worse for nourishment and digestion than the flesh of the donkey.

It signifies that inbred wantonness is more incorrigible and more harmful, and more infamous, in the illegitimate than in others: 'even the colt of a horse shall flee it; and where it did not hope, it shall be caught. And it shall be a disgrace to all, because they have not understood the fear of the Lord.'
The manifold multitude of the wicked shall not be profitable, and the bastard slips shall not take deep root, nor lay any fast foundation.
Sixth, according to the same author, there, and as Dioscorides says: its dung, burned and ground, tempered with vinegar, checks blood and avails against the stings of scorpions.

It signifies that the truly recognized nature of the base condition of the illegitimate, once kindled by the love of God and reconciled by the diligent meditation of Christ's passion, greatly restrains itself from every grave sin and resists the devil in temptations, Ecclesiasticus 13: 'humble yourself to God, and wait for his hands.'
The wisdom of the humbled man shall exalt his head.

bibl.author: Leo Magnus Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo: 'awake, O man, and acknowledge the dignity of your nature, which, though deformed in Adam, has nonetheless been reformed in Christ.'

...it stumbles, and watches cunningly for a chance to harm; on which account it is said, in the proverb, that it is never without a fault. It signifies the heretical man, or the vicious and malignant man, who greatly offend against the truth, in affection and in effect, and are very cunning for harming souls, on which account they are greatly to be guarded against: 'as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith; but they shall proceed no further, for their folly shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: Chrysostom, on Matthew: 'every malice is sometimes confounded by the reason of truth, but is never corrected, especially in those who sin by evil example and evil purpose.'

Eighth, according to universal judgment, it is worth nothing in war or danger, either for fighting or for fleeing. It signifies an effeminate man, of no strength in temptation, or in flight, or in a virtuous withdrawal from vices and sins and the dangers of souls, Hosea 4: 'they conversed with harlots, and offered sacrifice with the effeminate, and the people that does not understand shall be beaten.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke, on the prodigal son: 'what is more distant than to withdraw from oneself, and to have a divorce from the saints, poured over with the heat of worldly wantonness? For he who withdraws from Christ, withdraws from the fountain and the treasure.'
The mouse is known to have these properties, according to the ancient authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, according to Isidore, book 12, it is a tiny animal, named from earth, since it is born from the moisture of the earth. For the mouse is called 'earth,' whence also 'humus' (soil).
It signifies the worldly man, wholly earthly and small in virtue, Isaiah 16: 'her pride, and her arrogance, is more than her strength.'

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore De meditatione Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: Hugh of Saint Victor, in the book On Meditation: 'all have their eye turned outward, toward the appearance of the work, and not inward, toward the profit of virtue. And this is the reason why so few advance.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, its liver grows at the full moon, as certain sea-creatures then grow, which, as the moon wanes, diminish.

It signifies the worldly man in whom, as riches grow, the love of riches grows, together with a defect of virtues and graces, which grows, or is exalted, in prosperity, and fails, or is cast down, in adversity, Deuteronomy 32: 'the beloved grew fat, and kicked; grown fat, thick, and enlarged, he forsook God his maker, and departed from God his savior.'
The poet: 'the love of money grows, as the money itself grows.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Third, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it gnaws and cuts through everything like a saw, and so is called 'sorex.'

It signifies the devil, or the heretic, laying waste all the spiritual things of the soul, Lamentations 1: 'the enemy has put out his hand to all her desirable things; for she has seen the gentiles enter into her sanctuary, of whom you gave commandment that they should not enter into your church.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: He strikes charity in all who hear him, with a cursed tongue, and, as far as it lies in him, thoroughly kills and extinguishes it.

As Aristotle says, book 7: it does not drink; and if it should drink, it would die. This is not accepted by many, especially since it excretes much water. Nevertheless, since truth in a saying is twofold — namely, as to what is said, or as to the purpose for which it is said — the intention of sacred theology, as to conduct, is preserved in these words, as follows.

It signifies a religious man, abstaining, by vow and diligently, from the concupiscence of the flesh and of this world. If it should happen that a man of this kind is put to the proof, he dies in soul, Romans 8: 'if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live; but if you live according to the flesh, you shall die.'
Maximus, bishop, in the sermon On a Single Martyr: 'a holy man would live in vain in the body, if he were to die miserably in the soul.'
Fifth, as the same Aristotle says, it is a gluttonous animal, and is deceived by a modest bit of food, since it is provoked, by the smell, to its taste.

It signifies a young man who, at a modest suggestion of lust, follows the movement of the flesh, and thereby brings about the destruction of his soul, Proverbs 7: 'immediately he follows her as an ox led to be a victim, and as a lamb playing the wanton, and knows not that he is drawn like a fool to bonds, and that it concerns the peril of his soul.'
Against which, Ecclesiasticus 18: 'go not after your lusts, but turn away from your own will.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Nepotian: 'never mix with women.'
As the same author says, its urine is foul-smelling and contagious, and its bite is poisonous; its tail, too, is said to be venomous.

It signifies that detractors, and those who speak wickedly out of the abundance of their heart, are pestilent, harmful, and contagious to others, and that at the end of their words there is always found the venom of sin, Psalm 13: 'their throat is an open sepulcher; with their tongues they have dealt deceitfully; the venom of asps is under their lips.'
Jerome, at the end of the prologue on Joshua: 'we, hastening toward our homeland, ought to pass by, with a deaf ear, the deadly songs of the Sirens.'
Likewise, in the same place, toward the middle: 'for what use is it for us to sweat laboring at hearing or reading, and for others to labor at detracting?'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Seventh, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 28, certain of the more powerful mice gather food in their burrows and hide themselves away in winter. For in autumn, male and female gather ears of grain, and load one another on their bellies, and, holding by the tail, the male drags the female, thus laden, to the burrow. Once she is unloaded and the bundle stored in the cave, they return again to their work. And when a bundle has been gathered, the mouse lays itself on its back, which the female, in turn, loads, and, seizing its tail in her mouth, drags the male to the burrow. And so they carry their burdens, taking turns.

It signifies the avarice and cunning of the rich, and their gains and their danger, Ecclesiastes 5: 'there is also another very grievous evil, which I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the hurt of the owner. For they perish with very great affliction.'

Happy is the alms placed in the poor man's right hand; no slanderer can extort it from me, no envious man can accuse it, no robber can take it away, no thief by night can steal it, no fleeing servant can seize it, but it is always safe, always whole, always secure.
For truly happy is the alms that is always found strong before the sight of God.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Eighth, as Pliny says, book 29, chapter 7: its ash, with honey, dropped into the ears, soothes the pain in them. And if any creature has crept into the ears, the best remedy is to drop into the ears its gall, tempered with warm vinegar.

Its dung, too, according to Dioscorides, ground with vinegar, cleanses baldness, and keeps the head from losing its hair. Ground, too, and taken in a drink with wine, it wondrously loosens the belly. Its fresh skin, too, applied under the heel, brings its wounds to health.

These things signify that wicked men are, in some good and holy respects, useful, and that the lamb is sometimes of use to the wolf, so too the sinner to the just; there too: 'humble yourself to God, and wait for his hands.'
Augustine, in the sermon On a Single Martyr: 'whomever the cunning of Satan has bitten, let him look upon Christ hanging on the wood.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Ninth, as the same Pliny says, book 8, chapter 28, there are certain of the mice called dormice, which sleep for half the year and wake for half.

They signify, in an orderly man, a fit and discreet distribution of time, of action, and of leisure, 1 Timothy 3: 'these things I write to you, son Timothy, that you may know how you ought to behave yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul did nothing idly, but all things openly and with a plan and a reasonable purpose.'
The weasel is known to have these conditions, according to the ancient authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, the weasel, 'mustela,' is so called as it were 'mus longus' (long mouse); for 'telon' in Greek is called 'long' in Latin.
It signifies that the child of earthly things dies at a hundred years, and the sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed.
Augustine, treating that saying of Luke 16, on the mammon of iniquity: 'every rich man is either an unjust man or the heir of an unjust man.'
...its young.
It signifies a man deceitful and cautious toward others in his deeds and dealings, Jeremiah 4: 'they are wise to do evils, but to do good they have no knowledge.'
Ambrose, in the sermon for the Sunday of the Passion: 'every simulation and every duplicity is a lie.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As the same Isidore says, in the same place, it hunts serpents and flees, hates mice and eats them. It lies in wait for sparrows and other birds, and swallows their eggs, as Pliny sets forth.

It signifies a catholic soul, pursuing heretics and fleeing the greedy, detesting and reproving them, and manfully opposing and overcoming demons and their notions, 2 Timothy 3: 'know also this, that in the last days shall come dangerous times. Men shall be lovers of themselves,' and so on. 'Having an appearance indeed of godliness, but denying the power thereof. Now these avoid.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, on Ezekiel: 'nothing pleases God so much as zeal for souls, together with the detestation and reproof of every vice.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fourth, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 22: it heals its young, if by some chance they are injured or dead, with a certain herb; indeed, it is said even to revive them. It eats rue, and smears itself with its juice, and then, undismayed, attacks and kills the basilisk. For it knows the basilisk's den, and, entering it, destroys it.

It signifies a good man perfecting his own imperfections and weak works by the devotion of the Gospel of Christ Jesus, and, by the transformation of his passion, girding himself manfully against the devil, and fighting triumphantly against him: 'neither herb, nor poultice, healed them, but your word, Lord, which heals all things.' Indeed, the earth of blessed Mary brought forth a green herb when she bore a son who causes all the fruits of good work to flourish again, in herself and in others.
Fifth, as the same author says, it is an animal that sleeps much, and grows fat in sleep.

It signifies contemplatives, intent upon eternal life, and, above the mind, devoted to its devotion and sweetness, and refreshing themselves from the heart, Song of Songs 5: 'eat, O friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved. I sleep, and my heart wakes.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Augustine, On the Spirit and the Soul: 'nothing is more excellent, for a blessed life, than to be turned within oneself, and be made a stranger to desires.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As the same Pliny says, book 29, chapter 1: its gall avails against asps.

It signifies that wrath, through zeal, avails in the holy man against demons and heretical plagues and vicious actions, Numbers 25: 'Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, by being zealous with my zeal, has turned away my wrath from the children of Israel.'
Bernard: 'it is fitting to be impatient toward vices.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, On Consideration, to Eugenius: 'shepherds ought to show themselves as Phinehas toward transgressors,' and so on.
...of the asp.

It signifies that not only does a man avail, in his life, for the fruit of salvation and the remedy of every spiritual infirmity, but even his relics do, Acts 17: 'and God worked no small miracles by the hand of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons were brought from his body to the sick, and all diseases departed from them.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'do you wish to know the gifts of God? The garments of Paul were a terror to demons.'
The cat is found to have these properties, according to the ancient authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it sees so keenly that it overcomes the darkness of night with the brightness of its eyes. Whence it comes from the Greek 'cattus,' meaning 'clever,' as the same author says, in the same place.
It signifies the children of darkness, wiser in their generation than the children of light, according to that saying, Luke 16.

bibl.author: Leo Magnus Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo, in the sermon On the Circumcision: 'the devil has certain ones among them whom he has bound to himself so tightly that he makes use of their wits, deceits, arts, and tongues for the fulfillment of his will.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it is an animal of no fixed color, or fur. For now it is white, now black, now tawny, now varied, now even mottled on its feet, its face, and its ears.

It signifies hypocrites and apostates, showing their feigned representations here and there in manifold ways, and in no way fixing or steadying themselves in the truth, Matthew 7: 'beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you shall know them.'
'As Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith, but they shall proceed no further.'
For, as the panther shows itself with its varied colors, so a false man reveals himself, now this way, now that.
Third, as Aristotle and also Pliny say, it has a large mouth, serrated and sharp teeth, and a long, flexible, thin, and slender tongue.
It signifies talkative, or brazen and lying detractors, Psalm 13: 'their throat is an open sepulcher; with their tongues they have dealt deceitfully; the venom of asps is under their lips.'
'They have bent their tongue, as a bow, for lies. An arrow wounding, their tongue; he speaks peace with his friend, and secretly lays snares for him.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'he strikes charity in all, with a cursed tongue, and thoroughly kills and extinguishes it.'

Fourth, as the same Aristotle and Pliny say, it is a very wanton, playful, and petulant animal in its youth, agile and making a rush toward anything that moves near it; and it plays with a stick held out in front of it.

It signifies wanton young men, impetuously following the slipperiness, or wantonness, of the flesh, and every delight offered them, Proverbs 7: 'immediately he follows her as a lamb playing the wanton, and as an ox led to be a victim, and knows not that he is drawn like a fool to bonds, and that it concerns the peril of his soul.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'the prodigal son rightly squandered his inheritance, who, poured over with the heat of worldly wantonness, began to have a divorce from the saints, and, he says, began to be in want.'
Fifth, as the same Aristotle and Pliny say, in old age it is a very heavy and sleepy animal.

It signifies old men who, being young, did not care to advance, and therefore are found lying hidden and torpid in their old age, Ecclesiasticus 25: 'the goods you have not gathered in your youth, how shall you find them in your old age?'
Proverbs 22: 'a young man, according to his way, even when he is old, will not depart from it.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Nepotian: 'a new vessel long retains its smell alike and its flavor.'

As the same Aristotle and Pliny say, it lies in wait for mice with the greatest caution, and, sensing them more by smell than by sight, attacks them and hunts them in hiding. And, once it has caught a mouse, it plays with it; but, the play ended, it is devoured by the cat.

It signifies an evil lord, or temporal bailiff, lying in wait for the substance and life of poor peasants, and, under the appearance of good, impoverishing them and finally reducing them to nothing, Proverbs 28: 'a roaring lion, and a hungry bear, is a wicked prince over the poor people. A prince void of prudence shall oppress many by his power.'
But, as blessed James says, chapter 2: 'judgment without mercy shall be to him that has not done mercy.'
And as blessed Bernard says, in his letters: 'the insolence of the rich is tormented in hell.'

Seventh, as Aristotle and Pliny say, at the time of love a grave battle is fought among cats over their mates, and one is very gravely torn by another with claws and bites, and then a horrendous voice is emitted, when one is provoked by another to mutual combat.

They signify those who fight and quarrel with one another for benefices, James 4: 'from whence are wars and contentions among you? Are they not, from your concupiscences, which war in your members? You covet, and have not; you kill, and envy, and cannot obtain. You contend and war, and you have not, because you ask not. You ask, and receive not, because you ask amiss, that you may consume it on your concupiscences.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Whence such burning ambition of clerics, that they are in no way content with the stipends of the churches they hold?
Eighth, as the same Aristotle and Pliny say, when it falls from a height, it lands on its feet and rights itself, and is scarcely harmed at all by any fall, when it plunges downward.

It signifies the holy man who, falling from the height of some temporal prosperity into the calamity of some tribulation, always and infallibly rights himself upon the affections of eternity, and can never be harmed or cast down from the state of charity, 2 Corinthians 7: 'I am filled with comfort, I exceedingly abound with joy in all our tribulation.'
Paul counted death, and a thousand torments and punishments, as though a children's game, provided only that he might endure something for Christ.
For, confined in prison, he dwelt in heaven.
Ninth, as the same Aristotle and Pliny say, its dung, which it discharges, smells very foul, and so it naturally buries it under the earth, and covers it, hiding it with its feet.
It signifies infamous sinners who always excuse themselves and hide their sins and vices; against which, Psalm 140: 'incline not my heart to evil words, to make excuses in sins.'
He that hides his sins, shall not prosper; but he that shall confess, and forsake them, shall obtain mercy.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia and elsewhere: 'it belongs to good minds to recognize fault even where there is no fault.'
As the same Aristotle and Pliny say, when it has a beautiful coat, it becomes, as it were, wandering, glorying in it. But when its coat is scorched, then it stays hidden.

It signifies those, men or women, who glory and become vain over bodily beauty, and care nothing for inward virtue. And when their inward parts are touched by the man of truth, they blush, the last chapter of Proverbs: 'favor is deceitful, and beauty is vain; the woman that fears the Lord, she shall be praised.'
A golden ring in a swine's snout, a fair woman without discretion.

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore De meditatione Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: The reason why so few advance is this: that all have their eye turned outward, toward the appearance of things, and not inward, toward the profit of virtue.
Its skin, sought for its beauty, is what leads to it being devoured by a certain animal.

It signifies the wicked woman who, for the sake of her adornment, catches and is caught, and in the end is swallowed by hell, or by the devil, Proverbs 7: 'there met him a woman decked out like a harlot, prepared to catch souls.'
Proverbs: 'the lips of a harlot are as a dripping honeycomb, but her end is bitter as wormwood.'
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'if created things please you, praise the Creator in them, and turn your love back to him.'
Woe, Lord, to those who, for the sake of your nods, forsake you, their maker.
The firefly has these properties, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a modest little creature, many-footed and winged, and therefore is sometimes reckoned, out of abundance, among the flying things.

It signifies a humble man, disposed toward many holy desires, always inclined toward the flights of supermental contemplations, Job 5: 'wherefore I will pray to God, and address my speech to him, who sets up the humble on high, and comforts with health those that mourn. Man is born to labor, and the bird to fly.'
It is written of blessed Elizabeth: the more her noble humility submitted itself, the more her humble nobility shone forth.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it shines in the darkness like a candle, especially about its hindquarters; but in full daylight it is deformed and dark.

It signifies a holy man offering, among sinners, radiant examples of light, especially supporting the weak, and, in his whole outward habit, withdrawing from the prosperities of this world, holding them in contempt: 'he was a burning and a shining lamp.'
Bernard: 'John burned within with charity, without with the shining sanctity of his life.'
Isidore, in the same place: it stains the hands of one who touches it.
It signifies an evil man, whose familiarity is pernicious, Ecclesiasticus 13: 'he that touches pitch, shall be defiled with it, and he that communicates with the proud, shall put on pride.'
Seneca: 'the first step to innocence is to hate wicked things.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: ...little birds.

It signifies heretics, apparently shining among the faithful, yet, in truth, opposed to the light of grace and faith, and secretly and hiddenly intent on the teachings and deeds of darkness, and contrary to every faithful and wise person, John 3: 'every one that does evil hates the light, and comes not to the light, that his works may not be reproved.'
Chrysostom: 'the life of the good is a torment to the very worst.'

Fifth, as is found among the wise, and I myself have heard tell of it repeatedly from a great master of theology, a certain other small creature loves it and pursues it; and, once joined to it, the firefly at once loses its splendor and its light forever, and, sensing this, it at once kills that creature joined to it.

It signifies plainly those who lose wisdom and grace on account of lust, yet repent greatly and grieve, and contrive how they may triumph over the tempter, Ecclesiasticus 19: 'wine and women make even the wise fall away, and shall reprove the prudent.'

Blessed Gregory gives an example, in the third book of the Dialogues, of three bishops, at the time of the Arian persecution stirred up in Africa by the Vandals, whose tongues, for preaching and defending the truth and the faith, were cut out at the root, and, after this cutting, they spoke more brilliantly and effectively in defense of the faith; one of whom, having fallen into fornication, at once lost the gift and grace of the word and of the tongue, and was deprived of that office.
Augustine: 'bodily delight hinders the knowledge of spiritual good.'
The wild ass has these properties, according to the philosophers and the ancient authorities.
For first, as Isidore says, it is a wild donkey; for 'onager' is interpreted as 'donkey.'

It signifies a religious man serving the Lord singularly in the deserts, and a religious man continually and willingly bearing burdens, Jeremiah 2: 'a wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of her heart, drew in the wind of her love' — that is, the inspirations and breathings of the grace and consolation of the Holy Spirit.
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is a great and untamed animal, wandering in the deserts.

It signifies a religious man, great in virtue and unconquerable by temptation, Ecclesiasticus 46: 'he was great according to his name, the greatest in the salvation of the elect of God, in fighting down enemies rising up on every side.'

An example is found in blessed Anthony the monk, of whom Jerome relates, in the Lives of the Fathers, that he could never at any time be cast down by demons, so great was his constancy and perseverance and virtue.

Third, as the same Isidore says, single males preside over herds of females, and the males cut off the testicles of newborn males, lest they should gain dominion over the herds of females; and the mothers, guarding against this, hide their young in secret places.

It signifies effeminate and envious prelates, whom Mother Church ought to guard against, lest they should make sons such as they themselves are, that is, incapable of virtue, Isaiah 3: 'I will give children to be their princes, and the effeminate shall rule over them.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, On Consideration: 'shepherds seek the wool, and not the gain of souls.'
Fourth, as Pliny says, being a free animal, it is accustomed to frequent the mountains and the groves.
It signifies a religious man, above the mind, hungering after heavenly things, and abiding in the pleasantness of the eternal pasture, Philippians 3: 'but our conversation is in heaven.'
Chrysostom, on Paul: 'Paul, confined in prison, dwelt in heaven.'
Fifth, according to the same author, though it is in itself an unwarlike and harmless animal, by the sole benefit of flight it overcomes the lion and the wolf in the wilderness.
It signifies a religious man in the deserts, triumphing over the world and the devil, and consequently over them: 'leave the cities, and dwell in the rock. Flee, and let every one save his own soul.'

Gregory, of blessed Benedict, at the beginning of the second book of the Dialogues: 'when he saw many in the world going through the precipices of vices, he withdrew the foot he had, as it were, just set forth, fearing lest, if he should touch anything of that knowledge, he too might afterward go wholly into a monstrous headlong fall.'
...an animal very patient, long awaiting thirst until it finds a drink fit for it.
It signifies the patience of the just, persevering until their desire comes, Romans 8: 'but if we hope for that which we see not, we wait for it with patience.'
I will wait for your salvation, Lord.

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus De copia verborum

cit.quote: The remedy for every sorrow is patience. For, indeed, if you wish to conquer, learn to suffer.

As the Physiologus says, on the twenty-fifth day of March it roars twelve times in the day and as many times in the night, by which roaring the equinox is discerned among the Hebrews. Likewise, each single day and night it roars as many times as the day or night has hours, by which the number of the hours of the day and the night is known throughout the year.

It signifies that the frequency of confession and preaching, in prosperous times as much as in adverse ones, is, in a religious or a prelate, an argument of equanimity of mind, 2 Corinthians 12: 'most gladly will I spend, and be spent myself, for your souls.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Dominici fundatoris ordinis predicatorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Dominic, in his Life, that he gave the day to his neighbors, the night to God, knowing that in the day the Lord commanded his mercy, and in the night his canticle. He had a very firm equality of mind, except when he was moved to compassion and mercy.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis In Hieremiam prophetam Hieronymi

cit.quote: Eighth, as Jerome says, on Jeremiah 14: it is keen and lively of smell. Whence, when it burns with love and does not know where its mate wanders, it climbs a rock and, with nostrils spread wide, draws in the wind, by whose breath it discerns and judges where its mate is.

It signifies the keenness of the good in drawing to themselves the gifts of grace, and the lust of the wicked in drawing to themselves carnal things, Jeremiah 14: 'the wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in the wind like dragons.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'by the name of the wild ass is understood any solitary just man; likewise, one who does everything he desires in vain.'

Ninth, as the same Jerome says, it is accustomed to seek out, with great diligence, on high, grassy mountains, the green herbs it greatly loves, and, when it finds them, it at once roars for joy; and, unless it senses a beast or a man wishing to hunt it, it does not depart from its pasture as long as it finds green grasses.

It signifies a religious man refreshing himself only with the pleasantness of the ever-green paradise, and never departing from such desire, Job 39: 'to whom I have given a house in the wilderness, and his dwellings in the salt country. He looks round about the mountains of his pasture, and seeks out everything that is green.'

Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'my mother and I together touched the region of unfailing abundance, where you feed Israel forever with the food of truth, and we transcended our own minds.'
Tenth, as the same Jerome says, it greatly hates and flees the crowding of men, and greatly loves solitudes and deserts.
A man who hides himself from the wind, and shelters himself from the storm.
Bernard, in the sermon On the Nativity of the Baptist: 'John leaves the world, flees his parents, knows no homeland, and fixes his gaze on God alone, in blessed contemplation.'
The ass-centaur has these properties, or conditions, according to the ancient authorities.

For first, according to the Gloss on Isaiah 9, it is a monstrous animal, begotten of a bull and a she-ass. Whence it is an animal wanton after the manner of the ass, and stiff-necked after the manner of the bull.

It signifies demons, or those subjected to the vices of lust, who, on that account, lift up their neck, when they ought rather to be humbled, Jeremiah 2: 'what have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the river?' — that is, of lustful concupiscence — 'your own wickedness shall reprove you' — that is, your pride and your aversion, that is, your stiff-neckedness, shall rebuke you. 'I planted you a chosen vineyard, all true seed' — of humility. 'How then are you turned to be a degenerate vine' — of election — 'a strange vine?' — that is, estranged from the nature of innocence.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: By the name of the ass-centaurs are designated the carnal and the proud.
The ass-centaur and the hairy one shall cry out, one to another — supply, in hell. The carnal man, that is, the excessively proud and greedy one, shall howl for grief.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Second, as the Physiologus says — with whom Pliny agrees, book 8, chapter 3, though understanding it in another way — it is an animal composed of a human shape and an ass's shape. For from the navel upward it has the figure of a man, and from that point downward it takes on the form of the animal.

It signifies hypocrites, who are carnal in secret, but spiritual in the open, Matthew 23: 'woe to you, hypocrites, who are like to whited sepulchers, which outwardly appear to men beautiful, but within are full of filthiness and dead men's bones.'
Augustine, in his sermons and in many places: 'it has pleased God, at times, to manifest, in certain persons, a hidden wantonness by an open pride.'
The sheep is known to have these properties, or conditions, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a soft, wool-bearing, unarmed flock-animal, placid in temperament, so named from offering, since among the ancients it was placed in sacrifice.

It signifies the subject sheep, fruitful, kind, gracious, dedicated to God, Psalm 99: 'his people, and the sheep of his pasture: go into his gates with praise, into his courts with hymns; give glory to him.'
Pope Leo: 'we are sheep of the Lord's flock, and therefore we are set over the Lord's sheep.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is a fecund animal.
It signifies a good man, always growing in the progress of the virtues, Proverbs 4: 'the path of the just goes forward and increases even to a perfect day.'
Gregory and Bernard, in many places: 'not to advance daily in the way of God is to fall behind.'
A very obedient animal.
It signifies a man obedient to the Gospel and to his prelate: 'my sheep hear my voice, and I give them eternal life, and no man shall pluck them out of my hand.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis De contemptu mundi Bernardi Morlanensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On the Contempt of the World: 'the truly obedient gives up his own,' and so on.
Fourth, as the same Isidore says, it is a most patient animal.
'He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb.'
Bernard, On the Passion of Christ: 'no patience is more perfect than the patience of Christ.'
Fifth, as the same author says, it is a harmless animal.
It signifies a good man, innocent toward his neighbor, according to that saying, Psalm 36: 'keep innocence, and behold equity.'
Augustine, in the City of God: 'it belongs to the office of the innocent not only to bring evil upon no one, but also to restrain others from sin.'
Sixth, as Aristotle says, sheep conceive by drinking water.

They signify the humble and the subject, or the simple, made fruitful by the grace of God through devoted study of the sacred page, Proverbs 5: 'drink water out of your own cistern, and the streams of your own well. Let her be, as the loving hind, and most agreeable fawn, let her breasts inebriate you at all times, and be you delighted continually with her love.'
It is written of blessed Bernard, in his Life, that, by following divine Scripture, he was filled with grace, and, by following grace, was heaped up with heavenly wisdom.
The panther has these properties, or conditions, according to the ancient authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a friend of all animals, except the dragon, which it hates above all. It also rejoices in the company of its own kind, and gives back to it whatever it receives.

It signifies a charitable man, loving all, and sharing with all who bear the image of God the benefits received from God, and shuddering only at the devil and his deeds and members, 1 Thessalonians 2: 'we became little ones in the midst of you, as if a nurse should cherish her children. So, desirous of you, we would gladly have imparted unto you not only the Gospel of God, but also our own souls, because you were become most dear unto us.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is read of blessed Francis, in his Life: 'whom the force of the Creator's love had made a brother to other creatures, marked with his image; it is no wonder if the charity of Christ made him a still closer brother.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is a beast painted over with tiny circles, so that, from the variety of black, white, and tawny spots, its whole hide seems, from outside, covered with eyes.

It signifies a man conforming himself to the character of others, according to the diversity of persons, times, and places, 1 Corinthians 9: 'I became, to the Jews, a Jew; to them that are weak, weak; to them that are under the law, as if I were under the law. I became all things to all men, that I might save all.'

Ambrose, to Augustine, for his mother, who was inquiring, and it is found in a chapter of the Decretum: 'when I am at Rome, I fast on the Sabbath; when I am at Milan, I do not fast on the Sabbath. So too, whatever church you turn to, live according to its customs.'
Whence: 'when you shall be at Rome, live in the Roman manner; when you shall be elsewhere, live as they do there.'

...for when the cubs have grown strong in their mother's womb, and have already gained strength for birth, they hate their mothers, and tear their mother's belly with their claws, as though it resisted their birth; whence the mother, too, gives up her offspring in the pain of her womb.

It signifies Mother Church who, once her children have been completed and formed for the heavenly Father, is sometimes torn and lacerated by them, through heresies and schisms, by which, so afflicted with grief for them, she is almost, if it may be said, unwilling any longer to nourish, or even to conceive, such children: 'for it has been signified to me, my brethren, concerning you, by them that are of the house of Chloe, that there are contentions among you. I beseech you, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you.'

Romans 9: 'I speak the truth in Christ Jesus, I lie not, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sadness and continual sorrow in my heart. For I wished myself to be an anathema from Christ, for my brethren, who are my kinsmen,' and so on.
But above all things, the ruin and deceit of his own household tormented Paul; often he wept, was afflicted, and was thoroughly torn within, when he saw them perishing.

Fourth, as the Physiologus sets forth, in the larger volume: when it has eaten and is sated, it withdraws into a cave and sleeps continually for nearly three days. But, after three days, rising from sleep, it gives forth a cry, and from its mouth comes an aromatic fragrance, sweet beyond measure, on account of whose sweetness all living creatures follow it. But the dragon alone, hearing its voice, flees, terrified with fear, into a cavern, and, unable to bear its fragrance, fails and wastes away within itself; for it counts its fragrance as poison.

It signifies that those who truly partake of the sweetness of the Holy Spirit's grace, and refresh themselves with it, gladly and willingly withdraw from the consolations of the world, and, by this, lie open to the edification of their neighbor, both in life and in teaching and in great renown; and that only the wicked flee, shudder at, and defame their examples and their words, 2 Corinthians 2: 'thanks be to God, who always triumphs us in Christ Jesus, and manifests the odor of his knowledge by us in every place, for we are the good odor of Christ unto God, in them that are saved, and in them that perish. To the one, indeed, the odor of death unto death; but to the others, the odor of life unto life. And for these things, who is so sufficient?'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: He who does not sense your fragrance, Lord Jesus, is either foul-smelling or dead.
Blessed John the Evangelist said to Christ, at his death: 'your fragrance has stirred up in me eternal desires.'

It is also said, in the legend of blessed Nicholas: the fame of his goodness grew daily, which everywhere carried the praise of Nicholas — the powerful naming him from this side, the powerless from that.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fifth, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 18: toward those who help it in something, or concerning something, it is in no way ungrateful.

As the same Pliny gives an example of a certain man who freed the cubs of a panther, fallen into a pit, whom the panther led out of the wilderness, joyful and caressing, so that it easily appeared she was rendering thanks to him.

It signifies those who, serving freely or receiving services, or helping others in need, deserve, in their own time, equal or greater things in return, Colossians 3: 'be grateful. Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis De contemptu mundi Bernardi Morlanensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On the Contempt of the World: 'ingratitude dries up the fountain of piety.'
The panther-leopard is discerned to have these properties, according to our authorities.
A most swift beast, marked with circles of varied color.

It signifies hypocrites, swift to run into evil, deceitful and malicious, double-minded and false, Jeremiah 8: 'they are all turned to their own course; they have laid hold on a lie, and they would not return.'
Jeremiah 13: 'if the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots, you also may be able to do well, when you have learned evil.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, in his exposition on Luke, and elsewhere: 'feigned fairness is not fairness, but a doubled iniquity. Every simulation and duplicity is a lie.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is headlong toward blood.
It signifies hypocrites, swift to the destruction of souls, Proverbs 1: 'they make haste to shed innocent blood.'
Their feet are swift to shed blood.

Chrysostom, in the sermon for the third Sunday in Lent: 'the envious are jealous of the gentle, the wicked lie hidden with hostile rivalry against the mild; the wicked cannot bear to see what is good. O the unspeakable madness of the wicked!'
Aristotle, book 7: when it is sick, it eats human dung for the sake of medicine, and so hunters hang dung from a tree, to which, when it climbs, it is killed by them.
It signifies the greedy man, affectionately sick with a desire for riches, finding as the remedy for his sickness money, or gold, or temporal gain.

Demons, knowing this, make of that very money a bait for themselves, and, as it were, a snare in which they drag him to eternal death, Ecclesiasticus 31: 'many have been ruined by gold, and their destruction was made after its likeness. Gold is a stumbling-block to those who sacrifice to it; woe to those who eagerly follow it, and every fool shall perish by it.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, in the book On the Duties of Ministers: 'riches lend no support at all toward a blessed life,' and so on.
Fourth, as Isidore says, it is a lustful animal; for it mates with the lioness, from whose adultery the leopard is begotten.
It signifies the wolf and the Dionysian lily, secretly staining itself with various things, and others, Ephesians 5: 'for the things that are done by them in secret, it is a shame even to speak of.'
Augustine, in his letters and elsewhere: 'it pleases God, at times, to reveal to others a hidden wantonness through an open pride.'
Fifth, as the Gloss on Hosea 13 says, on that saying, 'I will be to them as a lioness, and as a leopard,' it is a very savage animal when its cubs are snatched from it.

It signifies that the devil, or the heretic, is greatly vexed by the withdrawal of those they have seduced, Hosea 13: 'the iniquity of Ephraim is bound up, his sin is hidden. The sorrows of a woman in labor shall come upon him; he is a son that is not wise.'
An example is found in Aristodemus, of whom is found in the legend of blessed John, of how, and how greatly, he grieved over those converted by blessed John.
The hairy ones have these conditions, or properties, according to our authorities.
They are monsters resembling men, and are called wild men, who are also called satyrs. Papias also says that their form begins from a human shape and ends in a beast-like one.
The Gloss on Isaiah 34 also says that they are apes; for it is a hairy and monstrous beast, imitating the human shape in many respects. All these things come, in the end, to the same thing.
