It signifies worldly men, living only after a worldly fashion, and lacking the dignity of the image of God, and therefore exulting, apart from the kindness of grace and the piety of the Church, together with demons like themselves, Psalm 48: 'man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to senseless beasts, and made like to them.'

An example is found in that holy man of whom blessed Gregory relates, in the Dialogues, that he said to the devil: 'well has it befallen you, wretch,' since, though you wished to raise your throne above the stars of heaven, now you are made like unto mice and cats, and dwell with them.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as Isidore says, book 7, chapter 5, and Papias likewise says this same thing, they are called and are 'incubi.' For they are often shameless toward women, and mate with them, and very often commit and carry out this uncleanness.
Whence demons of this kind are also called Gallic Dusii, or incubi, as Isidore says.

They signify men wholly given over to lust, Romans 1: 'and as they liked not to have God in their knowledge, God delivered them up to a reprobate sense, to do those things which are not convenient, being filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication. And they knew not that they who do such things are worthy of death.'

An example is found in a certain courtier, of whom Gregory relates, in the fourth book of the Dialogues, who incestuously knew a daughter he had received at baptism, and so died. From whose tomb a flame came forth, in the sight of all, and burned his bones for so long that all the surrounding earth was consumed, and the grave remained empty.
Going after strange flesh, they were made an example, suffering the punishment of eternal fire.
2 Peter 2: 'alluring unto themselves the unstable souls,' and so on.
The pygarg, of which is found in Deuteronomy 14, has these conditions, according to the authorities.
For first, as is found in Deuteronomy 14, it is an animal clean for eating.
It signifies a chaste religious man, wholly given to God, and accepted and gracious to angels and saints, Matthew 5: 'blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God.'
Jerome: 'to live in the flesh, apart from the flesh, is not an earthly nature but a heavenly one.'
Bernard: 'blessed is that chastity, God, in which God most delights, in these latter times.'
In the sequence beginning 'The Rod of Jesse': 'but in the house of chastity, chastity perseveres.'
Second, as Isidore says, it is a bearded animal, smaller than the deer, larger than the he-goat.
It signifies what those attending on divine things ought to be, namely, mature and of a middling condition, 1 Timothy 3: 'the saints ought to have a good testimony from them that are without.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Keep such companions as you will not be shamed by their company.
...he-goat, deer.
It signifies the due discretion in a prelate, or in any good man: 'that you may know how you ought to behave yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God.'
Paul did nothing idly, but all things with just cause and reasonable ground.
Fourth, as the same author says, it is a wild animal, of great swiftness, dwelling in the groves and the deserts.

It signifies the Cistercian Order, or also the Carthusian, in which there are austere men, not familiar with others, solicitous for the good of their monasteries, dwellers and inhabitants of forests and groves, Psalm 103: 'the highest hills are a refuge for the harts, the rock for the hyraxes. The birds of the air shall dwell above them; they shall give voice from the midst of the rocks.'

Bernard, in the sermon On the Nativity of the Baptist: 'the infant John leaves the world, knows no homeland, scorns his parents, and fixes his gaze on the summit of the Godhead alone, in contemplation.'
The pygmies have these conditions, or properties, according to the doctors.
For first, as Aristotle says, they are men of half a cubit in stature, or a cubit and a half, as Papias says.
They signify the brevity of the life of the good, and their true humility, Wisdom 4: 'being perfected in a short space, he fulfilled a long time; for his soul pleased God.'

Of the young King Hermenegild, son of the king of the Goths, whom his Arian father, having killed him in the flower of his youth as a most steadfast confessor of Christ, sent to heaven, as Gregory says, in the third book of the Dialogues.
Second, as Papias says, they hold, by day, the mountains in which there are precious stones, to which the ocean lies near.

They signify contemplative men, dwelling in heavenly things, above the mind, in desire, where the holy angels and holy souls are, and having compassion, in the world, for the wicked Christian people, Philippians 3: 'for many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ. But our conversation is in heaven.'
Paul, confined in prison, dwelt in heaven, and more gladly received torments than others snatch up prizes.
...cranes, by whom, armed with iron, they are sometimes defeated.

They signify religious fighting with the weapons of the virtues against temptations and all hostile assaults and the deadly persuasions of men, of whom some, at some time, not perfectly fortified, are overcome by those very temptations.
Wherefore the apostle says: 'put on the armor of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day, and to stand perfect in all things.'
An example is found in the hermit who served God for thirty years, as Jerome sets forth, in the Lives of the Fathers, and who at last succumbed to the devil transformed into a most beautiful woman.
Fourth, they are of perfect age in their third year, and grow old in their seventh, as Brito sets forth, from the authorities.
They signify those who, perfect in the faith of the Trinity, persevere in sevenfold grace, Mark, the last chapter: 'he that shall believe and be baptized shall be saved.'
It is sung of blessed Martin: 'Martin confessed the faith of the Holy Trinity, and received the grace of baptism. For indeed the strength of perseverance proceeds from sevenfold grace.'

Fifth, as is suggested, Ezekiel 27, verse 12: 'moreover, the pygmies also, that were in your towers, hung their quivers on your walls round about; they perfected your beauty.' They are the guards of towers, for the defense against enemies and the making good of the defects of others.

They signify religious, humble in themselves, yet effective for the benefit of the weak and the making good of the defects of prelates and of every rank, 1 Corinthians, the last chapter: 'I rejoice in the presence of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, for that which was wanting on your part, they have supplied. For they have refreshed both my spirit and yours. Know them therefore that are such.'
It is written, and is found in the histories of the Romans and the deeds of the ancients, that among the ancients there was an ordered city in which no one knew his own private feelings.

bibl.author: Valerius Maximus Facta et dicta memorabilia Valerii Maximi

cit.quote: Valerius, book 4, chapter 1, says that a certain man wept for his dead adversary, showing it with his mouth and grieving in his heart, because he had been useful to the commonwealth.
The pig has these meanings, according to the philosophers, or the ancient authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, 'it is called filthy. For it gorges and drowns itself in mud, and smears itself with slime,' and rests in foul-smelling places.
It signifies the lustful and the unclean: 'for that of the true proverb has happened to them: the dog is returned to his vomit, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke, on the prodigal son: 'poured over with the heat of worldly wantonness, the lascivious man begins to have a divorce from the saints.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, they love one another mutually, and recognize one another's voice.

It signifies wicked men cherishing one another, and recognizing one another in their evils, Job 41: 'one will cleave to another, and not so much as any air can come between them, and, once they hold together, they will not be separated.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni
Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: All wicked men are one body of the devil, and tend toward one snare of everlasting torment.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Third, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 51, a pig, once it loses an eye, is quickly extinguished.
It signifies that a man deprived of the light of heavenly wisdom quickly goes to eternal destruction, Baruch 3: 'and because they had not wisdom, they perished, through their folly.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'You are deceived, my son, you are deceived, if you think you can find the knowledge of God among the masters of this world, which only the disciples of Christ, who scorn the world, attain. For it is not reading that teaches this, but anointing; not the letter, but the spirit; not learning, but the exercise of God's commandments.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fourth, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, they are born with teeth.
They signify detractors, from the very beginning of their evil life: 'for their nation was wicked, and their own natural malice.' They were an accursed seed from the beginning.

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: He strikes charity in all, with a cursed tongue, and, as far as it lies in him, kills those who hear him.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fifth, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, it can live up to fifteen or twenty years.

It signifies the brief life of carnal, or wanton men, Job 20: 'as a dream that flies away, he shall not be found; he shall pass as a vision of the night. As a dunghill, he shall be destroyed in the end, and they that had seen him shall say: where is he?'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis De contemptu mundi Bernardi Morlanensis

cit.quote: Why should worms, in the tomb, devour your flesh with precious things? But you do not feed your soul with divine consolations, nor take care to adorn it with good works.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: ...males do not beget beyond their third year.

They signify the worldly man, able to multiply little in power, Psalm 36: 'I have seen the wicked highly exalted, and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon. And I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis De contemptu mundi Bernardi Morlanensis

cit.quote: Consider, man, what you were before your birth, and what you are from your birth to your setting. A sack of dung, food for worms. Why then does man grow proud, whose conception is a fault, whose birth is misery, whose life is a labor, whose death is a certainty? After man comes the worm, and stench, and horror.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Seventh, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, they are subject to many infirmities. When they are sick, too, they lie with their head bent to one side, rolling in the mud. They also lie more on their right side than on their left.

They signify carnal men, surrounded and wrapped up and ensnared by many spiritual infirmities, and turned away from a heavenly purpose, misusing the right hand of worldly prosperity in place of the right hand of eternity, Job 6: 'their paths are entangled; they shall walk in vain, and shall perish. At the time when they shall be scattered, they shall perish; and, as they grow warm, they shall be melted out of their place.'
'Upon my right hand rose up the calamities of the east, they have overthrown my feet, and have oppressed me with their paths as with waves.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: For those to whom all things prosperous succeed, the punishment of eternal damnation is manifest.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Eighth, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, they grow fat in forty days, but more so if, at the beginning of their fattening, they endure a three-day fast.

They signify Christians who, wishing to be fattened and refreshed from heaven in Lent, ought at the beginning willingly take up the three parts of penance, namely contrition, confession, and satisfaction, Joel 2: 'be converted to me with all your heart, in fasting, and in weeping, and in mourning,' and so on. 'Who knows but he will return, and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Ninth, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, once tamed, they learn to seek out their own lodging and home, and are accustomed to return to them, even without a guide, in the evening.
They signify disciples learned in the sacred —

— page, knowing how to live and to dwell with themselves and to gather themselves inward, without an outward teacher: 'coming into my house, I shall repose myself with her; for her conversation has no bitterness, nor her company any tediousness, but joy and gladness.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: 'I judge it the first proof of a well-composed mind to be able to remain with itself, and to dwell with itself.'
As the same author says, in the same place, they grunt going and lying down, and even while they sleep, especially if they are quite fat.

They signify complaining murmurers, drawing the origin of their continual murmuring from temporal happiness, Psalm 72: 'their iniquity has come forth, as it were, from fatness; they have passed into the affection of the heart. They have thought and spoken wickedness; they have spoken iniquity on high.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: You may see the adversaries of truth always speaking under a cloak, and in a murmur.
Eleventh, according to common experience, they are most voracious. For they seem to live only that they may eat, and they break down doors so as to find food quickly, and reach it with roaring.

They signify the gluttonous, wholly given over and enslaved to the voracity of the belly, Philippians 3: 'whose end is destruction; whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, and elsewhere in his sermons: 'the pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the breadth of two fingers, and takes away the knowledge of spiritual things.'
Twelfth, as Pliny says, they sleep more deeply in May than at any other time of the year.

They signify carnal men, more given over to bodily pleasures and self-indulgence in times of prosperity and favorable circumstances than at other times, Wisdom 2: 'let not the flower of the time pass by us. Let us crown ourselves with roses, before they be withered.'
Augustine, treating that saying of Song of Songs 3, 'in my bed,' and so on: 'in the bed of a dissolute mind, if the beloved is sought, he is not found.'
...a pig leaps, or plays, after the eighth month.

bibl.author: Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: It signifies new preachers who presume, before their time, to teach mysteries they have not yet well understood, and likewise parables, Song of Songs 2: 'behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, in the letter to Paulinus: 'I say nothing of those like myself who, if, after secular literature, they come to the sacred Scriptures, and soothe the ears of the people with a polished style, think that whatever they have said is the law of God. Nor do they deign to know what the prophets, what the apostles meant, but fit incongruous testimonies to their own meaning, as though it were a great, rather than a most vicious, kind of teaching, to twist sentences and drag Scripture, resisting it, to one's own meaning.'
As the same Aristotle says, those born in winter are better, and worse those born in summer, and those bred in their youth are of less worth.

They signify that good men are made, through and in tribulations, rather than through delights or in pleasures, and are more excellent when raised by their elders than by the young: 'the furnace tries the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation just men,' Ecclesiasticus 27.
No one chooses young men as leaders, since it is not agreed that they are prudent.
...a pig.

It signifies the wanton man, abounding in delights, not ceasing from pleasures, and especially in his youth, Wisdom 2: 'let no meadow be free from our riot. Let none of us go without his part in luxury; let us everywhere leave tokens of joy, for this is our portion, and this our lot.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bodily delight hinders the knowledge of spiritual good.
As Aristotle says, book 6, when a sow gives birth, she first gives her breast to her firstborn.

It signifies that he who is first called, or begotten, or promoted in the Church ought to be advanced first, and to that same one grace ought first to be divinely granted, Isaiah 43: 'since you became honorable in my eyes, I have loved you'; Isaiah 42: 'behold my servant, I will uphold him; my elect, in whom my soul delights.'
Whence the common proverb has grown up: 'he who is born first, is fed first,' since the Church holds this same manner in her promotions.
As the same Aristotle says, there, when she greatly desires mating, she does not let the male mount her until her little ears droop.

It signifies a young man, ardently desiring a woman who is cautious about being humbled and turned aside, allured and subjugated, and about extorting money, and who is more ardently desired by her, as a victim, like a lamb, or an ox led to sacrifice, Proverbs 7: 'she has entangled him with many words, and drawn him away with the flattery of her lips. Immediately he follows her as an ox led to be a victim, and as a lamb playing the wanton, and knows not that he is drawn like a fool to bonds, and that it concerns the peril of his soul.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, to Nepotian: 'lust also greatly desires and is desired.'
Origen, in the homily On the Canaanite Woman: 'woman is a weapon of the devil, the head of sin, the expulsion from paradise, the corruption of the ancient law.'
Eighteenth, as the same Aristotle says, in the same place, when she greatly desires mating, she does not let the male mount her until her ears droop.

It signifies that the wicked are to be separated from the good, and especially where infection of the whole congregation is feared, 1 Corinthians 5: 'know you not that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? Put away the evil one from among yourselves. For the diseased sheep must be cut off from the multitude, lest it corrupt others by its contagion.'
The louse has these properties, or conditions, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, the skin-worm is so named from the feet; for it harms the skin more by the movement of its feet, being generated from the moist and corrupted vapors settling beneath the skin, in the pores.
It signifies the gnawing of conscience, caused by sins and the corruptions of spirit and flesh, Job 20: 'yet his flesh, while he shall live, shall have sorrow, and his soul shall mourn over itself.'

Anselm, in the Proslogion: 'God will be angry against the sinful man; on the right hand, below, chaos and hell lying open; on the right, sins accusing; on the left, infinite demons dragging him to hell; within, conscience burning; without, the world blazing.' What shall the wretched sinner do? 'to hide will be impossible, to appear will be intolerable.'
Second, as the commentator on Constantine's Viaticum says, lice are of diverse color, sharpness, and size, according to the variety and quantity of the humors.

They signify the variety of evil thoughts and actions, according to the variety and quantity of evil and brutish affections, Jeremiah 3: 'you have played the harlot with many lovers; you have defiled the land with your fornications and your wickedness.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De divinis nominibus Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Divine Names: 'a multitude of demons is the cause of all evils, both to themselves and to others.'
Third, as the same author says, an excessive multitude of them in a body much putrid and corrupted is usually a sign of a general corruption, such as scurvy or leprosy.

They signify that the multiplying of evil thoughts and affections disposes toward mortal and wholly damnable sin, and toward the corruption of supermental habits, Jeremiah 2: 'the children also of Memphis, and of Tahpanhes, have deflowered you, even to the crown of the head. Has not this been done to you because you have forsaken the Lord your God, at that time when he led you by the way? And now what have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink turbid water?'
The Gloss explains that, through the accepted suggestions of the devil and demons, one arrives at the deflowering of the very summit of conscience.
Fourth, as the same author says, against their troublesomeness the frequent washing of the head avails, and combing, and medicinal cleansing.

For, as Constantine says, quicksilver with willow-ash kills them, if they are generated from a hot humor; the same is done by burnt lead with oil and vinegar. But if they are generated from a cold humor, stavesacre avails, and orpiment with oil and vinegar; likewise sea-water and brine with vinegar.

These things signify that, against the labyrinths of the gnawings of conscience, above all things avail penance and frequent confession, and, here and there, frequent remembrance of the Lord's passion and death, and consideration of divine mercy and kindness, and the intercession of blessed Mary and the angels and the saints, Ecclesiasticus 17: 'confess while you are living; whilst you live and are in health you shall confess, and shall praise God. For confession, from the dead, is as nothing.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Homilie 'super missus est' sive In laudibus Virginis matris Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard: 'in dangers, in doubts, in difficult matters, think of Mary, call upon Mary.'
Fifth, as Isidore says, every louse bites the more sharply, the more it withers away.

It signifies the greedy man, who then presses most sharply upon whomever he can, when he sees he can better provide for himself and his greed, Ecclesiasticus: 'the bread of the needy is the life of the poor; he that defrauds him is a man of blood. He that takes away the bread gotten by sweat, is like him that kills his neighbor.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: Jerome, in the letter to Paulinus: 'to the believer the whole world is a treasury of riches; but the unbeliever wants for a single coin.'
The flea has these properties, or conditions, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a modest worm, most troublesome and hostile to men, named from dust, since it makes the greatest use of dust.

It signifies every malignant spirit and quarrelsome man, intent on vanity alone, and acting for it as he can, and as much as he can, Ecclesiasticus 20: 'there is one that is hindered from sinning through poverty, and in his rest he shall be pricked.'
Dust is the serpent's bread.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is a little worm of wondrous lightness, escaping and fleeing dangers not by running but by leaping.

It signifies a humble man who knows how to redeem his evil times, not by power, but by wisdom, or holy cunning, Ephesians 5: 'see how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.'
Days are called good oxen when men are good and their deeds good; they are called bad oxen when men are bad and their deeds bad.
Isidore: in cold weather it grows sluggish and weak, but in the summer it grows bold.
It signifies a man who does not let up from doing evil and harming others except when he cannot, Ecclesiasticus 19: 'there is one that humbles himself wickedly, and his interior is full of deceit.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'those are pernicious in company who observe others only when they can do them harm.'

Fourth, as the same Isidore says, although it is not among the living things that reproduce by manifest mating, it nevertheless multiplies its kind by laying eggs. For it begets in itself certain eggs, from whose emission a single flea produces many.
It signifies that many evils arise and follow from one, Romans 5: 'for by the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam
Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: One disorder is followed by many disorders.
Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it is naturally white, but is suddenly changed into blackness.

It signifies those who are first chaste and clean from childhood, but afterward become infamous and unclean in old age, Galatians 3: 'are you so foolish, that, whereas you began in the Spirit, you now are made perfect by the flesh?'

For the soul is a widow, which, widowed of her heavenly bridegroom, does not act well, becoming useless, serving the desires of the flesh, and not attending to her salvation in the cultivation of virtues.

As the same Isidore says, it desires blood, and, boring and piercing the flesh where it strikes, sucks the more liquid part of the moisture beneath the skin, and, by sucking, leaves a reddish mark on the part of the body it strikes.

It signifies detractors and defamers of others, infecting, as far as they can, the inward goodness in their neighbors, and leaving evil traces everywhere, Ecclesiasticus: 'for he turns good into evil, and lies in wait, and shall put a stain upon the elect.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: He strikes charity in all, with a cursed tongue, and, as far as it lies in him, thoroughly kills and extinguishes it.
With a sharp bite, Isidore.
It signifies that the wicked disturb religious and contemplative men, and others who wish to serve God.
2 Peter: 'bold, self-willed, they fear not to bring in sects, blaspheming.'
An example is found in the wicked priest who disturbed blessed Benedict and his disciples, as Gregory relates, in the second book of the Dialogues.

Wormwood is a poison to it; likewise the leaves of the peach tree, as Constantine says. Colocynth also avails against them, ground and mixed with water, if sprinkled about in the places where they abound. Likewise the leaves of wormwood, by whose smell and taste they are said to die.
These things signify that canonical correction is deadly to the wicked, and that discreet correction represses the insolent, Proverbs 13: 'he that spares the rod, hates his son.'

Likewise they signify that the bitterness, or the remembrance and invocation, of Christ's passion is the safest remedy against the insolence of hostile temptations and the goads of demons, Lamentations 3: 'remember my poverty, and my transgression, the wormwood and the gall. I will be mindful and remember, and my soul shall languish within me.'
Whomever the cunning of Satan has bitten, let him look upon Christ hanging on the wood.

Ninth, as is clear by experience, on account of the swiftness of its leaping it is not easily caught. In hot weather, and when the weather is rainy, it bites more sharply. It signifies that demons and wicked men are not easily caught in their frauds and cunning by their own subtlety, and that they above all strive to do harm in adversities, 2 Corinthians 2: 'let us not be circumvented by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices.'
Thus it is said of the devil, that he is a lion and a dragon: a lion, for his onslaught; a dragon, for his ambushes.
The rhinoceros, the unicorn, which is the same thing, is found to have these properties.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a most savage beast, so called because it has one horn in the middle of its forehead, great, sharp, and strong, so that whatever it attacks it either tosses or pierces through.

It signifies Christ, growing strong in Paul, in zeal, or confounding the great and all the other Jews, Deuteronomy 33: 'his beauty as of the firstling of a bullock, his horns as the horns of a rhinoceros.'
But Saul increased much more in strength, and confounded the Jews, affirming that this is the Christ.

Chrysostom, in the book On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul suffered not even one day to pass idly and quietly, but, in the ardor of preaching, more vehement than fire itself, as he ascended from the saving fountain, he kindled the greatest flame within himself. Always girded for battle, and breathing a certain fire of war.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As the same Isidore says, in the same place: 'it is of such strength that it can be caught by no art of hunters, but, as is asserted, a virgin girl is set before it, who opens her lap to it as it comes, in which, laying aside all its ferocity, it lays its head. And so, lulled to sleep, as though disarmed, it is caught and killed with spears.'

It signifies the Son of God, most strong in majesty, humbly reclined only in the blessed Virgin, and thus afterward exposed to the death of the cross, Numbers 24: 'God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like to the rhinoceros. He shall lie down as a lion, and as a lioness, whom none shall dare to rouse.'
Ambrose: he entered into the womb of the Virgin, that he might appear visible to us, and went out through a closed gate, light and life, God and man, creator of the world.
Likewise, Ambrose, in the hymn On the Passion of Christ: 'the gentle body is pierced through, blood flows in a wave, the earth, the sea, the stars, the world, are washed by this stream.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: It is the greatest enemy of the elephant. For, always waging combat against it, it rubs and sharpens its single horn against the rocks, and so strikes the elephant's belly, which it knows to be the softer part of its body.

In this respect it signifies the devil, the chief enemy of a holy and great man in virtues, against whom he always girds himself, and, for his spiritual destruction, wherever he perceives him to be weaker, attacks and assails him with force.
Which was signified, 2 Kings 12: 'Joab therefore fought against Rabbah, of the children of Ammon, and stormed the royal city.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo, in the sermon On the Circumcision: 'for the ancient enemy does not cease to spread everywhere the snares of deception, and to press on, so that by whatever means he may corrupt the faith of believers. He has many among them whom he has bound to himself so tightly that he makes use of their wits and their tongues for the deception of others. He knows whom to deceive with joy, whom to trouble with sorrow, and there he seeks occasions of harm where he sees each one more eagerly occupied.' Thus far Pope Leo.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Fourth, as Gregory says, in the Moralia: it is a beast of an untamed nature, and, if it is somehow captured — supply, except when sleeping in a virgin's lap, as was set forth above — it can in no way be kept, and, impatient, as is said, it dies at once.

It signifies pestilent men, untamable and incorrigible, and most impatient and despairing of correction, Ecclesiasticus 31: 'an unbroken horse becomes stubborn, and a child left to himself becomes headstrong.'
Ephesians 4: 'who, despairing, have given themselves up to lasciviousness, unto the working of all uncleanness, unto covetousness.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Every proud man is utterly unbearable; his manner of dress is excessive, his gait pompous, his neck stiff, he strives from a loftier place, and desires to be preferred to his betters; he boasts of his own opinions and his own deeds, and keeps no reverence in his service.
Frogs have these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, chapter 3, among fish it is so named from the garrulity of its voice, since it makes a din, and gives back sounds of its voice with importunate cries, in the marshy places where it is generated.
It signifies swarming sophists and advocates; and this same thing is found in the mystery of Exodus 8: 'and the frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt.'
Origen, on Exodus, and it is found in the first part of the Decretum: 'by the name of the frogs are rightly understood the garrulities of the dialecticians.'
Second, as Aristotle says, book 4, it has its own tongue, or voice, and cries out, especially at the time of mating.

It signifies advocates who use their own, or invented, eloquence for the sake of subversion, and above all cry out for the hope of money or wantonness, Ecclesiasticus 21: 'the knowledge of a fool is words that cannot be numbered.'
Ecclesiasticus 31: 'he that loves gold shall not be justified'; Ecclesiasticus 19: 'wine and women make even the wise fall away, and shall reprove the prudent.'
Third, its eyes, at night, by the effort of stretching its jaws, shine like candles.

It signifies wicked men who, by a certain violence, not by grace, sometimes appear shining in their deeds, 2 Corinthians 6: 'what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what part has the faithful with the unbeliever? What agreement has Christ with Belial?' For a wolf is often clothed in a sheep's skin, when a double-minded man puts forward a dove-like simplicity, and, deceitfully wicked, displays innocence in his outward habit.
A soul quite pure is often accustomed to lie hidden beneath a skin.
Fourth, as Aristotle says, book 8, all little water-creatures, or fish, nourish their young, except the frog.
It signifies the wicked against their subjects, Job 39: 'she is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'bring forth the breasts, hold back the blows.'

Fifth, as the author says, and is proven by common experience, it is abominable to men and greatly hateful, on account of its garrulity, its venomousness, and its apparent disagreeableness and impudence.

It signifies carnal men and heretics, whom it would call those passing by the way and going on their journey, and it did not know that giants were there, and that the banquets of hell were in its depths.
The Ordinary Gloss explains this of heretical depravity.
Sixth, as the same authors say, and it is proven by experience, it lives equally on land and in water.
It signifies hypocrites and the double-minded, Ecclesiasticus 2: 'woe to the double heart, and to wicked lips, and to the hands that do evil, and to the sinner who goes upon the earth two ways.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke, and elsewhere: 'feigned fairness is not fairness, but a doubled iniquity.'

Seventh, as the same authors say, and it is proven by experience, when frogs are first formed, they seem to consist wholly of a head, with a certain tapering end hanging down like a tail. Then they widen in the belly, and, once the tail is entirely lost, feet grow on them, and they are transformed into a four-footed animal.

They signify demons and the wicked, 2 Corinthians 11: 'and no wonder, for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing, if his ministers be transformed as the ministers of justice.'
Ambrose, in the sermon for the Sunday of the Passion: 'every simulation and every duplicity is a lie.'
The salamander is found to have these properties, or conditions.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: For first, as Pliny says, book 12, chapter 48, it is like a lizard in shape. It never appears except in great rains; it fails, however, in clear weather.

It signifies hypocrites and false brothers, or wicked men, really and truly having such faces, or representations, and exercising their malice above all in the adversities of good men or of troubled churches, but withdrawing themselves in the prosperity of those same men and those same churches, Proverbs 26: 'as if one should set silver dross to adorn an earthen vessel, so are proud lips joined to a wicked heart. When he shall speak low, do not trust him, for there are seven mischiefs in his heart. He that covers hatred deceitfully, his malice shall be laid open in the public assembly.'
Chrysostom, on Paul: 'but above all things, the ruin and deceit of his own household tormented Paul.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Second, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, its coldness is so great that it puts out fire with its touch, like ice.
It signifies a holy man whose rigidity of life extinguishes the desire of carnal pleasure, 2 Corinthians 10: 'for walking in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis De assumptione sancte Marie Virginis Paschasii Radberti

cit.quote: Jerome, in the sermon On the Assumption of Blessed Mary: 'to live in the flesh, apart from the flesh, is indeed not an earthly life, but a heavenly one.'

Third, as the same Pliny says, it vomits from its mouth a milky matter, which, if it touches a man's body, causes his hairs to fall out daily, and whatever it touches becomes corrupted and changes into an ugly color.
It signifies a false man, or a hypocrite, who, under a pretense of good, seduces and progressively corrupts others, both by word and by example: 'evil communications corrupt good manners.'
For they spread much toward ungodliness, and their speech creeps like a cancer.

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'you see how great a multitude of souls a swiftly running speech of such great malice can infect!'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fourth, as Pliny says, book 29, chapter 3, it is a pestilent and supremely poisonous animal. For it infects the fruits of trees, corrupts waters, of which, if anyone eats or drinks, he is soon killed. But even if its spittle touches a foot, it infects and corrupts the whole man. And though the strength of its poison is so great, yet it is eaten by certain animals in place of food.

It signifies the plague and universal poisoning of heretics and schismatics, and at last their everlasting destruction by demons, 2 Timothy 3: 'as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith; but they shall proceed no further, for their folly shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Gregory, on that saying of Song of Songs 2, 'catch us,' and so on: 'this ought to be the praiseworthy care of prelates, that they catch the little foxes.'
Fifth, as the same Pliny says, alone among animals it lives amid the very fires.

It signifies those who, placed in tribulation, Ecclesiastes 8: 'there are wicked men who are so secure, as though they had the deeds of the just.' And again, there: 'a just man perishes in his justice, and a wicked man lives a long time in his wickedness.'
Blessed Andrew used to say, as is written in his Passion: 'the proconsul Aegeas does not fear to go to eternal punishments.'

As the same Pliny says, there is a kind of salamander whose skin is shaggy and hairy, from which belts are sometimes made for the use of kings, which, after long age, when cast into fire, are not burned up, but, after a lengthy burning, are drawn out unharmed and purified, and, as it were, renewed from the fires; and from that skin are made wicks for lamps and lanterns which are corrupted by no fire.

It signifies holy men who, serving the great and the small in the Church, never fail in tribulations, but rather are proven like gold, Wisdom 3: 'afflicted in few things, in many they shall be well rewarded, because God has tried them, and found them worthy of himself. As gold in the furnace he has proved them, and as a victim of a holocaust he has received them.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily on the Gospel 'This is my commandment': 'behold, the chosen of God tame the flesh, strengthen the spirit, command demons, gleam with virtues, despise present things, preach their eternal homeland with voice and character, and reach it through torments. They can be killed, but cannot be bent.'
Blessed Lawrence said to Decius: 'learn, wretch, how great is the power of Christ. For these coals do not burn me, but rather give me refreshment.'
And blessed Vincent said to Dacian, set upon the rack: 'I am borne up on high, and, set higher, I look down on the lowest things of the world.'
The leech has these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a water-worm, so named because it loves and sucks blood.
It signifies that the leech has two daughters, who say: 'bring, bring.'
The leech, according to the doctors, is the greedy and worldly man whose desire and concupiscence always cries out for having riches and obtaining delights.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it lies in wait for those drinking, and when it slips into their throat, or attaches itself anywhere, it draws blood, and, once it has sucked greatly to its fill, it vomits up what it drank, so as to suck fresh blood anew.

It signifies the envious man, lying in wait for neighbors who wickedly gain or advance, and, if he can, usurping and hoarding all their goods, or bestowing them on his own, and so receiving and procuring similar goods anew, Ecclesiasticus 14: 'there is no reason in the possessions of a covetous and grasping man, and what shall gold do to an envious man? He that gathers together, from his own soul, unjustly, gathers for others, and another shall be delighted with his goods.'
Ecclesiastes 5: 'riches kept to the hurt of the owner,' and so on.

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: Chrysostom, on Matthew, homily 47: 'if you wish to see the soul of one who loves gold, you will find it, like a garment gnawed by ten thousand worms, having nothing sound, pierced through everywhere, rotting from cares and sins, and full of rust.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, in the book On the Duties of Ministers: 'riches lend no support at all toward a blessed life, which the Lord clearly demonstrated in the Gospel, saying: blessed are the poor, and woe to you rich.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Third, as Isidore says, in the book cited above, it is somewhat black in color, soft, elongated, and pliable, marked with certain reddish streaks.

It signifies the heretical plague, or a malicious, deceitful, hypocritical, and pestilent person, Matthew 7: 'beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you shall know them.'
Ambrose: 'feigned fairness is not fairness, but a doubled iniquity.'
Dionysius, in his answer to the Architect: 'he sins doubly who, after sinning, justifies himself, or proves himself just.'
Fourth, as the same Isidore says, it has a triangular mouth, and, in its mouth, a channel with which it sucks blood.

It signifies detractors and defamers of others, cunning and ingenious for such things, Ecclesiasticus 11: 'a fire is kindled from a single spark, and by one deceitful man blood is increased. For the sinful man lies in wait for blood.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: He strikes charity in all, with a cursed tongue, and thoroughly kills and extinguishes it.

Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it settles on poisonous things, and therefore, when it must be applied to a limb for the sake of medicine, it ought first to be wrapped in nettles and salt, so as to be compelled to vomit up whatever poisonous thing it may perhaps have drunk. In warm water, and in warm weather, it more quickly applies itself to a limb, to suck.

It signifies that men who have consorted with heretics or other infamous or infected persons ought not to be admitted to familiarity or cohabitation before they have been purged, or tested, in grace —

— of the Holy Spirit and are fit and eager for evangelical discipline, Ecclesiasticus 11: 'bring not every man into your house; for many are the snares of the deceitful. For he turns good into evil, and lies in wait, and shall put a stain upon the elect.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus De copia verborum

cit.quote: One must first see with whom one eats, before what one eats.
The lizard is found to have these properties, or conditions, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is 'a little creature painted on its back, with shining spots in the manner of stars'; of it Ovid says: 'and it has a name fitting its color, starred with varied spots on its body.'

It signifies a holy man who, by the variety of his virtues and the brightness of his examples and the fair form of his character, edifies others variously and luminously and graciously, Philippians 2: 'as lights in the world, holding forth the word of life.'
The stars, moreover, gave light in their watches, and rejoiced.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'by the name of the stars are understood the souls of the good who live well, the holy prophets and blessed apostles, the doctors and pastors of the Church.'
It is written of blessed Bernard that, like a vessel of gold adorned with every precious stone, he shone forth among the people.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, 'it is so opposed to scorpions that, once seen, it brings them fear and numbness.'
It signifies that the just are opposed to demons and detractors, and bring upon them fear and numbness, Wisdom 1: 'but wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul,' proven virtue rebukes the foolish.
The north wind drives away rain, as does a sad countenance a backbiting tongue.
Do you wish to know the gifts of God? The garments of Paul were a terror to demons.
The Egyptians said: 'let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us.'
And God worked no small miracles by the hand of Paul, and so on.
...it lives, as Pliny says, chiefly on blood, and although it is a beautiful and painted animal, it is nonetheless greatly poisonous, since a most evil medicine is made from it.

It signifies hypocrites, living on the blood of others, and, although they appear good and gracious, are yet full of the poison of sin and vice, Matthew 23: 'woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like to whited sepulchers, which appear to men beautiful, but within are full of filthiness and iniquity.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke, and elsewhere: 'feigned fairness is a doubled iniquity.'
...a most swift animal, and yet it is not winged, but only by the swiftness of its feet, which serve it in place of hands, it creeps and climbs to the height of walls and houses.
It signifies good and simple men, advancing without worldly wisdom, Proverbs 11: 'the justice of the upright shall direct his way.'

Augustine, treating that saying of Matthew 11, 'learn from me,' and so on: 'those who have learned from the Lord to be humble and meek of heart profit more by praying and meditating than by reading and hearing.'

Fifth, as Pliny says, it hides in winter in caverns, and its sight grows dim; but, coming out of its caverns in spring, and sensing the defect in its sight, it changes its place, and seeks for itself a place and a cavern toward the east, and daily opens its eyes against the rising of the sun, until the moisture in the eye dries up and the film that induced darkness in its eyes is consumed.

It signifies the just man who, as long as he lives in this wretched world, always withdraws himself from the storms of the world, and shakes off the blindness of the world, and looks toward Christ, until the day of eternity dawns for him, Psalm 24: 'my eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he shall pluck my feet out of the snare. Look you upon me, and have mercy on me,' and so on.
It is sung of blessed Martin, that his eyes and hands were always intent upon heaven.
As the same author says, the serpent sheds its old skin in old age.

It signifies the putting off of the old man and the putting on of the new, according to the pattern of the apostle, Ephesians 4: 'be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who, according to God, is created in justice and holiness of truth.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Awake, O man, and acknowledge the dignity of your nature, which, though deformed in Adam, has nonetheless been reformed in Christ.
The serpent is proven to have these properties, or conditions, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as it is said, according to Isidore, book 12, because 'it creeps by hidden approaches, and does not walk about openly and publicly, but crawls hiddenly, striving with its scales.'

It signifies that demons and deceitful men always advance treacherously and maliciously toward others, Proverbs 26: 'when he shall speak low, do not trust him, for there are seven mischiefs in his heart.'
Thus it is said of the devil, that he is a lion and a dragon: a lion, for his onslaught; a dragon, for his ambushes; a lion rages openly; a dragon lies in wait secretly.
Second, as popular wisdom proves, it dreads a naked man, and leaps upon a clothed one.

It signifies that the devil is terrified by evangelical poverty, but is emboldened by worldly wealth, Isaiah 29: 'the meek shall increase their joy in the Lord, and the poor men shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.'
They that seek the Lord shall not be deprived of any good.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily on 'if any man will come after me': 'each man is cast down to earth clothed, since he has by what he may be held. Naked, therefore, we ought to struggle with the naked one.'
The poet: 'the empty-handed traveler will sing before the robber.'

Third, the spittle of a fasting man is especially poisonous to it. It signifies that the devil finds the rebuke or reproach of a man withdrawn from worldly things very pernicious to himself, and horrible, and confuting, James 4: 'draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.'

Blessed Gregory gives an example, in the book of the Dialogues, chapter 4, of Datius, bishop of Milan, who, lodging at Corinth in a house in which the devil was said to dwell, confounded and repelled the devil, with his ministers bleating, howling, running about at night in the likeness of sheep, pigs, lions, donkeys, and hissing serpents and mice, with these words: 'well has it befallen you, wretch, since you are the one who said, I will be like the Most High, and behold, now, on account of your pride, you have been made like unto pigs and mice.' And so it came about that he never again entered that house which he had claimed for himself.
Fourth, as Jerome says, it fights for its head, in which the seat of the heart is said to be, and, to protect that alone, it makes a shield of the rest of its body.

It signifies an evangelical man who, so as to preserve his soul alone for God, on whom, in the higher part of his reason, he has fixed his desire, his beloved and only Christ Jesus, exposes his whole body to sufferings and torments, persecutions and scourges, Matthew 10: 'be you wise as serpents, and simple as doves.'

Song of Songs, the last chapter: 'if a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he shall despise it as nothing. Many waters could not quench charity, neither shall the floods drown it.'

Blessed John the Evangelist said, in his Passion, when he was compelled by the proconsul, once seized, to deny Christ: 'therefore I will neither deny Christ my Lord, nor cease from preaching his name, until I finish the course of the ministry I have received.'
Blessed Andrew also said, to the proconsul Aegeas, in his Passion: 'the more I remain a confessor in torments for his name's sake, the more acceptable I shall be to my King.'

And blessed Agnes, in her Passion: 'but since I see that you strive for this, which you shall not be able to obtain, do whatever seems good to you.' Thus she spoke to the prefect Symphronian, a cruel tyrant.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fifth, as Isidore says, book 12, it has cold flesh, since it is of a cold nature.
It signifies a chaste man, estranged from pleasures, Galatians 5: 'and they that are Christ's have crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences.'
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions, speaking of the teacher Ambrose, before his own conversion: 'only his celibacy seemed a hard thing to me.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As the same Isidore says, in the same place, it renews itself each year, casting off its old skin by passing through a narrow opening.

It signifies the just man, always renewing himself in God with great zeal, and manfully casting off his defects, Colossians 3: 'stripping yourselves of the old man with his deeds, put on the new, who is renewed unto knowledge, according to the image of him that created him.'
Gregory and Bernard, in many places: 'not always to advance in the way of God is to fall back.'

bibl.author: Prosper Aquitanus Liber sententiarum ex operibus sancti Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, in the Sentences of Prosper, and elsewhere: 'it is not enough to abstain from evil, unless a man also does what is good.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily for Confessors Not Bishops: 'it is a lesser thing not to do evil, unless one also strives to labor at good works.'
As the same Isidore says, it licks moldy or putrid places, and loves shadowy places.

It signifies the devil, delighting in lusts and carnal pleasures, Job 40: 'he sleeps under the shadow, in the covert of the reed, and in moist places. The shadows cover his shadow; the willows of the brook shall compass him about.'
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'wretch that I was, I had chosen a softer place, unwilling to be without a woman's embraces.'
Eighth, as the same Isidore says, it never ceases to turn its tongue, from the force of its venom.
It signifies whisperers and detractors and murmurers, Proverbs 26: 'when wood fails, the fire shall go out; and when the talebearer is taken away, contentions shall cease.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'a heart bitter with the gall of envy cannot scatter, through the instrument of the tongue, anything but bitter things, the Lord saying: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.'
Ninth, as the author says, it looks sidelong, and moves crookedly, not straight.
It signifies the envious man, not rejoicing with truth and goodness, but opposing them, Ecclesiasticus 14: 'the eye of the envious is wicked; and he turns away his face, and despises his own soul.'
Chrysostom, in the sermon for the third Sunday in Lent: 'they do not wish the better man to live, lest they, degenerate, should have to bear reproaches for their own baseness.'
Tenth, as Isidore says, it hides its leprosy; it is even eaten for this reason, lest such an infirmity be revealed.

It signifies one who hides his crimes and sins, and does not reveal them, above all to a priest, Proverbs 28: 'he that hides his sins, shall not prosper; but he that shall confess, and forsake them, shall obtain mercy.'

bibl.author: Beda Venerabilis Expositio Bede in Marci Evangelium

cit.quote: Bede, on Mark: 'he who is ashamed now before one man will be exposed before the general judgment, on the last great day, when the hidden things of hearts shall be manifest.'
Eleventh, as the author says, it closes its ears, lest it hear the enchanter.
It signifies those unwilling, indeed scorning, to hear the word of God and the voice of the Gospel, Proverbs 28: 'he that stops his ear from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination.'
Augustine, and it is found in a chapter of the Decretum: 'he who scorns the Gospel sins no less than he who tramples the Lord's sacrament.'
It hisses before it bites, and kills all that it bites.

It signifies flatterers, fawning at first sight and, in the end, spiritually killing, Psalm 10: 'for the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul; and the unjust man is blessed. The sinner has provoked the Lord.'

bibl.author: Prosper Aquitanus Liber sententiarum ex operibus sancti Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, in the book of the Sentences of Prosper: 'the tongues of flatterers bind men fast in sins.'
...it is a most evil enemy to birds, since it kills them by its breath.
It signifies the devil, lying in wait especially for those seeking heavenly things, 1 Peter 5: 'your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour.'
Thus it is said of the devil, that he is a lion and a dragon: a lion, for his onslaught; a dragon, for his ambushes.
Fourteenth, as Isidore says, it takes back the poison it has cast out, once again.
It signifies a heretic renouncing and abjuring his heresy, and afterward falling back into it, Proverbs 25: 'as a dog that returns to his vomit, so is the imprudent man that repeats his folly.'

It had been better for them not to have known the way of truth, than, after they had known it, to turn back from that holy commandment which was delivered to them. For that of the true proverb has happened to them: the dog is returned to his vomit, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.
An example is found in Julian the Apostate, in the Tripartite and Ecclesiastical History.
As the same author says, it endures hunger for a long time, and at last is fed by dust.
It signifies the greedy man, eagerly awaiting to be satisfied by money, whose hope is found empty in the end, Isaiah 65: 'dust is the serpent's bread.'
Against which, Psalm 39: 'blessed is the man whose trust is in the name of the Lord; and who has not had regard to vanities,' and so on.
Augustine, in the sermon On the Holy Innocents: 'no one has unjust gain without a just loss. Gain is in the coffer, loss is in the conscience.'
The ape has these conditions, or properties, according to the ancient authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, the ape, 'simia,' is named from its flattened nose. Whence it is also called 'simia,' since its face is pressed in and disfigured, unpleasingly rippled with wrinkles. Others say that apes are named from their likeness in reason, since in many things they imitate the ways of man.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: But this is false, as the same Isidore says, in the book cited above.

It signifies, in general, hypocrites and the double-minded, who are one thing in reality, and another in outward show, and who present much in appearance which they do not have in the truth of the matter, 2 Timothy 3: 'know also this, that in the last days shall come dangerous times. Men shall be lovers of themselves,' and so on. 'Having an appearance indeed of godliness, but denying the power thereof; now these avoid.'
Ambrose, in the sermon for the Sunday of the Passion: 'every simulation and every duplicity is a lie.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, apes are keenly sensitive to the elements. For at the new moon they exult, but at the half-moon and the waning moon they grow sad.

They signify men rich, or wise according to this world, who rejoice in the flower of their age or their prosperity, but, as life proceeds, or at its end, descend sadly to hell, Job 21: 'their little ones go out like a flock, and their children dance and play. They take the timbrel and the harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ. They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment they go down to hell.'
For the glory of the world is the glory of the flesh, and there is no doubt that those who delight in it are carnal, Philippians 3: 'whose god is their belly, whose end is destruction.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Third, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, when it has two offspring, it carries in its arm the one it loves more, but bears on its shoulders the one it loves less, whenever the need to flee presses upon it. But when it is pressed hard in fleeing, it is compelled to throw away the one in its arms, and the other, sitting upon its shoulders, pressed down, makes its flight slower, and so it is more easily and quickly overtaken by the hunter.

It signifies that excessive lovers of their children, or their kinsmen, are exposed to the dangers of final damnation, Job 21: 'why then do the wicked live, are they advanced, and strengthened with riches? Their seed continues before them, a multitude of kinsmen, and of children's children, in their sight. They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment they go down to hell.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: man is caught, as though by the bait of prosperity, and led to the adversities of eternal calamity.
Fourth, as Aristotle says, book 2, it is a monstrous beast, yet greatly sharing in, and representing, the nature of man.

It signifies hypocrites, representing, or pretending to, the dignity of human nature in outward signs, but denying it in their deeds, or even in their affections, 2 Timothy 3: 'having an appearance indeed of godliness, but denying the power thereof; now these avoid.'
But above all things, the ruin and deceit of his own household tormented Paul.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fifth, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 54, seeing things done, it strives, with wondrous skill, to do them one by one. Whence, while it strives to be shod with the shoes hunters have deliberately left for it, it is caught again by them.
It signifies the presumptuous, or even the curious, striving with greater boldness to prove themselves sufficient for all things, though in the truth of the matter they are of little use or worth.

Against which, Ecclesiasticus 3: 'my son, do not many things beyond your power. Seek not the things that are too high for you, and search not into things above your ability. Be not curious in unnecessary matters, and be not inquisitive in many of his works. For many things are shown to you above the understanding of men. And the suspicion of them has deceived many, and has detained their minds in vanity.'
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions, and elsewhere: 'a curious race of men, eager to know the life of others, slothful to know their own.'
Sixth, as Pliny says, it is capable of instruction. Whence it is trained to dance and to play games in various ways.

It signifies beastly men who, though stupid by nature, are nonetheless made disciplined, or disciplinable, by much zeal and exercise, Ecclesiasticus 6: 'as one that plows, and sows, draw near to her' — that is, to wisdom. 'With your whole mind draw near to her, and with your whole strength keep her ways. For in the latter end you shall find rest in her.'
Jerome relates, in the prologue on Daniel, that a certain wise man said: 'unremitting labor conquers all things.'
It presents its young, showing them to men, rejoicing to have them handled sweetly with the hands, and knows those who congratulate it and applaud.

It signifies the worldly man, and the world itself, greatly loving and recognizing its own, John 7: 'the world cannot hate you; but me it hates, because I give testimony of it, that its works are evil.'
The body of Behemoth, that is, of the devil, is 'like molten shields, joined together with scales pressing one upon another; one is joined to another.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni
Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia and in a homily: 'all the wicked are one body of the devil.'

Eighth, as Aristotle says, book 5, being a beast, it is untamed and malicious by nature. It is nevertheless tamed by violence, by blows and chains, and is pressed down by a chain, lest it be able to run about freely, and so that its insolence may be repressed.

It signifies a wandering man, or a wanton woman, to whom caution, or guardianship, ought to be applied, and discipline added, according to the counsel of the wise man, Ecclesiasticus 26: 'keep a sure watch over a shameless daughter, lest at any time, finding an opportunity, she abuse herself. The fornication of a woman shall be known by the haughtiness of her eyes, and by her eyelids.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De diversis questionibus octoginta tribus

cit.quote: Augustine, book 83 Questions: beasts abstain from pleasures on account of blows.

Ninth, as the same author says, it eats every kind of food, but takes especial delight in unclean things. For, seeking out the lice of men, it eats them from their heads and their garments; and, like a man, it becomes drunk on wine.

It signifies the gluttonous, the unclean, and the drunken; against which, Ecclesiasticus 37: 'be not greedy in any feasting, and pour not yourself out upon any meat. For in many meats there shall be sickness, and greediness will turn to choler. By surfeiting many have perished; but he that is temperate, shall prolong life.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, and in his sermons, and elsewhere: 'the pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the length of two fingers.'
As Isidore and Pliny say, the lion desires its flesh, since it is said to recover, by eating it, when it is gravely sick.

It signifies that the devil, the wild ass's lion in the wilderness, feeds on the perverse life of the wicked, and, from this, on his own evil affections, insofar as he can find remedy or comfort there; Ecclesiasticus: the lion's prey is the wild ass in the wilderness.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: By the name of the wild ass in the wilderness is understood the one who does everything he desires in vain.
Ambrose, in the sermon for the Sunday of the Passion: 'thus the devil loves the sinner, so as to deceive him, just as a glutton loves a young pig — to eat it.'
Eleventh, as Avicenna says, book 2, it shares its form with man, and its hairiness with the wolf.

It signifies false brothers, sharing in the sacrament, or the outward habit, with the Church; but, in the old man, whom they never put off, sharing with demons, 2 Corinthians 11: 'in dangers from false brethren.'
Chrysostom, on Paul: 'but above all things, the ruin and deceit of his own household tormented Paul.'
The female ape, in her womb, is likened to a woman; but the male, in his organ, is likened to a dog.
They signify an unchaste soul and an unchaste body, Ephesians 4: 'who, despairing, have given themselves up to all lasciviousness, unto the working of uncleanness.'
The poet, and it is found in the Gloss near the end of the Decretum: 'it is asked: why did Aegisthus become an adulterer? The cause is plain: he was idle.'
As Pliny says, its bite is malicious, and especially that of those found to have tails.

They signify that the wounding detractions of those who bring them forth chiefly out of treachery are deadly, Jeremiah 9: 'an arrow wounding, their tongue, has spoken deceit; with his mouth one speaks peace with his friend, and secretly he lies in wait for him.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'he strikes charity in all, with a cursed tongue, and, as far as it lies in him, thoroughly kills and extinguishes those who hear him.'
Sirens are proven to have these various conditions, or properties.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as the Gloss on Isaiah 13 says, and Gregory and Isidore, book 12: they are winged and crested serpents, which run faster than horses.
And some say that they fly, especially Papias.
...great flying and crested dragons, as some think.

They signify the envious and the proud, or the ambitious, Proverbs 23: 'lift not up your eyes to riches which you cannot have, because they shall make themselves wings like those of an eagle, and shall fly toward heaven. Eat not with an envious man, and desire not his meats, because, like a soothsayer and diviner, he thinks of that which he knows not.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Every proud man is utterly unbearable; his manner of dress is excessive, his gait pompous, his neck stiff, he strives from a loftier place, and desires to be preferred to his betters; he boasts of his own opinions and his own deeds, and keeps no reverence.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as Isidore relates, book 11: 'three sirens are imagined to have existed, in part virgins, and in part flying creatures, each having wings, of whom one sang with the voice, another with the flute, the third with the lyre,' who, by their singing, allured sailors and drew them to shipwreck.

They signify the concupiscence of the flesh and of the eyes, and the pride of life, which draw sailors, by their pleasures, in the present age, down to hell, 1 John 2: 'all that is in the world, is the concupiscence of the flesh, and the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis Enarrationes in Psalmos Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, on the Psalms: 'a fear that basely humbles, and a love that basely inflames, are the tinder of vices.'
Third, as the Physiologus says, the siren is a sea-monster, having, from the navel upward, the form of a virgin, and below, the form or shape of a fish.
It signifies hypocrites, professing sanctity and hiding iniquity, 2 Timothy 3: 'having an appearance of godliness, but denying the power thereof.'
Ambrose, in the sermon of the Lord for the Passion: 'every simulation and every duplicity is a lie.'
Fourth, as the same author says, and the author sets forth, it is said to rejoice in a storm, but to grieve in clear weather.

It signifies perverse men and heretics who rejoice in the evils of the Church, and grieve at its goods, Proverbs 2: 'they are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in most wicked things; whose ways are perverse, and their steps infamous.'
Ambrose, on Paul: 'charity rejoices in the truth, when a good man rejoices at the happiness of his neighbors.'

Fifth, as the same authors say, by the sweetness of its song it lulls sailors to sleep, and, when it sees them fallen into a deep sleep, it draws them to the shore, and carries one of them to a dry place, and first makes him mate with it. But if he is unwilling, or unable, it kills him, and devours and swallows his flesh; and so it does afterward to others.

It signifies the malice of heretics in drawing men to themselves by their speeches, and making them give consent to their heresies, and so killing them in their souls, Romans, the last chapter: 'for they that are such, serve not Christ our Lord, but their own belly; and by pleasant speeches and good words seduce the hearts of the innocent.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: With an equal affection of shared malignity, a hateful conference is celebrated, and a huge multitude is destroyed.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Sixth, as Isidore says, book 12, their venom is such that death is felt before pain.

It signifies the destructiveness of the heretical plague, which kills the soul before its wickedness is detected, and therefore is, above all things, to be guarded against and fled, Matthew 7: 'beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you shall know them.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: he strikes charity in all who hear him, with a cursed tongue, and, as far as it lies in him, thoroughly kills and extinguishes it.
Seventh, as the author says, according to the truth, sirens were once certain harlots who led those who passed by them to destitution.

They signify lust and gluttony, impoverishing the wanton, and stripping them of virtues and graces, Proverbs 23: 'they that pass their time in wine, and that study to give banquets, shall be consumed; and drowsiness shall be clothed with rags. For a harlot is a deep ditch, and a strange woman is a narrow pit.'
As blessed Dionysius says, in his answer to the Architect: 'a man ought to be as ashamed of irrational movements as one is ashamed to be cast down from a position of leadership and dignity.'
The scorpion is found to have these conditions, or properties, from the natural authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12: 'the scorpion is an earthly worm, having in its tail an armed sting, so called because it bears, or fixes, its tail, and, with a curved wound, spreads its poison; and its peculiar quality is that it does not strike or harm the palm of the hand,' as the same Isidore says. And it is called 'scorpio' from 'scorte,' which means sweet, and 'poio,' which means to feign, since in its front part it feigns flattery, but in its rear part it stings.
It signifies malicious and deceitful men, and their trickery, Ezekiel 2: 'son of man, you dwell among rebels, subverters, and scorpions.'
But shun profane and vain babblings, for they grow much toward ungodliness; and their speech spreads like a cancer, of whom are Philetus and Hymenaeus, who have fallen away from the truth.

Jerome, to the virgin Metrias: 'what we have chosen must be kept, and we must walk as it were among scorpions and serpents, so that, with loins girded and feet shod and staves grasped in hand, we may make our journey through the snares of this world and amid its poisons, and may be able to reach the sweet waters of the Jordan, and enter the promised land, and ascend to the house of God.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Second, as Pliny says, book 11, chapter 26, scorpions bring forth little worms in the appearance of eggs, and destroy with an inopportune plague, being poisonous like serpents; for three days their poison greatly harms, and afterward they kill by a slow death, unless help is quickly given.

They signify souls poisoning men, and, unless guarded against, leading them, as though gently, to everlasting destruction, 2 Timothy 3: 'having an appearance of godliness, but denying the power thereof; now these avoid'; and below: 'men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke, and elsewhere: 'feigned fairness is not fairness, but a doubled iniquity.'
Beware of the pestilent man, for he devises evils, lest perhaps he burden you with his own evils.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: They strike virgins with a lethal blow when they sting them; likewise women, but not so quickly. They especially harm men. In the morning, when they come out of their dens, they are always ready to strike with their tail, if the occasion of harming is given them, and to strike with an oblique and bent blow, and to pour in their white venom.
