It signifies that demons tempt various people in various ways, according to how they can do worse or greater harm, and that they are ready for all evils against all ranks of the Church, and girded for all crimes, 1 Peter 5: 'watch, because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo, in the sermon On the Circumcision: 'for the ancient enemy does not cease to spread everywhere the snares of deception, and to press on, so that by whatever means he may corrupt the faith of believers. He knows to whom he should offer the incitements of lust, to whom he should press the enticements of gluttony, to whom he should apply the heats of desire. He knows whom to deceive with joy, whom to trouble with sorrow. He examines the habits of all, weighs their cares, and seeks occasions of harm wherever he sees each one more eagerly occupied.' Thus far the words of blessed Leo.
Fourth, as the author sets forth, nine kinds of scorpions are described by their colors.

They signify the varied malice and pestilent fraud of wicked men, 2 Timothy 3: 'know also this, that in the last days shall come dangerous times. Men shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, haughty, proud, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, unmerciful, without kindness, traitors, stubborn, puffed up, and lovers of pleasures more than of God.'

Ambrose, and it is found in the Decretals, on heretics, 'we excommunicate,' and so on: 'having indeed different faces, but tails bound together to one another, since out of vanity they agree upon the very same end.'
Fifth, as Pliny says, book 11: the scorpion harms no animal that lacks blood.

It signifies that demons cannot harm spiritual men, Romans 8: 'who shall rise up against the elect of God? For I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God,' and so on.
Do you wish to know the gifts of God? The garments of Paul were a terror to demons.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Sixth, as the same Pliny says, in the same place: to one struck by a scorpion, the ash of scorpions, drunk in wine, is a remedy, and, in oil, helps against the danger that stinging animals have brought about.

It signifies that there is no better way to escape and guard against demons and heretical persuasions than through the raging and victorious contrition of their malice, through humility and the gift of God's grace, James 4: 'draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.'
Blessed Cecilia said, in her Passion, preaching to her own: 'come, soldiers of Christ, cast off the works of darkness, and put on the armor of light.'
The Egyptians said, Exodus 14: 'let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Seventh, as Isidore says, book 12, scorpions so fear the lizard that, once they have seen it, they waste away and become numb.
It signifies that detractors fear to speak before holy men, Proverbs 25: 'the north wind drives away rain, as does a sad countenance a backbiting tongue.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Francis, in his Life, that he supremely abhorred detractors.
The sow, which is also called the pig, is found to have these conditions, according to the natural authorities.

For first, as Isidore says, it is called 'sus,' from subduing, since it subdues the earth for the sake of food, and roots in so deeply that it reaches to the roots with its teeth. It signifies moneymaking preachers and advocates, greedy for gain and eager for earthly profit, and deeply zealous and cunning toward this end: 'the wranglings of men corrupted in mind, and who are destitute of the truth, supposing gain to be godliness.'
Augustine, in various places: 'while other vices grow old with a man, avarice alone grows young again.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Second, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 51, and Solinus too, and Aristotle, book 6: it conceives around the spring equinox, gives birth twice a year, carries in the womb for four months, and sometimes produces twenty offspring. But it cannot raise them, and sometimes devours them all, except for the firstborn, which it loves the most, and to which it first offers its first teat.

It signifies worldly men multiplied in temporal things and devouring everything; likewise ecclesiastical prelates who give the first and choicest benefices to their kinsmen, Psalm 4: 'they are multiplied from the fruit of corn, and wine, and oil.'
'To sit on my right or left hand is not mine to give to you, but to those for whom it is prepared by my Father.'

To such men blessed Eugenia said, as she replied to Melania, a very wealthy citizen, who was urging her to consent to her, believing her to be a man: 'let those like you have your riches; it delights us to beg with Christ.'
A gluttonous and unclean animal, greedily devouring whatever is foul and unclean, and thinking mud, in which it rests, to be a bath, and being fattened by it.
It signifies gluttonous and wanton men: 'the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.'
While other animals eat that they may live, the pig seems to be signified as living that it may eat.
Fourth, as Aristotle says, book 7, when it has young, it is of great ferocity, and fights for them against the wolf.

It signifies usurers, or the greedy rich, who, for the sake of their children, are unwilling to see the poor, and fight and strive to enrich their children, and to protect them from every violence, Job 21: 'why then do the wicked live, are they strengthened, and lifted up with riches? Their seed continues before them, a multitude of kinsmen, and of children's children, in their sight. The ox has conceived, and not cast her calf, and the cow has calved, and is not deprived of her fruit.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: But against this, Ambrose, in the book On the Duties of Ministers: 'riches lend no support at all toward a blessed life,' and so on; 'otherwise the Lord would not say: woe to you rich,' and so on.
Fifth, as Aristotle says, book 7, it grows fat in rest, and a seventh part of its food passes into hair and blood and similar things.
It signifies that a man idle from good things is multiplied in vices and sins and the thoughts of the old life, Ecclesiasticus: idleness has taught much evil.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Always do something, so that the devil may find you occupied.
The bull is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, the bull is a male ox, not castrated, and its name is Greek, as is that of the ox. It signifies wanton and petulant young men.
Against which, Matthew 19: 'there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. He that can take it, let him take it.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Eustochium

cit.quote: Jerome, in the letter to Eustochium: 'I had made myself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven, yet I was still present among the choirs of maidens — in thought, that is.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is tawny, and swift, and vicious.
It signifies outstanding — indeed, distinguished — young men, according to that saying, Ezekiel 23: ready for evils, and malicious.
Against which, the last chapter of Proverbs: 'favor is deceitful, and beauty is vain; the woman that fears the Lord, she shall be praised.'

Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'if beauty pleases you, let it turn your love back to its maker, lest the things that please because they are creatures should displease you in place of him.'
Stiff-necked and proud, whose greatest strength is actively in its neck and its horns.

It signifies the devil and every member like him, swollen and inflated with pride and stiff-neckedness and the arrogance of worldly power, Job 15: 'he has stretched out his hand against God, and has strengthened himself against the Almighty. He has run against God with his neck outstretched, and is armed with a fat neck.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, and elsewhere: 'every proud man is utterly unbearable; his manner of dress is excessive, his gait pompous,' and so on.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fourth, as Isidore says, book 17, although it is of wondrous ferocity, once bound to a fig tree it loses all its fierceness, and suddenly grows gentle.

It signifies the tyrants of this world, who laid aside their fierceness against the faith, at once, after the humbling and subjection of their affections and the capture of their understanding, at the Lord's cross, 1 Corinthians 1: 'we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, and unto the Gentiles foolishness; but unto them that are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God; because the foolishness of God is wiser than men.'

Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'Victorinus, the great rhetorician of the city of Rome, was not ashamed to become a child of your font and a proclaimer of your faith, his brow tamed to the reproach of the cross.'
Fifth, as Aristotle says, book 7, it has a liver round like a man's liver, and feeds alone before the time of mating and love, but then joins itself to cows, and then also fights most fiercely.

It signifies lustful and gluttonous, or wanton and petulant men, given over uselessly to the love of carnal pleasures, and fighting continually for temporal things, and eagerly clinging to youthful vanities, and inciting others, as much as they zealously can, to love and do similar things, Philippians 3: 'for many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; whose god is their belly,' and so on.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Oceanum de vita clericorum

cit.quote: Jerome, on the letter to the Ephesians: 'a belly seething with wine easily boils over into lust.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Sixth, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 41, it is a noble animal, whose nobility appears in its face and horned brow, and in its ears and horns.
...of the bull, of the rhinoceros.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: By the name of the bull is designated the fair disposition of Christ's youth.
Aristotle, book 7: with figs and dried grapes.

It signifies that young religious are spiritually fattened and made rich by heavenly anointing and devotion, 1 John 2: 'you have the unction from the Holy One. Let the unction which you have received abide in you.'
Bernard: 'many see our crosses, who do not see our anointings.'
...of horses.

It signifies that a religious disciple should love no teaching except a chaste and clean one, namely sacred theology, shining with chastity and cleanness: 'the words of the Lord are chaste words, silver tried by fire, purged from the earth, refined seven times.'

Augustine, in the eleventh book Against Faustus: 'holy Scripture contains nothing absurd. But if you should find anything of that kind there, you should say that either the interpreter erred, or the scribe corrupted it, or you yourself do not understand.'
Likewise, to Volusian, speaking of this same matter: 'for it is a sincere and solid thing,' and so on.

Ninth, as the same Aristotle says, in the same place: bulls fight over females, and the one that wins mounts the female; and when he is weakened by much mating, the one he had defeated comes and fights against him, and then whichever wins mounts the female, as though rejoicing in his triumph.

They signify lustful men, fighting and being jealous over women in turn, and, once their desire is achieved or obtained, rejoicing, devoting themselves to the miserable consolation of the flesh, 2 Peter 2: 'you have nourished your hearts in luxury.' 1 Corinthians 4: 'one is puffed up against another.'
By chastity we are gathered together into one, from whom we had flowed away into many.

Bulls, as long as they are not castrated, are fierce and proud, but, their testicles removed, they are made humble and gentle, unwarlike, harmless, and they grow in body and become fat, and submit themselves to the yoke of the plowmen.

They signify that the yoke of evangelical chastity and religion tames all pride and puts on Christian humility and meekness, and brings about true penance, and pours in an increase of graces and virtues: 'it is good for a man, when he has borne the yoke from his youth.'
It is sung of blessed Francis: 'he grows gentle, though not entirely, first through the languors that, once heavenly arms are taken up, fully change his character.'
It is also written of blessed Nicholas that, as a youth, he began to be of good disposition.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Eleventh, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 22, there are certain wild and most fierce bulls, larger and swifter than the others, having a back as hard as flint, so that they cannot be wounded. They hunt all wild beasts, and cannot be caught except in pits; and, once caught, they die out of indignation.

They signify that the bull and the lion, the wrathful and the elated, troubling all their inferiors and, as it were, disdaining them, at last find themselves shamefully troubled, Ecclesiasticus 6: 'extol not yourself in the thoughts of your soul like a bull, lest perhaps your strength be quashed by folly, and it eat up your leaves, and destroy your fruit, and you be left as a dry tree in the wilderness. Be not as a lion in your house, terrifying those of your own household.'
Against which, it is read of blessed Nicholas that he showed himself humble in receiving his brothers, and affable in exhorting them.
The mole is proven to have these conditions, or properties, according to the doctors.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a certain little beast like the mouse, condemned to perpetual blindness; for it is in darkness, and without eyes.

It signifies heretics, going about after the likeness of mice, and persevering in the darkness of errors, and dwelling without the eye of sound understanding, 1 Timothy, the last chapter: 'who are destitute of the truth, supposing gain to be godliness.'
The Gloss on Matthew 12: 'heretical depravity casts down into the lowest of all vices; nor can they have the spirit of understanding, who do not have the head of wisdom.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it has a snout like a pig's, with which it digs the earth and casts it out. It eats and gnaws roots under the earth; it hates and flees the sun, nor can it live long above ground.

It signifies the teaching and life of heretics, seeking only earthly things, hating and fleeing the truth, and shunning the sight of good and perfect men in the Church, John 3: 'he that does evil, hates the light, and comes not to the light, that his works may not be reproved. They loved darkness rather than light; for their works were evil.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'dark spirits always do dark works.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: It has a black skin, shaggy and soft.

It signifies heretics, contemptible in outward habit, composed and feigned in affection, smooth and sweet in speech, against whom one must be especially guarded, Matthew 7: 'beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you shall know them.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus De copia verborum

cit.quote: One must first see with whom one eats, before what one eats.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As the same Isidore says, in the same place, it has very short legs, and broad feet, divided into fingers after the manner of a hand.
It signifies those who do few good things, but strive, out of deliberation and discretion, to do many evil ones, Jeremiah 4: 'they are wise to do evils, but to do good they have no knowledge.'
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'no one does anything good unwillingly, even if the thing he does is good.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'affection gives its own name to your work.'

Fifth, as Aristotle says, although the mole does not have visible eyes, nor does it see in any way, yet, if someone should cut delicately into its skin, he will find within traces of hidden eyes. And some have thought that this skin bursts, out of distress, at death, or when it begins to die, and that then, in dying, it begins to open the eyes it kept closed while living.
It signifies that heretics could, from that very light of nature given them, come to the knowledge of the truth, and will not.

For these, indeed, eternal punishment opens, in death, the eyes which the fault of error and faithlessness had closed, 1 John 1: 'he is in darkness, and walks in darkness, since darkness has blinded his eyes.'
Augustine: 'the sinner is struck with this punishment, that, dying, he forgets himself, since, while he lived, he forgot God.'

Gregory, in the Dialogues: 'punishment opens the eyes that guilt closes'; and they shall have as their tormentors, in punishments — supply, eternal ones — those whom they had as their inciters in vices.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Sixth, as Pliny says, book 10, chapter 49, 'the mole, buried under thick earth, hears more clearly,' and, by this second sense of nature, if it hears a man speaking, it flees from afar.

It signifies the rich of the world, or lovers of earthly things, who quite eagerly, or intently, hear the word, and seem to lend an ear more than others, but, when they hear it, scorn to follow Christ's humanity and life, Luke 8: 'that which fell among thorns, are they who, when they have heard the word, go their way, and are choked with the cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and yield no fruit.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: If you truly desire to be rich, brothers, love the true riches, and hasten as quickly as you can to that heavenly homeland.
The badger, which is also called the 'melus,' is proven to have these conditions, or properties.
For first, as the Gloss on Hebrews 11 says, it is an animal the size of a fox, whose skin is very rough and shaggy, and is called 'melota.'
It signifies the habit of religion, or of penance: 'and John had his garment of camel's hair,' and so on.
'They wandered about in sheepskins, and in goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy.'
It is read of blessed Dominic that he was a true lover of poverty, using cheap garments.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As Pliny says, book 8, chapter 39, it is of wondrous cunning. For, pursued by dogs, it holds its breath, inflated, and stretches its skin in this way, and so escapes the bites of dogs and the blows of men.
It signifies patience, which makes a man strong against adversity, Luke 21: 'in your patience you shall possess your souls.'
A noble kind of conquering is the virtue of patience. He conquers who suffers. If you wish to conquer, learn to suffer.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Badgers, or 'meli,' foresee a coming storm, and therefore make for themselves underground dens with various exits. Whence, when the north wind blows, they block the northern entrance with the shagginess of their tails, and then leave the southern one open, and conversely. In these same hiding-places, moreover, they provide for themselves against the winter with food, and, if food should ever fail them, sleep serves them in place of provisions. For they are among the kinds of animals that live, for the most part, on sleep, and hide themselves in winter, as the same author says.

They signify those who cautiously provide for themselves in adversity and prosperity, and religiously withdraw from the world's vanity toward the contemplation of God and the supermental absorption into God, Isaiah: 'he shall be as one that hides himself from the wind, and shelters himself from the storm.'
In peace, in the very same, I will sleep, and I will rest.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: He truly ascends to God who, penetrating himself, is turned within himself, and is made a stranger to desires.

As the Physiologus says, there is a certain species of badger which, freely, gathers and stores food in summer against the winter, together with its mate, and, when the cold of winter comes, the male, fearing lest the food gathered should run out too quickly, restrains the female from eating, and does not permit her to eat her fill. She, feigning peace, and, as though yielding to the male badger, secretly leaves the den, and, entering the hiding-place by the opposite side, unknown to the male, opens her jaws and devours and consumes the long-gathered food.

It signifies the wives, or mistresses, of usurers, like the females of the snake, who, gathering gains with their husbands, and, once told to stop hoarding the accumulated money, dissemble and afterward secretly filch it as they wish, and sometimes bring about great losses, Ecclesiasticus 25: 'there is no head worse than the head of a serpent; and there is no wrath above the wrath of a woman. From the woman came the beginning of sin, and by her we all die.'
Origen, in the homily On the Canaanite Woman: 'woman is the head of sin, a weapon of the devil, the expulsion from paradise, the corruption of the ancient law.'
Fifth, as the same author says, this beast hates the fox, and is accustomed to fight with it.
It signifies good and religious men opposing wicked and vicious men, Proverbs 24: 'they that rebuke shall be more acceptable, and upon them shall come the blessing.'
Ephesians 5: 'have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Nothing pleases God so much as zeal for souls.
The tiger is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to the natural authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is a beast most swift in flight, after the manner of an arrow; for arrows, that is, tigers, are so named for this.
They signify demons, or robbers, very swift to evil, Proverbs 1: 'their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Evil spirits beset our journey, like a band of robbers.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it is a beast marked with varied spots, and wondrous in strength.

It signifies the hypocrite, or the false and double-minded man, appearing virtuous in many things and being so in none, Matthew 23: 'woe to you, hypocrites, who are like to whited sepulchers, which outwardly appear to men beautiful, but within are full of dead men's bones.'
Ambrose, in the sermon for the Sunday of the Passion: 'every simulation,' and so on, 'is a lie.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Third, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 19, the female tiger is an animal supremely devoted to its young, so much so that, when it finds its lair robbed by hunters, its cub pursues them headlong by scent, and the hunter, sensing its pursuing roar, throws down one of the cubs in the middle of the road; the mother, finding it, at once carries it back to the lair, and quickly returns for the others, but meanwhile the hunter boards his ship, while she, left behind, is frustrated and greatly enraged.

It signifies the worldly man, loving his children too much out of affection, around whom his labor and zeal are always found, in the end, useless, Ecclesiastes 5: 'there is also another very grievous evil, which I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the hurt of the owner. For they perish with very great affliction. He has begotten a son, who shall be in extreme want. As he came forth naked from his mother's womb, so shall he return, and shall take nothing away with him of his labor. What does it profit him, then, that he has labored for the wind?'
Augustine, in the sermon On the Holy Innocents: 'no one has unjust gain without a just loss. Where there is gain, there is also loss,' and so on.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fourth, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, the male tiger cares nothing for its offspring.

It signifies wicked men who are hardened toward their own children and toward others of the household of the faith, as though they were not their own, according to what is found in Job 39: 'she is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers. She has labored in vain, no fear compelling her. For God has deprived her of wisdom, neither has he given her understanding.'
Against which, in the gloss on 1 Timothy 4, Ambrose says: 'the sum of the Christian religion consists in godliness,' and so on.

Fifth, as the same author says, the female tiger is wondrously deceived by a mirror. For when the hunter intends to carry off with him all its cubs from its lair, while it is away hunting for food, he leaves great shining mirrors along the way. The mother, pursuing her sons, finds them and, seeing herself in them, believes them to be her sons — the varied reflection of herself in the mirrors. And so, held fast in the shadow of herself, and occupied with drawing out from the glass the images of her imagined sons, she gives the robber time to flee, and so is deceived by the shadow, so that she pursues the robber no further, for the freeing of her sons.

It signifies those who embrace earthly things and follow what is fleeting, and contend for such things, and in the end find themselves wholly deceived, Ecclesiasticus 34: 'the hope of a senseless man is vain and false; and dreams lift up fools. He that regards lying visions, is like to him that catches at a shadow, and follows after the wind.'
Jerome relates, in the Lives of the Fathers, that a holy father, asked what truth was, replied that whatever was below heaven was a lie, and whatever was above heaven, truth.
The cow has these conditions, or properties, according to the natural authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is the female of the bull, so called, that is, 'uacca,' as it were 'boacca.'

It is, moreover, as the same Isidore says, a wanton and lustful animal, since, as Aristotle says, book 6, cows are moved to mating after a year, or perhaps after eight months, and the time of a cow's pregnancy is nine months, and her calving in the tenth. And a cow's mating is likened to that of males, and they then become wild, so that herdsmen cannot tame them. And their desire is shown by a swelling of their claws and continual lowing, since cows low in desire for mating, and leap upon bulls, and follow them, and stand with them.

It signifies the wantonness, or petulance, of certain lesser prelates and young ministers of the Church, who anticipate their season, or age, in lust, and sometimes exceed the act or measure of nature, whose dishonorable and base appetite is shown by their outward habit and words and signs and familiarities: 'like a wanton heifer, Israel has turned aside,' that is, the clergy who ought above all to devote themselves to contemplation, since 'Israel' is interpreted as 'seeing God.' Daniel 13: 'and two elders of the people were appointed judges that year, of whom the Lord said, that iniquity came out from Babylon, from the ancient judges, who seemed to govern the people. These men frequented the house of Joachim, and saw Susanna daily entering and walking in her husband's orchard, and they were inflamed with lust for her,' and so on.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: He ministers dangerously to you whose face you gaze upon frequently.

Second, as the same Aristotle says, in the same place, men say that their time of pregnancy is ten months, and if the calf is born before this time, it will not live, nor will its hooves be fully formed; and for the most part it bears one, and perhaps two.

It signifies those who, before their time, and too soon, wish to preach in the Church of God, and therefore profit little, since they depart from the pattern and example of Christ: 'and Jesus himself was beginning about the age of thirty years,' and so on.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Rusticum monachum

cit.quote: Jerome, to the monk Rusticus: 'learn for a long time what you will afterward teach.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Regula pastoralis Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Pastoral Rule, chapter 49: 'our Redeemer, though he was the founder in heaven, and, by the display of his power, the teacher of angels always, was unwilling, before the age of thirty, to be, in reasoned account, a teacher of men; that is, hastening down, he might, by the force of most wholesome fear, instill it, since he himself, though he could not fail, would not preach the grace of a perfect life except at a perfect age. For it is written: and when he was twelve years old, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem. Of whom, sought by his parents, it is added a little after: they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, hearing them, and asking them questions.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: And on Ezekiel, in the second homily: 'according to the use of reason, the discourse of teaching does not suffice, except at a perfect age. Whence the Lord himself, in the twelfth year of his age, sitting in the midst of the doctors in the temple, wished to be found not teaching, but asking questions.'

Third, as the same Aristotle says, females live, for the most part, fifteen years, and males likewise. But when they are castrated, they become stronger, and live twenty years. And after calving, a cow has good milk, but before, none; and if she has any, it is little and worth nothing. And when it is afterward curdled, a cow's milk becomes like a stone; but this happens when it is mixed with water.

They signify that, through chastity, men are made more powerful against hostile wickedness, and, after a good life, after the example of Christ, Acts 1, follow a better teaching, and a more effective and solid edification, especially when holy devotion is shared.
'Let no man despise your youth. Command these things, and teach. Be an example to the faithful, in conduct, in charity, in integrity, in chastity.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily On a Simple Confessor: 'chastity is nothing without good work, nor is good work anything without chastity.'
Ambrose, in the sermon On a Bishop Confessor: 'let us, therefore, resist the manifold assaults of this world by chastity and chaste deeds.'
Fourth, as the same Aristotle says, when cows are often impregnated and produce many young, it is a sign — as men think — that there will be much rain in winter.

It signifies that, when and where good men and good works are multiplied, in every adversity and tribulation, the grace and blessing and consolation of God is present, Proverbs 29: 'when just men increase, the people shall rejoice; when the wicked shall bear rule, the people shall mourn.'
In whatever and however great tribulations, when good men are present, all sad things are softened and lightened.
Fifth, as the same Aristotle says, cows live in a herd, and if they withdraw from the herd, they often perish, since they are eaten by wild beasts.
They signify that the life of man consists in concord and unity, but danger in discord and schism, John 17: 'I pray for them, that they may be made perfect in one, as we also are one.'
Ephesians 4: 'careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Commentarii Hieronymi in Evangelium Matthei

cit.quote: Jerome, on Matthew: 'as by concord small things grow, so by discord the greatest things collapse.'
...cows, which have a voice deeper than the males'.

They signify certain women of good will who confess their sins and their defects more expressly and effectively, and praise God better and more, than ordinary men, Judges 5: 'blessed among women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, and blessed be she in her tent. He asked her water, and she gave him milk, and offered him butter in a dish fit for princes.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Learn with what grief Mary — the spider that does not blush to weep, even amid feasting. As many delights, then, as she had within herself, so many burnt offerings she found from herself.
A cow has stronger and thicker horns than the male, and more knotted, though not as large in light, or brightness; but, if warmed, they can be widened, or made larger.
They signify certain religious women, more powerful and effective, or more manly, in fighting down hostile temptations, than ordinary men.

For although they are more fragile by nature, they are fortified and strengthened by the heat, or the inflaming, of grace, Proverbs: 'who shall find a valiant woman?' and so on. 'She has girded her loins with strength, and has strengthened her arm. She shall not fear for her house the colds of the snow,' and so on.
It is written of blessed Lucy that she confounded Paschasius with her public voice.
As the same Aristotle says, when cows are sick in their feet, medicine for them is if, between their horns, they are anointed with oil and pitch and other remedies.

They signify that works of mercy are remedies against all sins, both of the affections and of the deeds, 1 Timothy 4: 'exercise yourself unto godliness. For bodily exercise is profitable to little; but godliness is profitable to all things,' and so on.
The Gloss, there: 'the sum of the Christian religion consists in godliness, which, whoever has it, even if he suffers the slipperiness of the flesh, will obtain mercy in the end.'
Ninth, as Bede says, cows love to drink clear water, and rarely, or never, drink turbid water.
They signify those who study more gladly and eagerly in holy Scripture, Proverbs 5: 'drink water out of your own cistern, and the streams of your own well.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Love the knowledge of the holy Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.
Tenth, as the same author says, they suffer from gout, from which they die. And the sign of this is when they droop their ears and do not eat.

They signify the lazy and the disobedient, depriving themselves of heavenly grace and consolation, and incurring the death of sin, and likewise of hell, Proverbs 21: 'desires kill the slothful, for his hands have refused to work at all.'
The poet: 'it is asked: why did Aegisthus become an adulterer? The cause is plain: he was idle.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: Therefore Jerome says: 'always do something, so that the devil may find you occupied.'
Eleventh, as the same Aristotle says, it grows fat in its own dung, and the more it is spared from labor, the more it grows sluggish and fat.

It signifies the lustful and the sensual, beasts of burden wholly devoted to the stench of wantonness and to the consolation, or rest, of the flesh, even unto death, and always withdrawing themselves more and more from divine things: 'the beasts have rotted in their own dung.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'the beasts...'
...a pregnant cow casts off the yoke, though at other times she submits herself to it willingly.

It signifies enriched men casting off the observance of the commandments, who nevertheless, when they were poor, were willingly obedient, Jeremiah 5: 'they are grown fat and rich, and have most wickedly forsaken my words.'

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore Soliloquium de arrha anime Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: Hugh of Saint Victor, On the Betrothal-Gift of the Soul: 'the harlot soul loves the yearly gifts of the giving God more than the goodness of so generous a God.'
Bernard: 'ingratitude dries up the fountain of piety.'
...the ox-fly, which lifts its tail, and, wondrously maddened, roams and runs about the fields at will.

It signifies apostates who, once struck by apostasy, are, as it were, carried freely toward every evil, and, as though placed outside themselves, become wanderers through the various spaces of the world, Proverbs 6: 'an apostate man, an unprofitable man,' and so on, 'at all times he sows discord.'
As I have never found better men than those who have advanced in monasteries, so I have never found worse than those who have fallen away in monasteries.
The wild cow has these properties, or conditions, according to the natural authorities.
For first, as Avicenna and Aristotle say, in the land of the Parthians it has, on its neck, a mane like a horse's, and likewise in the size of its body. Whence it is called, by many, the horse-deer.
It signifies worldly and secular men, rich and proud, or their overabundant substance, Ecclesiasticus 11: 'if you are rich, you shall not be free from sin.'
Augustine, treating the mammon of iniquity, on Luke 16: 'every rich man is either an unjust man or the heir of an unjust man.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, in the book On the Duties of Ministers: 'riches lend no support at all toward a blessed life.'
Second, as the same Avicenna and Aristotle say, it lacks horns, and dwells in the mountains, with beautiful eyes and sharp sight.

It signifies the humble and the poor and the religious, who do not have the power of the world, but the hope of the empyrean heaven and a keen and pleasant contemplation of paradise, Hebrews 11: 'for we have not here a lasting city, but we seek one that is to come.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'Paul, confined in prison, dwelt in heaven. And so he walked on earth, as though he enjoyed the company of angels.'
As the same Avicenna and Aristotle say, some are sometimes found to have fawns of deer, but small, like a fawn of the deer, and curved back like a goat's.

They signify humble and religious persons who, though they do not have the horns of worldly power, have, in their place, the horns of evangelical justice and truth: 'we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, On Consideration: 'it is fitting to be impatient and steadfast against vices.'

Fourth, as the same Avicenna and Aristotle say, in its heart is found a bone, as in the heart of the deer and the camel. And that bone, when the blood grows warm, tickles and moves the substance of the heart, and is the cause exciting the animal to a movement of joy and exultation. Whence, from such tickling, it suddenly rises up, moves its head, leaps more quickly, and runs about.

It signifies that Christ is found in the heart of the just man, and begets a loving joy in his affections and character and deeds, Colossians 3: 'let the peace of Christ rejoice in your hearts, and be grateful.'

Jerome, to the virgin Metrias: 'happy is that conscience, and blessed the virginity, in whose heart, besides the love of Christ, who is wisdom, chastity, patience, and justice, and the other virtues, no other love dwells. Nor does it ever breathe at the remembrance of a man, nor desire to see one whom, once seen, it would be unwilling to let go.'
He is found by those who love him, and appears to those who have faith in him.

Fifth, as Aristotle says, since it cannot help itself with horns — which it either lacks, or, if it has them, they are curved back and small — against dogs approaching it, it helps itself by casting out dung, which burns the dogs themselves. Other dogs, too, who find dung of this kind, occupy themselves with its smell until the unwarlike beasts flee and escape.

It signifies that in no other way can one better triumph over all hostile assaults than through a perfect contempt for all temporal things, which are signified by the dung, Philippians 3: 'I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them as dung, that I may gain Christ.'
Jerome, in the letter to Eliodorus: 'do you wish to be perfect, and to stand at the first pinnacle of dignity? Do what the prophets did, what the apostles did: naked, follow the naked Christ.'
The calf has these conditions, or properties, according to our doctors.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, it is named from the greenness of its age. For, as soon as it is born, it rises up and lifts itself to seek its mother's udders, and is at once refreshed and suckled by its mother's udders.

It signifies a young man of good disposition who, by the constant zeal of Christian piety, green in mind, is joined by faith wholly, from the flower of his early age, to the grace of God and to Mother Church, by whose sacraments and gifts he is spiritually refreshed and suckled, Proverbs 5: 'let her be, as the loving hind' — that is, Mother Church, lovingly embracing her children — 'and most agreeable fawn' — that is, the Son of God made man — 'let her breasts inebriate you at all times, and be you delighted continually with her love.'

Augustine, book 7, Lord: 'your Word, Lord, was made flesh, that your wisdom, by which you made all things, might give milk to our infancy, and that we, seeing your divinity brought low before our feet, might fall down, prostrate before it; and that it, rising, might lift us up.'

Second, as the same Isidore says, as soon as it is born, it is licked with its mother's tongue, and purged from every uncleanness contracted in the womb, and is wiped clean out of the womb. And a certain black pustule is born on its forehead, as on the horse's forehead, which they call the excitor of love, which its mother at once cuts away, nor does she admit it to her udders until she takes it away and cuts it off.

These things signify that grace purges the soul, and that Mother Church, through Baptism, blots out original sin, and that those who are in original sin are not children of the Church, nor are they to be nourished or cherished by her until they have Baptism, Acts 2: 'do penance, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.'
Ambrose, On the Sacraments: 'you have come to the fountain; you are baptized, you are restored, you are reformed to your original innocence.'
It loves its mother and follows and recognizes her lowing; it shakes off, with its forehead, the udders it sucks, and so seeks a more abundant flow of milk from its mother.

It signifies the children of the Church, recognizing their spiritual origin, and pupils of the true shepherd, Christ, eager and zealous for the draught of heavenly consolations. To whom it is said, both by eternal Wisdom herself and by Mother Church: 'come over to me, all you that desire me, and be filled with my fruits. For my spirit is sweet above honey, and my inheritance above honey and the honeycomb.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Divine consolation is a delicate thing, and is not given to those who possess what belongs to another.
Fourth, as the same author says, satisfied with milk, it leaps joyfully and runs about; but, in leaping, it does not depart from its mother's footsteps.

It signifies the supermental joy that is always in one well fed with grace and spiritual consolation, and in the man who always holds himself close to God, Habakkuk 3: 'but I will rejoice in the Lord, and I will joy in God my Jesus.'
The Gloss on 1 Kings 2, chapter, at the beginning: 'if you rejoice in Jesus, your heart is enlarged.'

Fifth, as Aristotle says, book 8, calves are castrated after one year, and if they are not castrated at that time, they will be small. And their castration is done in this manner: the calves are laid down and stretched out on the ground, their skin is cut, and the testicles are pressed out, and their roots are drawn out upward, and their sinews likewise. The incision is then bound until the blood comes out; and if an abscess should occur, they will burn the testicle, and apply it to the abscess, and so the place will be healed.

They signify that novice religious ought not to be bound to a vow of continence before a year's trial, and that men are made chaste only through great violence, and that, by vehement zeal for honesty, a man is removed from the mortal infirmity of an assailing concupiscence, Matthew 11: 'the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent bear it away.'

Gregory and Augustine, likewise in various places: 'the kingdom of heaven is then violently seized, when the proud man strives toward humility, the incestuous toward chastity, the impatient toward kindness.'
The bear has these properties, or conditions, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, the bear, 'ursus,' is so called as it were 'orsus,' since it forms its young with its mouth.
For Avicenna says that they generate unformed offspring, and that a certain flesh is born, which the mother, by licking, shapes into limbs.

Thus the tongue shapes the young the she-bear has brought forth. But this haste hastens the birth; indeed, she gives birth on the thirtieth day. Whence it comes that a hastened fecundity produces an unformed creature.

It signifies those who make so young in age, in the Church, clerics, or religious, or prelates, and promote them so untimely, that, being as it were unformed and too much hastened, they wholly need the shaping of their character, affections, and deeds, Galatians 4: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'
'I gave you milk to drink, not meat; for you were not able as yet; but neither indeed are you now able.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'there are two breasts of the faithful soul: understanding and affection. From the first breast is pressed the milk of truth, by which the ignorant and the erring are fed; from the second is pressed the sweetness of charity, by which the bitterness of vices, and especially of anger, hatred, and envy, is cut away. With these two breasts the Lord feeds and gives drink to the just.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the author says, and it is found in Isidore, book 12, the bear, 'ursus,' is named from pressing, since it strongly presses and binds what it seizes.
It signifies the devil, or sin, which most strongly binds and chains whomever it subjugates, or subjects, to itself, 2 Peter 2: 'for by whom a man is overcome, of the same also he is the slave.'
He that commits sin, is the servant of sin.

Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'from a perverse will, lust was made; and while lust was not resisted, habit was made; and while habit was not resisted, necessity was made, by which the soul is bound to itself, as if by little hooks intertwined.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Its head is weak; but it has the greatest strength in its forelegs and its loins.

It signifies those who are weak in mind and purpose toward every true and chief good, but strong toward every temporal and carnal evil, Jeremiah 4: 'they are wise to do evils, but to do good they have no knowledge.'
'His strength is in his loins, and his force in the navel of his belly.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis Epistola Augustini ad Probam

cit.quote: Against which, Augustine, to Proba, on praying to God: 'a man's mind is not sound unless it prefers eternal things to temporal ones.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fourth, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 38, bears mate at the beginning of winter, and do not mate in the common manner of four-footed animals, but, both lying down and embracing, then withdrawing from one another, and entering their den separately.

It signifies those who devote themselves, above all, to the consolations of the flesh, when generally others are cold and troubled, and, against the general course of nature, are occupied with private pleasures, withdrawing to their own secret places, and caring nothing for the whole rest of the multitude, Philippians 2: 'for all seek the things that are their own, not the things that are Jesus Christ's.'
Augustine: 'every part that does not agree with its whole is shameful.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fifth, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, they build their dens with branches and fruits, covered against the rains with soft foliage, penetrable by them.

They signify those who so build themselves up, spiritually or even temporally, that they do not resist grace and heavenly influence, but rather, adapting themselves to it with pious and devoted affection, dispose themselves toward it; which is the opposite of those who resist the grace of God and the kindness of the Holy Spirit, James 4: 'God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.'
It is written of blessed Francis that he was solicitous to adapt his soul to the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As the same Pliny says, in the same place, when they lie hidden in caverns after mating, separately, for the first fourteen days, they are so overwhelmed by heavy sleep that they cannot be roused even by wounds, and then they grow fat in a wondrous way.

They signify those who, having obtained the desires of the flesh and intent on themselves, with a private love, are so oppressed by the sleep of sin, negligence, and sloth, that they can scarcely be roused, and, at last, through the scourges of infirmities and the losses of adversities — indeed, then above all — cling to themselves and are made dull, as is clear in Pharaoh, throughout Exodus, and in Antiochus, 2 Maccabees 9, who, after many offenses against God, did not come to their senses even amid the very scourges and singular plagues terribly inflicted upon them from heaven, but rather strove the more to fulfill their own evil will, and for this reason perished utterly, the last chapter of Acts, taken from Isaiah 6, according to the Septuagint: 'the heart of this people has grown fat, and their ears have been dull of hearing, and they have shut their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia and elsewhere: 'a sin that is not washed away by penance soon draws, by its own weight, to another.'
Isaiah 5: 'woe to you who draw sin like a long rope.'
Its fat is useful against the loss of hair.
It signifies that the anointings, or consolations, of grace greatly avail against the flowing out, or wasting, of vices.
For this reason David says: 'let my soul be filled as with fat and marrow.'

Against which: 'their iniquity has come forth, as it were, from fatness; they have passed into the affection of the heart.' For there is a fat of inward consolation, and a fat of worldly prosperity, or of bodily consolation, according to what the two aforesaid authorities plainly testify, and the doctors and saints distinguish.
Theophrastus believes — a thing wondrous to relate — that their flesh, cooked after a long hiding in caverns, grows, if kept in another vessel.
It signifies the progress and increase of those who turn themselves, in the wilderness, to God, for the edification of the people.
'The word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zachary, in the desert. And he came into all the country about the Jordan, preaching the baptism of penance for the remission of sins.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know or spread divine things.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Ninth, as Pliny says, book 8, when they come out of their caverns, fattened and sated from sleep, they seek a certain herb, which they eat so as to loosen their belly, which they then feel to be bound up.

They signify that spiritual remedies, or saving medicines, are to be sought and obtained by those fattened on temporal goods, and consequently constipated and hardened toward spiritual things, and that the divine words are to be fulfilled: 'for neither herb nor poultice healed them, but your word, Lord, which preserves those who have believed in you.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis Epistola Augustini ad Probam

cit.quote: In the riches of this world there can be no true solace, that is, no remedy for the soul.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Tenth, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, when they come out of their caves and feel their eyes dulled, they run to the honeycombs of bees, so that their mouth, wounded by the stings of bees, may relieve, by bleeding, the heaviness and pain of their eyes.
It signifies those who seek the salvation of the body's belly to the loss of their own soul, Philippians 3: 'whose god is their belly, whose end is destruction.'
Augustine, in the sermon On the Holy Innocents: 'no one has unjust gain without a just loss. Where there is gain, there is loss,' and so on.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Eleventh, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, their brain is poisonous, and therefore, when they are killed, their heads and shoulder-blades are burned, lest anyone tasting them be turned to the madness of the bear.

They signify heretics, corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith, who are rightly burned, and their power annulled, lest the rest be corrupted, 1 Corinthians 5: 'put away the evil one from among yourselves. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?'
Chrysostom, on 1 Corinthians: 'leaven in dough is a heretic in the Church.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As the same Pliny says, in the same place, it fights against bulls, and, seizing them with its mouth, facing them, and hanging by all its feet, bends them by its weight, and, so dying, tears and kills them. Nor is there such skill in any animal, as in bears, for working evil.

It signifies the battle of the wicked with the good, and of tyrants with martyrs, and also the singular malice of the devil and the Antichrist, Galatians 4: 'but as then he, that was born according to the flesh, persecuted him that was after the spirit, so also it is now. But what does the Scripture say? Cast out the bondwoman and her son.'
Augustine, in the sermon On the Holy Innocents: 'the profane enemy could never have benefited the blessed little martyrs so much by favor as he did by hatred.'
'Fear not them that kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.'

The bear eats everything indiscriminately. For it eats fruit when it climbs trees; it also breaks open hives and eats honey, and bees attack its eyes and sting its tongue, and it eats crabs and ants for medicine, and eats meat for great strength, and it fights with bulls and wild deer and pigs and dogs, and it lays them low, and stands upright against them, and holds their horns with its paws, and often overcomes them.

It signifies that the devil and the Antichrist, and the men who are their members, desire to devour all souls indiscriminately, and kill spiritual fruits and heavenly consolations in souls, and, under the appearance of what is right, draw to themselves the great and the small as much as they can, and, without ceasing, harass the good and the wicked, the great and the weak, and often overcome, though many are found opposing them, on account of all of which, 1 Peter 5: 'be sober, and watch, because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour. Whom resist, strong in faith.'
A roaring lion, and a hungry bear, is a wicked prince over the poor people.

Augustine, in the gloss on James, chapter 1, 'count it all joy': 'do not wonder if the wicked flourish in the world, and you suffer, for it is not the way of the Christian religion,' and so on, 'but, by the hope of that good toward which you strive, bear with equanimity all the evils that shall befall you.'

The bear is an impatient and wrathful animal, wishing to avenge itself on all who touch it. And so, if it should attack someone who strikes it, and another should touch it, it lets go of the first and attacks the second; and if a third should then strike it, it lets go of the first and second, and at once rises up against the third.

It signifies the wrathful and the impatient, wishing to avenge every wrong down to the last detail, and striving as much as they are able, against that saying, Deuteronomy 32: 'revenge is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord.'
And Romans 12: 'not revenging yourselves, my dearly beloved, but give place unto wrath.'
Let the harsh, then, quarrel over bodily and temporal things; but blessed are the meek, for...
As the same author says, in the same place, when it is captured, it is blinded by the sight of a burning basin, is bound with chains, and is compelled to play, and is tamed by blows.

It signifies that the burning of the greed of avarice blinds a man, and reduces him to the slavery of the devil, and makes him play along with sins and temptations, and, at last, through well-deserved blows, joins and unites him wholly with the devil, into hell, 2 Peter 2: 'for by whom a man is overcome, of the same also he is the slave.'
Terrors shall go and come upon him.
Wisdom 2: 'their own malice has blinded them.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: He whose portion is God ought to care for nothing but God.

As the same Aristotle says, in the same place, it is an unstable and restless animal. Whence, all day long, it circles round the stake to which its feet are bound with chains, and licks and sucks them, and delights wondrously in their moisture. It knows how to climb trees, up to their very highest tops. And where bees are accustomed to make honey in the hollows of trees, it perceives this by scent and climbs up, makes an opening with its claws, and draws out the honey from there, and sometimes, growing used to this, especially when it is hungry, it is caught there in snares by a hunter. And, out of indignation, it strives so violently and heavily to shake itself free from those very snares that, falling, weak-headed, by its own folly, it kills itself, falling below upon stakes.
Theophrastus relates this manner of hunting, and this same manner of hunting he learned from hunters in the German regions.
It signifies the unstable, the wandering, and those who delight in evil desires, striving after high and delightful things, who, by evil habit, are caught in sins by their own evil desire.

And, detected and caught, they despair on account of their iniquity, and, violently, on account of their own folly, destroy themselves and their own together with their possessions, Baruch 3: 'the sons also of Hagar, that search after the wisdom that is of the earth, the merchants of Merrha, and of Theman, and the tellers of fables, and searchers of prudence and understanding, but the way of wisdom they have not known, neither have they remembered her paths.' And it follows: 'and because they had not wisdom, they perished through their own folly. These the Lord has not chosen,' and so on.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De sancta virginitate Augustini

cit.quote: No rest of the soul is found otherwise than in a tumor of pride quietly digested.
The she-bear, the female of the bear, has these properties, or conditions.

For first, as Aristotle says, book 6, it is a most savage beast, and especially when its cubs are snatched from it. For it takes care for the safety of its young; it licks them, suckles them, and nourishes them most diligently, and, against those who oppose it, it sets itself against them with all its strength.

It signifies the fervor, and the boldness, and the vigor, that a prelate ought to have for the care and instruction, the salvation and defense, of the souls entrusted to him, or of his spiritual children, 2 Kings 17: 'you know your father, and the men that are with him, to be very valiant, and bitter in mind, as a bear raging in the wood when her whelps are taken away; and your father also is a warrior.'
Proverbs 17: 'it is expedient rather to meet a bear robbed of her whelps,' and so on.
The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep; but the hireling —

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Nothing pleases God so much as zeal for souls.
Second, as Aristotle, Pliny, and Avicenna say, the male keeps apart, and does not approach again, until the shaping of the young is complete.

It signifies that a wife ought not, fittingly and honestly, to be known by her husband after conception, until after the birth and purification, 1 Corinthians 7: 'defraud not one another, except perhaps by consent, for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer; and return together again, lest Satan tempt you for your incontinence.'
For honesty, in itself, is desirable, as something good and beneficial, as is also found in philosophy.

Third, as the same Aristotle, Pliny, and Avicenna say, at the time of mating it hides itself, and is ashamed to be seen at the time of love. The males, too, spare it then, and, for the sake of pleasure, do not approach it within the times of birth.

It signifies the modesty that ought to be in married and other women, and in men and young people, 1 Timothy 4: 'but fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not so much as be named among you, as becomes saints. For God has not called us unto uncleanness, but unto sanctification.'
It is written of blessed Nicholas that, although he shuddered at the company of women from the time of his boyhood, yet, once made a bishop, he fled from it as though from a kind of plague.
Joseph, Genesis 39.
Rebecca, a most beautiful girl, did likewise, when, seeing her husband, she covered her face, Genesis 24.

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fourth, as Pliny sets forth, book 10, chapter 73, a she-bear, with her young, does not lap up drink as beasts with serrated teeth do, nor does she sip it as those with continuous teeth do, like sheep and men, but devours water by biting it.
It signifies the gluttonous and the voracious, insatiable, Proverbs 13: 'the just eats and fills his soul; but the belly of the wicked is never to be filled.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: The pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the breadth of two fingers.
The fox has these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12: 'the fox is named as it were "uolupes" (rolling-foot). For the fox is nimble on its feet, and never advances by straight paths, but always by twisting and winding turns.'

It signifies deceitful men and hypocrites, who never walk in the truth, 2 Timothy 2: 'of whom is Philetus and Hymenaeus, who have fallen from the truth, saying that the resurrection is past already, and have subverted the faith of some.'

John the Evangelist said, as the Gloss says on 2 John, and it is found in a chapter of the Decretum, when he saw the heresiarch Cerinthus wishing to enter the bath in which he himself, with his disciples, happened to be: 'let us flee from here,' he said, 'lest even the baths themselves should fall in, in which Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, wishes to bathe.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it is a faithless and deceiving animal. For when it has no food, it feigns itself dead, and so birds, coming down in safety as though to a carcass, it seizes, devours, and swallows.
It signifies those who defraud and lie in wait for others: 'he lies in wait, that he may catch the poor man; to catch the poor man, while he draws him to himself.'

Chrysostom, in the sermon for the third Sunday in Lent: 'O the unspeakable madness of the wicked! It is not permitted for Joseph to be unpunished, because he is good. The wicked cannot bear to see what is good, but hasten to destroy it.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Third, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, the fox always limps, since its right legs are shorter than its left.

It signifies heretics, always turning aside from the way and the footsteps of the Gospel, Baruch 4: 'I am forsaken of many, for the sins of my children, because they departed from the law of God. But they have not known his justice, nor have they walked by the paths of the commandments of God, nor entered by the paths of his truth, with justice.'
Paul was torn apart, Paul was anguished, when he saw his neighbors perishing.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fourth, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it has a hairy and shaggy hide, and also a large tail, which, when a dog thinks to catch it, it fills and stops up the dog's mouth and teeth with its hairs.

It signifies the demonic, or even heretical, illusions which the devil and heretics, on every side, most cunningly work upon a man, even a defender and champion of truth, through the circumvention of temporal things, in a treacherous and manifold intrusion into his affections, under the appearance of what is right, 2 Corinthians 11: 'it is no wonder if the ministers of Satan are transformed as the ministers of justice. For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light; whose end shall be according to their works.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: 'The ancient enemy, transforming himself into an angel of light, does not cease to spread everywhere the snares of his deceptions, and to press on, so that by whatever means he may corrupt the faith of believers. He has very many among them whom he has bound to himself so tightly that he makes use of their wits and their tongues for the deception of others.' Thus far Leo.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fifth, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, there is a natural hatred between it and the badger, or the 'melus.' For it fights with him over dwellings, and pollutes and befouls his den with urine and dung. And it triumphs over him, not by violence, but by fraud. For the badger greatly dreads its urine and dung, and so yields the place to it. And so the fox overcomes him by cunning rather than by strength.

It signifies the devil, fighting against a religious man for the possession of his soul, and often, through the foulness of the flesh, obtaining more by malicious harassment than by violence, which he cannot inflict on one who is unwilling.
Wherefore it is said, Revelation 2: 'hold fast that which you have, that no man take your crown.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia and elsewhere: 'the enemy is weak, who cannot conquer any but the willing.'
Sixth, as Aristotle says, book 16, it is a swift and gluttonous animal, and therefore produces blind young.
For, as Solinus says, in all animals producing incomplete offspring, the cause is gluttony, since, if nature waited until completion, it would kill the mother by suckling.

It signifies that the headlong and the gluttonous make and have their works blind, that is, without perfection, without the deliberation of decision, Proverbs 21: 'he that loves wine, and fat things, shall not be rich.'
A drunken workman shall not become rich.
'Have you seen a man swift,' and so on. Folly is more to be hoped for than the correction of such a man.
Jerome: 'it was not the hen, but the apple, that cast Adam out of paradise.'
An example is found in Esau, who, as a glutton, without consideration, sold his birthright, Genesis 25.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As Isidore says, book 12, it inhabits and frequents dens and underground places. It signifies that demons inhabit the souls of heretics lurking in the depths of heresies, and deeply loving earthly things and subjected and enslaved to earthly things, Matthew 8: 'the foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests; but the Son of man has not where to lay his head.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'by the name of foxes are understood demons and heretics.'
'Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines.'
Eighth, as Aristotle says, book 8, it seizes and devours domestic animals more than wild ones.

It signifies that heretics exercise their depravity and malice more against those of the household of the faith than against other unbelievers and those outside the Church, Matthew 7: 'beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly are ravening wolves.'
'Having an appearance of godliness, but denying the power thereof. Now these avoid.'
But above all things, the ruin and deceit of his own household tormented him.
Ninth, as Aristotle says, in the same place, and Solinus likewise, it is a foul-smelling and corrupt animal, and habitually renders the places it frequents sterile and corrupted.

It signifies that heretics share and leave the leaven and corruption of their errors wherever they dwell, and are, above all, to be expelled and avoided, 1 Corinthians 5: 'put away the evil one from among yourselves. Do you not know that a little leaven,' and so on.

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: Chrysostom, on Matthew: 'every malice is sometimes confounded by the reason of truth. But it is never corrected, especially in those who sin by an evil purpose.'
Tenth, as the same author says, its belly and throat are white and delicate, its tail and back are reddish.
It signifies the gluttonous, gladly using, in general, clean and delightful things, and clinging, in particular, on this side and that, to various worldly things, both in clothing and in company.
Against which, 1 Corinthians 6: 'meat for the belly, and the belly for meats; but God shall destroy both it and them.'
The pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the breadth of two fingers.
Eleventh, as Pliny says, its breath is foul-smelling and its bite somewhat poisonous.
It signifies detractors, Psalm 13: 'their throat is an open sepulcher; with their tongues they have dealt deceitfully; the venom of asps is under their lips.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'he strikes charity in all who hear him, with a cursed tongue, and, as far as it lies in him, thoroughly kills and extinguishes it.'

...dogs, it, its tail, the tail, its own, urine, dogs, it itself, tail, its own, stench, to preachers, to prelates, to brothers, its own, them, strangers: 'such is the way of an adulterous woman, who eats, and wipes her mouth, and says: I have done no evil.'
Dionysius, in his answer to the Architect: 'she sins doubly who, after sinning, justifies herself.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Thirteenth, as the same Pliny says, book 28, although it is a very cunning and malicious animal, it is nonetheless useful in many respects for the practice of medicine. For its fat and marrow are said to avail greatly against the contraction of the sinews. Its blood, too, is said to be diuretic; whence it is believed to avail greatly against stone in the bladder, and for the strengthening of the kidneys.
The same author also says of the fox that, if anyone has a fox's tongue in a ring or a bracelet, he will not suffer — according to the magicians — dimness of the eyes.

It signifies that no man is so wicked that he does not have some usefulness or goodness in himself, or even some grace freely given, for his own use, or, above all, for that of others. Just as few, or no, good men exist who do not have some grace or goodness, whether of nature, or of grace, or of acquisition, which some others, especially those around them and of their own age, do not have.
By this manner is understood that saying, Ecclesiasticus 44, which is sung of each confessor-bishop: 'there was none found like unto him, who kept the law of the most High.'
'Good is set against evil, and life against death; so also look upon all the works of the most High: two and two, and one against one.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: 'There is no sin which one man has done that another man could not do.' So too we may turn this saying about: that there is nothing so useful found in, or belonging to, one man that it could not, in its own way — God willing — be found and exist in another.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De diversis questionibus octoginta tribus

cit.quote: Augustine, in the book of 83 Questions: 'no man's friendship is to be spurned on account of the sight of some infirmity in him.'
The worm has these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore sets forth, book 12, it is an animal that is often born from flesh and from herbs, and often is produced from vegetables too; sometimes from the corruption of humors alone, sometimes from the mingling of the sexes, sometimes from laying eggs, as is clear in tortoises, scorpions, and lizards.

It signifies the manifold generation of good and wicked men in the present Church, in whose consideration and memory the eternal God, who makes all good things, and only tolerates and permits evils, and orders them to their due end, is always to be praised and admired, Psalm 78: 'we will declare your praise, unto generation and generation.'
'To him be glory in the Church, and in Christ Jesus, unto all generations, world without end. Amen.'
The Gloss on Psalm 102, 'bless the Lord, O my soul': 'so, where God does not rule, there let him not be blessed; but since he rules everywhere, let him be blessed in every place.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, the worm, 'uermis,' is named as it were 'uerens,' since it turns itself into many parts, or since it turns, that is, draws itself toward opposite parts. For it does not creep, as serpents do, by the effort of scales, but draws its little body into various parts.
It signifies wicked and unstable men who pervert themselves, in words and deeds, to the opposites of truth and virtue, Proverbs 16: 'he that turns his tongue, shall fall into evil.'

'Woe to the double heart, and to wicked lips, and to the hands that do evil, and to the sinner who goes upon the earth two ways.' The same, chapter 4 of the same book: 'for so is the sinner proven by his double tongue.'
Ambrose, in the sermon for the Sunday of the Passion: 'every simulation and every duplicity is a lie.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Worms come out from their hiding places, and so perhaps they took their name from their springtime emergence.

It signifies sinners coming out, in the time of new grace, from the hiding places, or the darkness, of their faults, into the light of the virtues and the pasture of heavenly consolations, or the solace of spiritual refreshments: 'go out from the midst of Babylon, my people, and let every one save his own soul.'

Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'we transcended our own minds, and touched the region of your unfailing abundance, your fountain, which is with you, Lord, where you feed Israel forever with the food of truth. And my mother said to me: nothing now delights me in this life, but, having scorned earthly happiness, I see you a servant of Christ; and this world grew worthless amid our words.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Fourth, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, there are many differences among worms. For some are aquatic, some terrestrial. And of these, some live in herbs, like caterpillars and their like; some in trees, like wood-worms; some in clothing, like moths; some in flesh, like maggots, which are generated from corrupted moisture in decaying flesh; some in living creatures, like intestinal worms, roundworms in the bowels, mites in the hands, lice and nits in the head, all of which are generated within animals or within corrupted bodies, inwardly or outwardly. There are also other, long and round worms of the earth, soft and slippery, which moles hunt out beneath the ground, and with which fish are caught in the waters when hooks are baited with such worms.
