It signifies the various differences of vices and of worldly men who, like worms, settle now upon waters, that is, the concupiscences and lusts of the flesh, now upon earth, that is, avarice, now upon corrupted bodies, that is, the foulness and familiarities of wicked persons and depraved manners, Proverbs 29: 'when the wicked are multiplied, crimes shall be multiplied; but the just shall see their downfall.'
Daniel 13: 'they perverted their own mind, that they might not remember the just judgments, nor look up to heaven.'
'Know this also, that in the last days shall come dangerous times. And men shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, haughty, disobedient to parents,' and so on.

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De divinis nominibus Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Divine Names: 'a multitude of demons is the cause of all evils, both to themselves and to others.'
The viper has these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities and natural philosophers.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, book 12, the viper is a kind of poisonous serpent, so named because 'it gives birth by force. For when its belly groans in labor, its young, not waiting for nature's own time, gnaw through its sides, and burst forth by force, with their mother's death.'

It signifies poisonous men who, born or begotten of poisonous parents, destroy the Church, or religion, by their schisms and heresies, Luke 3: 'generation of vipers, who has shown you to flee from the wrath to come?'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'the generation of vipers is the evil offspring of evil parents, that is, poisonous children, born of poisonous fathers.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Second, as the same Isidore says, in the same place, it is said that 'the male, its mouth inserted into the mouth of the female viper, pours forth its seed. But she, turned from the pleasure of lust into rage, bites off the male's head. And so it happens that each parent perishes: the male while mating, the female while giving birth.'

It signifies violent lustful men, whose end is everlasting destruction and perpetual fire, Job 20: 'his bones shall be filled with the vices of his youth, and they shall sleep with him in the dust. He shall suck the head of asps, and the viper's tongue shall kill him. A fire that is not kindled shall devour him; he shall be afflicted, left in his own tabernacle.'

Blessed Gregory gives an example, in the third book of the Dialogues, of a certain courtier who received a certain woman's daughter at baptism, and afterward had her as his own. And so he died, from whose tomb a flame came forth, in the sight of all, and burned his bones for so long that all the earth was consumed, and the grave remained empty, as a certain proof of the eternal damnation of his soul.
From the viper are made the little cakes called theriac lozenges, from which theriac is made, and a remedy against poison.

It signifies that poisons are a singular remedy against vices and sins, especially mortal or capital ones, Acts 2: 'do penance, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the remission of your sins.'
The Gloss on Matthew 3: 'the first virtue is to kill the old man through penance.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fourth, as Pliny says, book 8, chapter 40, the viper alone among serpents hides itself in caverns of the earth; but all the others hide themselves in the hollows of rocks or trees in the depth of winter, and, having first vomited out their venom, sleep there until the time of spring. But when, by the sun's heat, the pores of the earth are opened, the viper, roused, comes forth.

It signifies those who, in a time of adversity, cease from evil for an hour, but who, when prosperity comes on, return to evil, Ecclesiasticus 20: 'there is one that is hindered from sinning through poverty.'
If he shall find an occasion for blood, he shall not be satisfied.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke, and elsewhere: 'feigned fairness is not fairness, but a doubled iniquity.' Likewise: 'every simulation and duplicity is a lie.'

Fifth, as Avicenna sets forth, when its sight has contracted dimness from long dwelling underground, it seeks the root of fennel, or the herb itself, and anoints its dulled eyes with its juice, so as to recover the sight it had lost.

It signifies that the drinking-in of the grace of God, or of saving Scripture, is a remedy against ignorance and spiritual dullness, Isaiah 60: 'behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and a mist the people; but the Lord shall arise upon you, and his glory shall be seen upon you. Then shall you see, and abound, and your heart shall wonder and be enlarged.'

Chrysostom and Damascene likewise, in various places: 'many great goods, indeed, have been given by the merciful God to men. But the first and greatest of the gifts is the teaching of the Scriptures. For the sun and the moon, and all the harmony of the stars, the rivers, the pools, the wells and the fountains, were made for the care of bodies; but the holy Scriptures were given for the direction of souls. And by as much as the soul is superior to the body, by so much is the divine Scripture superior to those other gifts. Wherefore the Savior said: search the Scriptures, for,' and so on.

Sixth, as Ambrose says, in the Hexameron, of all serpents the most wicked kind is that of the viper, which, when it is seized with the desire of mating, seeks the union of the moray eel, and goes forth to the water's edge, where it believes the little moray eel to lie hidden, and, by hissing, invites the moray eel to its embrace. She, called, is at once present; but the viper, seeing her ready for union, vomits out all its venom, and comes to the moray eel's embrace. But once the mating is complete, the viper takes back the venom it had vomited out, and so, its venom retaken, returns to its den.

It signifies the heretic, or the devil, seeking, by many cunning devices, to fulfill their pleasures, or their evil intentions. These, too, sometimes show themselves to have no venom, and yet are always convicted of laboring to poison, and of always drawing in and holding venom.

Whence heretical depravity says, Proverbs 7, to the senseless young man: 'come, let us be inebriated with the breasts, and let us enjoy the desired embraces. Immediately he follows her as an ox led to be a victim, and as a lamb playing the wanton, and knows not that he is drawn like a fool to bonds, and that it concerns the peril of his soul.'
The Gloss on Matthew 12: 'heretical depravity casts down into the lowest of all vices.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: As Pliny says, book 29, the viper swallows a certain stone; and the Scythians, perceiving this, open up the viper itself, and use that stone against poison.

It signifies certain men who, drawn out from the womb of the devil, are made, through grace, most excellent against heretics and adversaries of the truth, as is clear in the case of Paul and Augustine, Galatians 1: 'but when it pleased him, who separated me from my mother's womb, and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me, immediately I condescended not to flesh and blood,' and so on.
Augustine, in the sermon On the Conversion of Paul: 'the apostle Paul, from a persecutor of Christians, was made a proclaimer of Christ.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: When a dragon or an asp wounds a viper, the viper's head, applied to the wound, heals it; and, conversely, whomever a viper stings, the flesh of the asp is accustomed to heal.

It signifies that opposites are healed by opposites, spiritually, Galatians 5: 'for the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are contrary one to another, so that you do not the things that you would.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, on the Gospel 'This is my commandment': 'for as, in the art of medicine, cold things are cured by hot ones, and hot things by cold ones, so too our God, Jesus Christ, applied contrary remedies to sins, so that he might prescribe continence to the slippery, generosity to the grasping, meekness to the wrathful, and humility to the elated.'
Jerome, in his letters and elsewhere: 'for not everything that heals the eye heals the heel.'
